Cardiac hemangioma.description: A rare benign vascular tumor of the heart composed of proliferating blood-filled vascular channels. It may arise in the ventricular myocardium and often shows progressive contrast enhancement on cardiac MRI.

Cardiac fibroma.description: A benign tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen, usually arising within the ventricular myocardium. It is more common in children but can rarely occur in adults.

Cardiac myxoma.description: The most common primary benign cardiac tumor, usually arising in the left atrium from the interatrial septum. Ventricular myxomas are uncommon and may cause obstruction or embolization.

Cardiac angiosarcoma.description: A malignant endothelial-cell tumor of the heart that most often arises in the right atrium and may invade surrounding structures or metastasize. It can have hemorrhagic and highly vascular imaging features.

Splenic infarction associated with Mycop.normalized_text: Splenic infarction associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Splenic infarction associated with Mycop.description: Ischemic injury of splenic tissue from impaired splenic arterial perfusion or thrombosis; Mycoplasma pneumoniae can rarely cause a prothrombotic inflammatory state and extrapulmonary vascular complications.

Splenic infarction due to splenic arteri.normalized_text: Splenic infarction due to splenic arterial or venous thrombosis
Splenic infarction due to splenic arteri.description: A splenic infarct occurs when blood flow to part of the spleen is blocked, commonly producing peripheral wedge-shaped areas of ischemia on imaging. Causes include thrombosis, emboli, infection, hematologic disease, and hypercoagulability.

Splenic abscess.description: A splenic abscess is a localized bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infection within the spleen. It can cause fever, inflammatory marker elevation, and left upper quadrant pain, with focal splenic lesions on ultrasound or MRI.

Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragm.normalized_text: Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragmatic pleurisy
Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragm.description: Lower-lobe pneumonia can irritate the diaphragm and present with upper abdominal pain rather than prominent respiratory symptoms, particularly in children.

Infectious mononucleosis with splenic in.description: Epstein-Barr virus infection can enlarge or inflame the spleen and, rarely, lead to splenic infarction through transient hypercoagulability or altered splenic blood flow.

Amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histoly.description: A hepatic abscess caused by invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection, often occurring months to years after travel to endemic regions. It can cause fever, inflammatory-marker elevation, diarrhea, and pleuritic upper abdominal or diaphragmatic pain.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection within the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, streptococci, or anaerobes. It typically produces fever, neutrophilia, high inflammatory markers, and a focal liver lesion on imaging.

Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.normalized_text: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkho.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and parts of Southeast Asia. It can cause acute febrile illness with abscesses in the liver, spleen, lungs, or other organs.

Fascioliasis (acute hepatic infection wi.normalized_text: Fascioliasis (acute hepatic infection with Fasciola species)
Fascioliasis (acute hepatic infection wi.description: Fascioliasis is a parasitic liver infection acquired by ingesting contaminated water or aquatic plants. During the acute hepatic migratory phase it can cause fever, abdominal or pleuritic pain, and focal liver lesions.

Portal pylephlebitis with hepatic microa.normalized_text: Portal pylephlebitis with hepatic microabscesses from intra-abdominal infection
Portal pylephlebitis with hepatic microa.description: Pylephlebitis is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system, usually arising from an intra-abdominal infection such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, or bowel infection. It may produce liver abscesses and systemic inflammation.

OPA1-associated hereditary spastic parap.normalized_text: OPA1-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia with dominant optic atrophy (DOA-plus syndrome)
OPA1-associated hereditary spastic parap.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, characterized by slowly progressive bilateral optic neuropathy/optic atrophy and upper-motor-neuron spastic paraplegia; additional neurologic features may occur.

Multiple sclerosis, progressive spinal-p.description: An immune-mediated central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory disturbance, bladder dysfunction, and optic neuritis or optic neuropathy.

SPG7-related hereditary spastic parapleg.description: A genetic, often mitochondrial, complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by SPG7 variants. It commonly causes progressive lower-limb spasticity and may include optic atrophy, ataxia, neuropathy, and bladder dysfunction.

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degener.description: An autosomal-recessive ATP7B-related disorder of impaired biliary copper excretion, causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. The reported homozygous ATP7B c.2333G>T (p.Arg778Leu) pathogenic variant, Kayser-Fleischer ring, and basal-ganglia MRI abnormalities strongly support this diagnosis.

Drug-induced liver injury from Chinese h.normalized_text: Drug-induced liver injury from Chinese herbal medicines
Drug-induced liver injury from Chinese h.description: Liver injury caused by herbal or traditional medicines may produce hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed hepatitis with jaundice and pruritus. Herbal exposure for approximately 9 months is a relevant potential contributor, although it does not explain the ATP7B mutation, corneal ring, or brain MRI findings.

Autoimmune hepatitis.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that often affects girls and young women and can present with chronic hepatitis, jaundice, and progression to cirrhosis if untreated.

Chronic viral hepatitis.description: Chronic hepatitis caused by viruses such as hepatitis B or hepatitis C can cause persistent liver inflammation, jaundice, impaired coagulation, and eventual cirrhosis, although this presentation is less specifically supported than Wilson disease.

Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (dru.normalized_text: Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (drug-induced acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (dru.description: A hypersensitivity-type neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, and systemic inflammation; it can be triggered by azathioprine soon after initiation.

Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome.description: A systemic adverse drug reaction occurring days to weeks after azathioprine exposure, commonly causing fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, elevated inflammatory markers, and neutrophilia; it is distinct from dose-related azathioprine toxicity.

Serum sickness-like reaction.description: An immune-mediated drug reaction that typically presents one to two weeks after medication exposure with fever, rash, arthralgias or arthritis, and inflammatory marker elevation.

Erythema nodosum.description: A panniculitis producing tender erythematous nodules, most often on the shins, often accompanied by fever, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers; it may be associated with drugs, infections, inflammatory disease, or systemic conditions.

Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bact.normalized_text: Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bacteremia
Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bact.description: Bacterial infection can cause fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, painful joint swelling, and erythematous skin lesions; diabetes and immunosuppression increase susceptibility.

Traumatic retropharyngeal hematoma.description: Bleeding into the retropharyngeal space after neck trauma, producing posterior pharyngeal wall swelling and potentially severe upper-airway narrowing.

Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.normalized_text: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal ed.description: Injury to the larynx after blunt neck trauma that can cause edema, internal bleeding, vocal-cord dysfunction, and airway obstruction.

Traumatic cervical soft-tissue hematoma.description: A collection of blood within the anterior or deep soft tissues of the neck following trauma, which may expand and compress the pharynx or airway.

Traumatic carotid or vertebral artery in.normalized_text: Traumatic carotid or vertebral artery injury with expanding neck hematoma
Traumatic carotid or vertebral artery in.description: Blunt injury to a cervical blood vessel, such as arterial dissection, pseudoaneurysm, or vessel rupture, can cause an enlarging neck hematoma and airway compression.

Insulinoma.description: A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that autonomously secretes insulin, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia (Whipple triad).

Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.normalized_text: Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia due to pancreatic nesidioblastosis
Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.description: Diffuse overgrowth or hyperfunction of pancreatic beta cells causing excessive endogenous insulin secretion and recurrent hypoglycemia, more commonly seen after bariatric surgery but possible in adults without surgery.

Sulfonylurea- or meglitinide-induced hyp.description: Hypoglycemia caused by insulin secretagogue medications, which increase endogenous pancreatic insulin release and therefore produce elevated insulin and C-peptide levels.

Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous i.normalized_text: Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous insulin administration
Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous i.description: Deliberate or inadvertent administration of insulin causing hypoglycemia, usually associated with high insulin levels but suppressed endogenous C-peptide production.

Slipping rib syndrome.description: A hypermobility disorder of the false ribs, usually the 8th to 10th ribs, caused by laxity or disruption of interchondral attachments. The mobile rib cartilage can sublux beneath an adjacent rib and irritate the intercostal nerve, producing focal sharp lower anterior chest-wall pain. The ultrasound appearance of altered relationship/mobility of the 8th rib relative to adjacent ribs supports this diagnosis.

Intercostal muscle strain.description: Overstretching or repetitive overuse injury of an intercostal muscle, commonly occurring with vigorous exercise, twisting, coughing, or forceful trunk movement.

Costochondral or interchondral sprain.description: A mechanical injury or inflammation involving the cartilage junctions between ribs or between rib cartilage and the sternum, often caused by repetitive loading or forceful movement.

Rib stress injury or stress fracture.normalized_text: Rib stress injury or stress fracture
Rib stress injury or stress fracture.description: A repetitive-load injury of a rib that may progress from bone stress reaction to fracture, seen in athletes performing repeated high-intensity upper-body or trunk movements.

Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.normalized_text: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not other.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia, abnormal eosinophil maturation, cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities, and possible organ damage from eosinophil infiltration.

Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.normalized_text: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangement
Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophi.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms, often involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangements, that can cause marked eosinophilia, abnormal myeloid cells, anemia, and eosinophil-mediated lung disease.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with pulmonary involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A disorder of persistent eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated organ injury after secondary causes and defined clonal hematologic neoplasms have been excluded. The lungs, heart, skin, gastrointestinal tract, and nervous system may be involved.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia.description: An eosinophilic lung disease characterized by subacute cough, dyspnea, wheezing, blood eosinophilia, and pulmonary eosinophilic infiltrates; it is usually corticosteroid responsive.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A systemic eosinophilic small-vessel vasculitis typically associated with adult-onset asthma, eosinophilia, sinus disease, neuropathy, skin lesions, and variable pulmonary infiltrates.

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma

Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma.normalized_text: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), ALK-positive
Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: An aggressive pediatric T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by large CD30-positive anaplastic lymphoid cells, often ALK-positive, with systemic symptoms and frequent extranodal disease.

Burkitt lymphoma.description: A rapidly growing high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly affects children and may present with abdominal masses, bowel involvement, systemic symptoms, and tumor-related anemia.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells that usually presents with painless lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms; extranodal abdominal disease can occur.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, impaired growth, weight loss, and iron-deficiency anemia.

Abdominal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, or abdominal lymph nodes can cause prolonged fever, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia, inflammatory marker elevation, and bowel symptoms.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria (potential.normalized_text: Plasmodium falciparum malaria (potentially severe malaria with hemoglobinuria)
Plasmodium falciparum malaria (potential.description: Mosquito-borne malaria caused by P. falciparum, which can produce high parasitemia, cyclic fever with rigors, hemolysis, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine (blackwater fever). The rapid malaria test and blood smear images show findings consistent with P. falciparum ring-form parasites.

Plasmodium vivax malaria.description: A mosquito-borne malaria species that commonly causes intermittent fever, chills, headache, malaise, and gastrointestinal symptoms. It is generally less likely than P. falciparum to cause severe hemolysis, renal failure, or marked hemoglobinuria.

Leptospirosis.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, myalgias, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine.

Dengue fever.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral illness causing acute fever, severe headache, myalgias, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes liver dysfunction. Severe dengue can cause bleeding, plasma leakage, and shock.

Enteric fever (typhoid or paratyphoid fe.description: A systemic Salmonella infection acquired through contaminated food or water, causing prolonged fever, headache, malaise, anorexia, abdominal symptoms, diarrhea or constipation, and occasionally hepatitis.

Delayed esophageal perforation from cerv.normalized_text: Delayed esophageal perforation from cervical spinal hardware erosion
Delayed esophageal perforation from cerv.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which plates or screws erode into the esophageal wall, causing perforation and possible fistulous communication with adjacent infected spaces.

Esophagomediastinal fistula with mediast.description: An abnormal communication between the esophagus and mediastinum that permits leakage of saliva, food material, and bacteria into the mediastinum, resulting in severe mediastinal infection and pus collection.

Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.normalized_text: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with vertebral osteomyelitis and paraspinal abscess
Cervical spinal instrumentation infectio.description: Infection involving prior cervical fixation hardware and/or adjacent vertebrae, potentially causing osteomyelitis, loosening or migration of hardware, and formation of a large paraspinal abscess.

Descending necrotizing mediastinitis sec.normalized_text: Descending necrotizing mediastinitis secondary to cervical infection or esophageal perforation
Descending necrotizing mediastinitis sec.description: A rapidly progressive deep neck or esophageal infection that spreads along fascial planes into the mediastinum, producing purulent mediastinal collections and systemic infection.

Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophage.description: A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, classically occurring after forceful vomiting, causing leakage of air and gastric contents into the mediastinum and pleural spaces. Imaging is consistent with pneumomediastinum, cervical subcutaneous emphysema, and pleural fluid/air, particularly on the left.

Pneumomediastinum secondary to esophagea.description: Air within the mediastinum, often due to disruption of the esophagus after vomiting. It may extend into the neck and coexist with pleural effusions or pneumothorax.

Acute aortic dissection.description: A tear in the aortic wall causing separation of its layers, typically presenting with abrupt severe chest pain that may radiate to the back. This is an important emergency differential diagnosis for this pain pattern.

Acute coronary syndrome.description: Myocardial ischemia or infarction due to reduced coronary blood flow, commonly causing pressure-like chest pain with diaphoresis, nausea, and autonomic symptoms.

Mallory-Weiss tear.description: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by forceful retching or vomiting, most often producing upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than a full-thickness esophageal rupture.

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES).description: Paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are not caused by abnormal epileptic cortical electrical activity. They are commonly associated with psychological trauma, PTSD, depression, anxiety, and other functional neurologic symptoms; ictal EEG often shows movement or muscle artifact without an evolving epileptiform seizure pattern.

Generalized tonic-clonic epileptic seizu.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures involve sudden tonic body stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking, often with loss of consciousness, falls, injuries, urinary incontinence, postictal confusion, elevated lactate, and elevated creatine kinase.

Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.normalized_text: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral t.description: Focal seizures begin in a localized brain region and may progress to bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions. Auras can include visual symptoms, autonomic symptoms, nausea, cognitive changes, or focal pain, followed by impaired awareness and generalized convulsive activity.

Convulsive syncope.description: Transient cerebral hypoperfusion, often from vasovagal or cardiac causes, can produce loss of consciousness with brief tonic stiffening or myoclonic jerks. Palpitations and nausea may precede an episode, but convulsive movements are usually brief and recovery is relatively rapid.

Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.normalized_text: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
Incarcerated right obturator hernia caus.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal, typically occurring in thin, elderly multiparous women. Entrapment of bowel can cause mechanical small-bowel obstruction, and obturator nerve compression can cause medial thigh, hip, or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign).

Strangulated obturator hernia.description: An obturator hernia in which the trapped bowel has compromised blood supply, potentially progressing to ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. It often presents with bowel obstruction and may initially lack obvious abdominal wall findings.

Femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstr.description: A hernia through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, more common in older women and prone to incarceration and strangulation. It can produce bowel obstruction but is anatomically distinct from an obturator hernia.

Adhesive small-bowel obstruction.description: Mechanical obstruction caused by fibrous intra-abdominal adhesions, most commonly after prior abdominal surgery or inflammation.

Susac syndrome.description: A rare autoimmune microangiopathy affecting small vessels of the brain, retina, and inner ear, classically causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. Corpus callosum lesions on MRI are characteristic.

Multiple sclerosis.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause recurrent neurologic deficits, visual disturbances, sensory symptoms, and characteristic brain MRI lesions.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: An inflammatory vasculitis limited to the brain and spinal cord that may produce headache, multifocal ischemic lesions, focal neurologic deficits, and abnormal cerebrospinal fluid findings.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune prothrombotic disorder that can cause arterial or venous thrombosis, including retinal vascular occlusion and cerebral ischemic events, often in young adults.

Mitochondrial myopathy due to an MT-TL1.normalized_text: Mitochondrial myopathy due to an MT-TL1 m.3243A>G mutation (MELAS-spectrum mitochondrial disease)
Mitochondrial myopathy due to an MT-TL1.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder with highly variable manifestations, including myopathy, exercise intolerance, sensorineural hearing loss, cardiac conduction abnormalities, cognitive impairment, seizures, and cerebellar involvement. Muscle biopsy may show ragged-red fibers and mosaic cytochrome-c oxidase deficiency.

MERRF syndrome due to an MT-TK m.8344A>G.normalized_text: MERRF syndrome due to an MT-TK m.8344A>G mutation
MERRF syndrome due to an MT-TK m.8344A>G.description: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers is a mitochondrial disorder that can cause myopathy, elevated CK, ataxia, hearing loss, cognitive decline, seizures, and cardiac abnormalities. Expression varies substantially among maternal relatives.

Mitochondrial recessive ataxia syndrome.normalized_text: Mitochondrial recessive ataxia syndrome / POLG-related mitochondrial disease
Mitochondrial recessive ataxia syndrome.description: POLG-related disorders are nuclear-gene mitochondrial diseases that may present with adult-onset ataxia, myopathy, seizures, neuropathy, hearing loss, cognitive changes, and mitochondrial abnormalities in muscle.

Myofibrillar myopathy, particularly myot.normalized_text: Myofibrillar myopathy, particularly myotilin-related or desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy
Myofibrillar myopathy, particularly myot.description: Myofibrillar myopathies are inherited muscle disorders characterized by progressive weakness, muscle atrophy, elevated CK, and abnormal protein aggregates in muscle. Desmin-related disease can additionally cause cardiomyopathy or arrhythmias.

SELENON-related myopathy (rigid-spine mu.description: SELENON-related myopathy is a congenital or slowly progressive muscle disorder marked by prominent axial weakness, spinal rigidity or scoliosis, neck weakness, and respiratory muscle involvement. CK can be mildly elevated.

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma of childhood, often involving extranodal sites and potentially disseminating to marrow and blood. Tumor cells typically express surface immunoglobulin and mature B-cell markers, and commonly have MYC rearrangement.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not other.description: A mature B-cell lymphoma composed of large malignant lymphoid cells. It can present as a nodal or extranodal soft-tissue mass and may occasionally involve peripheral blood or bone marrow.

High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.normalized_text: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rearrangement
High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rear.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with high-grade morphology and genetic abnormalities involving MYC, sometimes with additional BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements. These tumors may resemble Burkitt lymphoma but can show atypical morphology or immunophenotype.

B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly affects children and can involve marrow, blood, lymph nodes, bone, and soft tissue. It usually expresses precursor markers such as TdT and CD34 rather than surface immunoglobulin.

Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.normalized_text: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni (periportal fibrosis/Symmers fibrosis)
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Sch.description: Chronic hepatointestinal infection caused by Schistosoma mansoni eggs lodged in portal venules, producing granulomatous inflammation and characteristic periportal fibrosis that may lead to portal hypertension and splenomegaly.

Acute or chronic intestinal schistosomia.description: Intestinal disease caused by Schistosoma mansoni egg deposition in the colonic wall, resulting in granulomatous inflammation, abdominal symptoms, diarrhoea, and possible progression to hepatosplenic disease.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver that can produce fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and a focal hepatic lesion, usually with imaging evidence of a fluid-containing collection.

Traumatic hepatic injury or resolving he.normalized_text: Traumatic hepatic injury or resolving hepatic hematoma
Traumatic hepatic injury or resolving he.description: Liver contusion, laceration, or hematoma following blunt abdominal trauma can cause right upper-quadrant pain and may appear as a focal low-attenuation hepatic abnormality on imaging.

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.icd11_title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings consistent with anterior/anterolateral ST-segment elevation.

Polycythemia vera.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red-cell production and often associated leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, aquagenic pruritus, and arterial or venous thrombosis.

Essential thrombocythemia.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm with persistent high platelet counts that can cause arterial thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis and myocardial infarction.

Acute coronary thrombosis secondary to a.normalized_text: Acute coronary thrombosis secondary to a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Acute coronary thrombosis secondary to a.description: Coronary artery thrombosis may occur in polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia because of increased blood viscosity, platelet activation, and abnormal blood-cell production.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) o.description: Acid reflux or esophageal inflammation can cause burning substernal discomfort, sometimes with nausea or vomiting, and may improve with antacids or proton-pump inhibitors.

Pulmonary sequestration (likely intralob.normalized_text: Pulmonary sequestration (likely intralobar sequestration of the left lower lobe)
Pulmonary sequestration (likely intralob.description: A congenital nonfunctioning segment of lung that lacks normal bronchial communication and receives an anomalous systemic arterial supply, typically from the descending thoracic aorta. It may cause neonatal respiratory distress and can appear as an abnormal lower-lobe pulmonary opacity or hyperinflated region.

Hybrid congenital pulmonary airway malfo.normalized_text: Hybrid congenital pulmonary airway malformation and pulmonary sequestration
Hybrid congenital pulmonary airway malfo.description: A hybrid congenital lung lesion combines features of congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) with an anomalous systemic arterial supply characteristic of pulmonary sequestration. These lesions can produce cystic, hyperinflated, or consolidated lower-lobe abnormalities and respiratory compromise in newborns.

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation.description: CPAM is a developmental malformation of the lung characterized by abnormal bronchiolar and alveolar tissue, often producing cystic or hyperinflated lung areas. Large lesions can cause respiratory distress immediately after birth.

Neonatal pneumothorax or pulmonary air-l.normalized_text: Neonatal pneumothorax or pulmonary air-leak syndrome
Neonatal pneumothorax or pulmonary air-l.description: Air leakage into the pleural space or pulmonary interstitium can occur after vigorous resuscitation, positive-pressure ventilation, meconium aspiration, or underlying congenital lung disease. It may cause sudden respiratory decompensation and unilateral hyperlucency on radiographs.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, aHUS)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: A complement dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and severe acute kidney injury. It may be triggered by cocaine use, hypertension, or infection and can be associated with inherited complement abnormalities.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can cause acute endothelial damage in renal arterioles, producing thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrinoid vascular injury, onion-skin arteriolar thickening, hemolysis, and rapidly progressive kidney failure.

Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.normalized_text: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy and hypertensive renal injury
Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangio.description: Cocaine can cause intense vasoconstriction, severe hypertension, endothelial injury, platelet activation, and renal thrombotic microangiopathy. Levamisole-adulterated cocaine may also contribute to vascular and immune-mediated injury.

Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
Hepatitis C-associated membranoprolifera.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, particularly mixed cryoglobulinemic membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, leading to proteinuria, hematuria, renal dysfunction, and complement consumption.

Chronic kidney disease with superimposed.normalized_text: Chronic kidney disease with superimposed acute kidney injury due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Chronic kidney disease with superimposed.description: Long-standing hypertension causes progressive arteriolar sclerosis, glomerular ischemia, proteinuria, and small echogenic kidneys. A hypertensive emergency can precipitate acute deterioration and volume overload.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.normalized_text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies. Lesions in the dorsal medulla/area postrema can cause intractable nausea and vomiting, while additional brainstem or spinal cord involvement can produce neurologic deficits.

Wernicke encephalopathy.description: A neurologic emergency caused by thiamine deficiency, often after prolonged vomiting or malnutrition. It classically causes encephalopathy, eye movement abnormalities, and gait ataxia.

Brainstem encephalitis.description: Inflammation of the brainstem due to infectious, autoimmune, or paraneoplastic causes. It may produce cranial nerve dysfunction, eye movement abnormalities, long-tract signs, weakness, and respiratory compromise.

Posterior circulation ischemic stroke in.normalized_text: Posterior circulation ischemic stroke involving the medulla/brainstem
Posterior circulation ischemic stroke in.description: An infarction in the vertebrobasilar circulation can affect the medulla or pons, causing vomiting, nystagmus, cranial nerve abnormalities, weakness, pyramidal signs, and potentially respiratory failure.

Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infective e.description: A rare, subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a gram-positive rod often associated with animal or animal-product exposure. It has characteristic intrinsic resistance to vancomycin and is usually susceptible to penicillin.

Subacute native-valve infective endocard.description: Infection of a native heart valve causing persistent fever, systemic inflammatory symptoms, valve vegetation, and progressive valvular regurgitation. It may be caused by unusual gram-positive organisms including Erysipelothrix species.

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) endocarditis.description: A culture-negative or difficult-to-culture subacute endocarditis caused by Coxiella burnetii, usually occurring in patients with pre-existing valvular disease and often involving the aortic valve.

Brucella infective endocarditis.description: A rare but severe complication of brucellosis in which Brucella species infect a heart valve, commonly producing a prolonged febrile systemic illness and destructive aortic-valve disease.

Venous air embolism.description: Entry of air into the venous circulation during an invasive procedure, potentially causing acute pulmonary vascular obstruction and hypoxaemia.

Paradoxical air embolism through a paten.normalized_text: Paradoxical air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
Paradoxical air embolism through a paten.description: Venous air enters the right heart and crosses a patent foramen ovale into the systemic arterial circulation, allowing embolization to the cerebral and coronary arteries.

Transient ischaemic attack or acute isch.normalized_text: Transient ischaemic attack or acute ischaemic stroke due to cerebral air embolism
Transient ischaemic attack or acute isch.description: Temporary or persistent focal neurological dysfunction caused by air embolization to cerebral arteries; rapid symptom resolution supports a transient ischaemic event.

Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary air embolism
Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.description: Myocardial ischaemia or infarction caused by air entering a coronary artery, in this case plausibly after paradoxical embolization through a patent foramen ovale.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), BRA.description: A rare, usually superficial astrocytic brain tumor that often arises in the temporal lobe and commonly presents with long-standing seizures in younger patients. Many PXAs harbor a BRAF V600E mutation and are WHO grade 2, although some may progress.

Recurrent pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: Regrowth or persistence of a previously resected PXA. Recurrence may appear as a new or enlarging contrast-enhancing lesion with surrounding FLAIR/T2 signal abnormality at or near the prior tumor site.

Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.description: A higher-grade, more aggressive form of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and a greater tendency toward recurrence or progression. BRAF V600E mutations may still be present.

Ganglioglioma.description: A typically slow-growing glioneuronal tumor, often located in the temporal lobe and strongly associated with chronic focal seizures. Some gangliogliomas also carry BRAF V600E mutations and can resemble PXA radiologically and histologically.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle weakness due to muscle inflammation.

Anti-MDA5 antibody-associated dermatomyo.description: A dermatomyositis subtype often associated with painful ulcerative or inflammatory hand lesions, periungual changes, and potentially rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease; muscle weakness may be variable.

Antisynthetase syndrome.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome characterized by myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and sometimes mechanic's hands.

Polymyositis.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle inflammation, but without the characteristic skin findings of dermatomyositis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis overlap
Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rashes, inflammatory muscle disease, edema, pulmonary manifestations, and constitutional symptoms; overlap with dermatomyositis can occur.

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia.description: Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through increased vitamin D breakdown leading to impaired bone mineralization, hypocalcemia or hypophosphatemia, muscle weakness, bone pain, and insufficiency fractures.

Vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia.description: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of mature bone, commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency. It produces diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy, fragility or insufficiency fractures, and Looser’s zones.

Hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.description: Osteomalacia due to chronic low phosphate availability, which may result from renal phosphate wasting, medications, malabsorption, or tumor-induced osteomalacia. It causes bone pain, proximal weakness, and pseudofractures.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome, usually caused by small phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors that produce excess FGF23, leading to renal phosphate wasting, osteomalacia, diffuse bone pain, weakness, and insufficiency fractures.

Native mitral valve infective endocardit.normalized_text: Native mitral valve infective endocarditis caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus
Native mitral valve infective endocardit.description: Infection of the native mitral valve endocardium with vegetation formation, caused here by bloodstream infection with group A Streptococcus. It can produce valvular destruction, emboli, fever, and systemic inflammation.

Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke seco.normalized_text: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke seco.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected material from a cardiac valve vegetation. The brain image is consistent with a focal ischemic lesion in the left cerebral hemisphere, which can cause contralateral motor coordination deficits and dysarthria.

Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to.normalized_text: Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to infective mitral valve destruction
Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to.description: Severe backward flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium due to infection-related mitral leaflet or chordal damage. This can cause an apical pansystolic murmur, pulmonary congestion, respiratory distress, ventricular enlargement, and elevated natriuretic peptide levels.

Splenic infarction from septic embolizat.description: Ischemic injury of splenic tissue caused by embolization from infective endocarditis. Abdominal ultrasonography can show focal hypoechoic splenic lesions consistent with infarction or embolic involvement.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (Sensenbrenne.description: A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy characterized by craniofacial abnormalities, ectodermal defects involving hair, teeth and nails, skeletal dysplasia with narrow thorax and short limbs, and progressive tubulointerstitial kidney disease that may cause renal failure.

Jeune syndrome (asphyxiating thoracic dy.description: An autosomal-recessive skeletal ciliopathy causing a narrow thorax with short ribs, short limbs, brachydactyly, and variable renal disease including nephronophthisis and progressive chronic kidney disease.

Mainzer-Saldino syndrome.description: A ciliopathy with skeletal dysplasia, particularly cone-shaped epiphyses and phalangeal abnormalities, progressive renal disease often resembling nephronophthisis, and possible retinal or ocular involvement.

Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia.description: A rare autosomal-recessive multisystem disorder caused by SMARCAL1 variants, characterized by progressive renal disease, skeletal dysplasia with short stature, facial dysmorphism, sparse hair, and susceptibility to infections due to immune dysfunction.

Dermatomyositis.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle inflammation and distinctive cutaneous findings, including Gottron papules over the knuckles. It may be associated with an underlying malignancy in adults.

Cancer-associated (paraneoplastic) derma.description: Dermatomyositis occurring as a paraneoplastic syndrome, particularly in older adults. The inflammatory muscle and skin disease can precede or accompany discovery of a solid malignancy, including upper gastrointestinal cancers.

Oesophageal carcinoma with paraneoplasti.description: A malignant tumour of the oesophagus that may cause dysphagia and can rarely trigger dermatomyositis as a paraneoplastic autoimmune syndrome. PET avidity in the oesophagus and abnormal endoscopy raise concern for this diagnosis.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing prominent proximal weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase, sometimes associated with malignancy, medications such as statins, or autoantibodies.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head epiphysis in children, leading to femoral-head fragmentation, flattening, and possible lateral extrusion on radiographs.

Transient synovitis of the hip.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, often following a viral illness, that commonly causes acute limp and hip pain in young children.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).description: Posteroinferior displacement of the femoral-head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in adolescents during growth spurts.

Septic arthritis of the hip.description: An acute bacterial infection of the hip joint that can rapidly damage cartilage and bone and usually requires urgent treatment.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A bacterial abscess within or immediately adjacent to the liver that contains gas, often causing severe systemic inflammation and right upper quadrant peritonism.

Subphrenic abscess.description: A localized infected collection beneath the diaphragm, commonly occurring after upper abdominal surgery and potentially containing gas, which can mimic free intraperitoneal air on chest radiography.

Delayed abscess caused by dropped gallst.normalized_text: Delayed abscess caused by dropped gallstones after laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Delayed abscess caused by dropped gallst.description: A late complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in which spilled or retained gallstones act as a nidus for infection, causing a perihepatic, subhepatic, or subphrenic abscess years after surgery.

Perforated peptic ulcer with pneumoperit.description: A full-thickness gastric or duodenal ulcer perforation causing free intraperitoneal air and acute peritonitis.

Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion syndro.description: A chromosomal deletion disorder caused by loss of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, facial/ocular abnormalities, and occasional congenital heart defects.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: A congenital viral infection that can cause microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, brain abnormalities, hearing loss, and growth restriction.

Rett syndrome.description: An X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, usually caused by MECP2 variants, characterized by initially apparently normal early development followed by developmental regression, loss of hand skills, impaired speech, microcephaly, gait abnormalities, and stereotyped hand movements.

Angelman syndrome.description: A neurogenetic disorder involving loss of maternal UBE3A expression, causing severe developmental delay, absent or minimal speech, ataxia, seizures, a happy/excitable demeanor, and acquired microcephaly in many affected children.

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.icd11_title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.normalized_text: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of t.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor occurring outside the gonads. Yolk sac tumors commonly produce very high serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and may arise in the gastrointestinal tract, including the jejunum.

Hepatoblastoma with metastatic or ectopi.normalized_text: Hepatoblastoma with metastatic or ectopic abdominal disease
Hepatoblastoma with metastatic or ectopi.description: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary liver malignancy in young children and often causes major AFP elevation. Advanced disease can spread within the abdomen, although a primary jejunal mass would be unusual.

Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the small.normalized_text: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the small bowel
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the small.description: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is a pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma that can rarely involve the gastrointestinal tract and present as an intestinal wall mass with abdominal pain.

Small-bowel lymphoma.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including Burkitt lymphoma, can involve the ileum or jejunum in children and cause bowel-wall masses, abdominal pain, ascites, and abdominal lymphadenopathy.

Small-intestinal adenocarcinoma.description: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor of the intestinal lining that can form an infiltrative bowel-wall mass. It is very rare in children but may occasionally show AFP production in unusual AFP-producing variants.

Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.normalized_text: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopi.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration and potentially severe lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The scintigraphic appearance is consistent with a Meckel scan showing an abdominal focus of uptake appearing with gastric uptake.

Intussusception, potentially with a Meck.normalized_text: Intussusception, potentially with a Meckel diverticulum as a lead point
Intussusception, potentially with a Meck.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, usually ileocolic in infants. It causes episodic severe colicky pain and may progress to bowel ischemia and bloody stool. A Meckel diverticulum can serve as a pathologic lead point.

Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.normalized_text: Enteric duplication cyst containing ectopic gastric mucosa
Enteric duplication cyst containing ecto.description: A congenital duplication of the gastrointestinal tract that can contain gastric mucosa, resulting in ulceration, bleeding, abdominal pain, obstruction, or intussusception. It can occasionally demonstrate uptake on a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan.

Food protein-induced allergic proctocoli.description: A non-IgE-mediated inflammatory reaction to dietary proteins, commonly cow's milk or soy protein, causing blood-streaked stools in otherwise well young infants.

diagnoses.name: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia

Multiple pulmonary arteriovenous malform.description: Abnormal direct communications between pulmonary arteries and veins, producing enhancing rounded vascular lesions with feeding and draining vessels. Multiple PAVMs may be idiopathic or associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.normalized_text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, commonly involving the lungs, nose, gastrointestinal tract, liver, and brain. Multiple PAVMs strongly raise this possibility.

Bronchiolitis obliterans (constrictive b.description: A small-airway disorder involving inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of bronchioles, causing fixed severe airflow obstruction and progressive exertional dyspnea. CT may show mosaic attenuation and air trapping, particularly on expiratory imaging.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease du.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to non-smoking-related small-airway disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease du.description: Chronic obstructive airflow limitation can occur in non-smokers because of asthma, environmental or occupational exposures, prior infections, or other bronchiolar disorders. It causes dyspnea and reduced FEV1 but would not usually produce vascular nodules.

Pulmonary sarcoidosis associated with un.normalized_text: Pulmonary sarcoidosis associated with unicentric Castleman disease
Pulmonary sarcoidosis associated with un.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disorder characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving the lungs and lymph nodes. The supraclavicular node histology is compatible with hyaline-vascular-type unicentric Castleman disease, a benign lymphoproliferative disorder that can coexist with sarcoid-like granulomatous lung disease.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis is a mycobacterial infection that commonly causes chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, upper-lobe infiltrates or cavitation, and granulomatous inflammation. It must be excluded carefully despite initially negative sputum studies.

Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary d.description: Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, such as Mycobacterium avium complex or M. kansasii infection, can produce upper-lobe cavitary disease, nodules, bronchiectasis, chronic cough, hemoptysis, and granulomatous lung inflammation.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated vasculitis that can cause cough, hemoptysis, pulmonary nodules or cavitary infiltrates, systemic inflammation, and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in the respiratory tract.

Necrotizing sarcoid granulomatosis.description: Necrotizing sarcoid granulomatosis is a rare sarcoid-spectrum disorder characterized by pulmonary granulomas, variable granulomatous vasculitis, nodular or cavitary lung lesions, fever, cough, and occasionally hemoptysis.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.normalized_text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating infection of the brain caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, especially in patients receiving natalizumab or other immunosuppressive therapies.

Multiple sclerosis relapse.description: An acute or subacute episode of new inflammatory demyelination in the central nervous system causing new neurologic deficits in a patient with multiple sclerosis.

PML-associated immune reconstitution inf.description: An inflammatory worsening of JC-virus brain infection that may occur after stopping natalizumab, removing immunosuppression, or changing disease-modifying therapy, as immune cells regain access to the CNS.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: A lymphoma confined to the brain, spinal cord, leptomeninges, or eyes; it is more likely in immunosuppressed patients and may cause focal deficits and seizures.

Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.normalized_text: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-ga.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants resulting in deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity and accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular, neural, renal, cardiac, and other cells. This case is strongly supported by markedly reduced alpha-Gal-A activity, a hemizygous GLA mutation, and characteristic clinical findings.

Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid accumulation in cardiomyocytes, producing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, chest pain, arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, and progressive myocardial fibrosis.

Sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: An inherited myocardial disorder, usually caused by sarcomeric gene variants, characterized by otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy that may cause chest discomfort, dyspnea, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death risk.

Infected intrahepatic hematoma (post-tra.description: A pre-existing traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected, producing a pyogenic abscess with systemic inflammatory signs.

Pyogenic liver abscess.description: A localized bacterial infection within the liver that forms a pus-containing collection; it may occur after trauma, biliary infection, bacteremia, or infection of a hematoma.

Infected biloma.description: A biloma is a collection of leaked bile caused by disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts, often after liver trauma. Infection of the collection can cause fever and sepsis.

Gas-forming pyogenic liver abscess.description: A severe subtype of bacterial liver abscess in which gas-producing organisms, such as Klebsiella species or anaerobic bacteria, create gas within an infected hepatic collection.

Iododerma (bullous/vegetative iodide-ind.description: A rare neutrophilic skin reaction caused by exposure to iodide-containing substances, including iodinated radiographic contrast. It can produce pustules, vesicles, bullae, and vegetating plaques, often with sterile cultures and neutrophilic histology.

Acute generalized exanthematous pustulos.description: A severe acute drug eruption characterized by rapid development of numerous sterile, nonfollicular pustules on erythematous skin, usually accompanied by neutrophilia. Iodinated contrast material is a recognized trigger.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal.description: A severe mucocutaneous drug reaction with extensive keratinocyte death, epidermal necrosis, blistering, and skin detachment. Although iodinated contrast can rarely trigger it, pustules are not a usual dominant feature.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.normalized_text: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), bullous variant
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis that typically causes abrupt painful erythematous plaques or nodules and may rarely become vesiculobullous or pustular. It may be triggered by medications or systemic disease.

Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.normalized_text: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant seps.description: A rapidly progressive gram-negative zoonotic bloodstream infection transmitted by dog bites or saliva exposure. Severe disease is especially associated with heavy alcohol use, immunocompromise, and asplenia, and may cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpuric skin necrosis, and limb ischemia.

Necrotizing fasciitis due to dog-bite wo.normalized_text: Necrotizing fasciitis due to dog-bite wound infection
Necrotizing fasciitis due to dog-bite wo.description: A life-threatening deep soft-tissue infection involving fascia and subcutaneous tissue, often caused by polymicrobial infection or organisms introduced through traumatic wounds. It can rapidly produce necrosis, systemic toxicity, septic shock, and skin discoloration.

Pasteurella multocida infection with sep.description: Pasteurella multocida is a gram-negative bacterium commonly found in dog and cat oral flora. It can cause rapidly developing cellulitis after bites and, less commonly, invasive bacteremia and septic shock in people with alcohol-related liver disease or other comorbidities.

Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with hemorr.normalized_text: Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with hemorrhagic bullous/purpuric skin lesions
Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with hemorr.description: A severe gram-negative infection acquired from seawater exposure or raw seafood, particularly in people with heavy alcohol use or chronic liver disease. It can cause fulminant sepsis with painful purpuric lesions, hemorrhagic bullae, tissue necrosis, and shock.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome.description: A syndrome caused by abrupt cessation or reduction of heavy alcohol intake. Symptoms can begin within hours to a few days and include anxiety, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tremor, hypertension, agitation, seizures, or delirium tremens.

diagnoses.name: MELAS syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: MELAS - [Mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes] syndrome

MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.normalized_text: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) due to MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mutation
MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalom.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variants, commonly involving the tRNA leucine gene. It causes impaired oxidative phosphorylation, myopathy, elevated lactate, neurologic deficits, and recurrent stroke-like episodes at a young age.

Mitochondrial myopathy.description: A neuromuscular disorder caused by impaired mitochondrial energy production in skeletal muscle, resulting in exercise intolerance, weakness, hypotonia, muscle wasting, and lactic acidosis.

Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke invo.normalized_text: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke involving the right middle cerebral artery territory
Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke invo.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolic occlusion of a cerebral artery, often originating from a cardiac thrombus. The diffusion-weighted MRI lesion and MR angiographic arterial obstruction are compatible with an acute large-vessel ischemic infarction.

Left ventricular thrombus associated wit.normalized_text: Left ventricular thrombus associated with mitochondrial cardiomyopathy
Left ventricular thrombus associated wit.description: Mitochondrial disease can involve cardiac muscle and cause cardiomyopathy, impaired ventricular contraction, and formation of mural thrombi. A left ventricular thrombus can embolize to the cerebral circulation and produce ischemic stroke.

Extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (distal.description: A malignant adenocarcinoma arising from the extrahepatic bile ducts that causes progressive biliary obstruction, often with ductal dilation, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and elevated CA 19-9. The imaging and pathology are consistent with an obstructing pancreatobiliary-type adenocarcinoma.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the.description: A pancreatic adenocarcinoma arising near the pancreatic head can obstruct the distal common bile duct, producing painless or minimally painful obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, anorexia, and elevated CA 19-9.

Gallbladder adenocarcinoma.description: Gallbladder cancer is usually an adenocarcinoma and may cause right upper quadrant discomfort, anorexia, jaundice, and biliary obstruction when it extends into or compresses the extrahepatic bile ducts.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis with domi.normalized_text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with dominant biliary stricture
Primary sclerosing cholangitis with domi.description: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease of the bile ducts that can produce multifocal strictures, cholestatic liver injury, pruritus, jaundice, and recurrent biliary obstruction. It also substantially increases the risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

Choledocholithiasis causing obstructive.description: A stone in the common bile duct can obstruct bile flow and cause jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, nausea, right upper quadrant pain, and elevation of bilirubin and liver enzymes.

Gallstone ileus with cholecystocolonic f.normalized_text: Gallstone ileus with cholecystocolonic fistula and rectal gallstone impaction
Gallstone ileus with cholecystocolonic f.description: A large gallstone enters the bowel through an abnormal fistula between the gallbladder and colon, travels distally, and may become impacted in the rectum, causing obstructed defecation (gallstone coleus).

Rectal fecal impaction.description: Accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum that causes impaired evacuation, rectal pressure, and occasionally minor bleeding from mucosal irritation.

Crohn's disease with anorectal involveme.description: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect the colon, rectum, and anus, causing inflammation, ulcers, strictures, fistulas, bleeding, and altered bowel habits.

Colorectal or rectal stricture due to Cr.normalized_text: Colorectal or rectal stricture due to Crohn's disease
Colorectal or rectal stricture due to Cr.description: Chronic intestinal inflammation from Crohn's disease can lead to fibrotic narrowing of the rectum or colon, producing obstructive defecatory symptoms and occasional bleeding.

Acute lateral patellar dislocation.description: Displacement of the patella out of the trochlear groove toward the lateral side of the knee, commonly occurring after twisting or minor trauma in adolescents with ligamentous laxity.

Osteochondral fracture associated with p.normalized_text: Osteochondral fracture associated with patellar dislocation
Osteochondral fracture associated with p.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, often occurring when the patella dislocates laterally and shears cartilage from the medial patella or lateral femoral condyle. The fragment may become a loose body in the joint.

Intra-articular loose body of the knee.normalized_text: Intra-articular loose body of the knee
Intra-articular loose body of the knee.description: A free fragment of cartilage, bone, or osteochondral tissue within the knee joint, often resulting from an osteochondral injury after patellar dislocation. It can mechanically obstruct movement.

Patellofemoral instability related to ge.normalized_text: Patellofemoral instability related to generalized ligamentous laxity
Patellofemoral instability related to ge.description: A predisposition to recurrent or first-time patellar subluxation/dislocation due to laxity of stabilizing structures, sometimes accompanied by anatomical or connective-tissue-related risk factors.

Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome.description: A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules, often with intense itching.

Lichen planopilaris.description: A lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory hair disorder that destroys hair follicles and produces scarring alopecia; follicular keratotic papules and perifollicular inflammation may occur, particularly in its Graham-Little variant.

Lichen spinulosus.description: An uncommon follicular keratosis presenting with groups of rough, spiny keratotic papules that can produce a sandpaper-like texture, usually on the trunk and extremities.

Complement-mediated atypical hemolytic u.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by uncontrolled alternative-complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period. It causes microvascular thrombosis, severe kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, and sometimes cutaneous thrombotic lesions.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP.description: A life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy usually due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with variable neurologic, renal, and systemic manifestations. Pregnancy can precipitate episodes.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can damage small vessels, producing endothelial injury, ischemic renal disease, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. It may overlap clinically with complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy.

Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated.normalized_text: Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets syndrome (HELLP syndrome) or persistent preeclampsia-related thrombotic microangiopathy
Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated.description: HELLP syndrome and severe preeclampsia are pregnancy-related endothelial disorders that can cause hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and kidney injury. They generally improve after delivery; persistence or worsening postpartum raises concern for aHUS.

Antiphospholipid syndrome-associated thr.description: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune prothrombotic disorder that can cause pregnancy complications, renal vascular injury, hypertension, thrombocytopenia, and skin necrosis or ulcers. Catastrophic forms can produce multiorgan microvascular thrombosis.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Small intestinal gastrointestinal stroma.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells, commonly driven by activating KIT mutations. Ileal GISTs can present with occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding and anemia. The exon 11 KIT deletion strongly supports this diagnosis.

Small intestinal leiomyoma or leiomyosar.description: A smooth-muscle tumor of the gastrointestinal tract. Benign leiomyomas are uncommon in the small bowel, while leiomyosarcomas are malignant smooth-muscle neoplasms that may form an enhancing bowel-wall mass and cause bleeding.

Small intestinal schwannoma.description: A rare benign or low-grade peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall. It may present as a submucosal small-bowel mass and can occasionally cause bleeding, but is much less common in the ileum than GIST.

Small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (i.normalized_text: Small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (ileal carcinoid tumor)
Small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (i.description: A neuroendocrine neoplasm commonly arising in the distal ileum. These tumors can cause abdominal pain, obstruction, mesenteric fibrosis, or metastatic disease; bleeding and anemia may occur but are less characteristic.

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

Adult pancreatoblastoma.description: A rare malignant pancreatic epithelial tumor with acinar differentiation and characteristic squamoid corpuscles. Although predominantly a childhood tumor, it can rarely occur in older adults and often presents as a large, well-circumscribed pancreatic mass.

Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma.description: A rare malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor composed of cells showing acinar enzyme-producing differentiation. It commonly occurs in older adults and may form a large, relatively circumscribed mass.

Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic endocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors may become large before detection and can present with mass effect, abdominal fullness, or digestive symptoms.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from pancreatic ductal epithelium. It typically causes obstructive symptoms, pain, weight loss, and jaundice, but may occasionally present as a pancreatic mass with digestive impairment.

Hailey-Hailey disease (benign familial p.description: An autosomal-dominant acantholytic skin disorder caused by impaired keratinocyte adhesion. It produces recurrent painful, pruritic, erosive and crusted plaques in flexural areas, often exacerbated by heat, sweating, and friction.

Darier disease (keratosis follicularis).description: An inherited disorder of keratinization characterized by greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas, frequently aggravated by heat and sweating. Histology typically shows acantholysis with dyskeratosis.

Pemphigus vegetans.description: A rare flexural variant of pemphigus vulgaris in which flaccid blisters evolve into erosive, vegetating, crusted plaques, often involving the axillae and groin.

Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or f.normalized_text: Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or fungal infection
Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or f.description: Inflammation of opposing skin folds caused by moisture, friction, and heat, often complicated by Candida or bacterial overgrowth, producing maceration, odor, erosions, and crusting.

Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma of the ilium.description: A rare aggressive cartilage-producing malignant bone tumor that often affects adolescents and young adults and may arise in the pelvis. Imaging commonly shows a destructive osseous mass with a large soft-tissue component and areas of chondroid mineralization/calcification.

Conventional chondrosarcoma of the pelvi.description: A malignant cartilage-forming bone tumor that commonly occurs in the pelvis and can produce lobulated soft-tissue masses with rings-and-arcs, stippled, or peripheral calcification. It is more common in older adults but can occasionally occur in younger patients.

Ewing sarcoma of the ilium.description: An aggressive small round cell malignancy of bone occurring mainly in children, adolescents, and young adults. Pelvic Ewing sarcoma may present as a painful enlarging mass with destructive bone changes and a large soft-tissue component.

Osteosarcoma of the pelvis.description: A malignant bone-forming tumor that can occur in young people and may arise in the iliac bone. Pelvic lesions often present late as large painful masses and may contain mineralized osteoid matrix.

Giant cell tumor of bone with secondary.normalized_text: Giant cell tumor of bone with secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change
Giant cell tumor of bone with secondary.description: A locally aggressive benign bone tumor usually arising after skeletal maturity, often in women aged 20 to 40 years. It can affect the pelvis and cause an expansile lytic lesion with pain and a palpable mass; secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change can enlarge the lesion rapidly.

Stiff-person syndrome (SPS), likely anti.description: A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder causing progressive axial and limb rigidity with painful stimulus-sensitive muscle spasms. Electromyography may show continuous motor-unit activity, and symptoms often improve with benzodiazepines and IVIG.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.normalized_text: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigid.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person-spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, characterized by rigidity, painful spasms, exaggerated startle, myoclonus, brainstem involvement, autonomic dysfunction, and possible respiratory compromise.

Hereditary spastic paraplegia.description: A group of inherited disorders causing slowly progressive upper-motor-neuron dysfunction, predominantly affecting the legs, with spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and impaired gait.

Multiple sclerosis with spastic parapare.description: An immune-mediated central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause upper-motor-neuron weakness, leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, sensory symptoms, visual symptoms, and bladder dysfunction.

Tetanus.description: A toxin-mediated neurologic illness caused by Clostridium tetani, producing generalized rigidity, painful stimulus-triggered spasms, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability, and possible respiratory failure.

Takayasu arteritis.description: A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often occurring in younger women and causing stenosis or occlusion of carotid and subclavian arteries. Reduced scalp and cerebral perfusion can cause scalp ischemia, ulceration, syncope, and stroke.

Giant cell arteritis.description: A granulomatous vasculitis involving medium and large arteries, especially cranial branches of the carotid artery. It can produce scalp tenderness, scalp necrosis, visual loss, and ischemic stroke.

Severe premature atherosclerotic carotid.normalized_text: Severe premature atherosclerotic carotid and arch-vessel disease
Severe premature atherosclerotic carotid.description: Atherosclerosis can cause progressive narrowing of carotid and subclavian arteries, resulting in transient cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and rarely tissue ischemia when collateral blood supply is poor.

Antiphospholipid syndrome.description: An autoimmune thrombophilia that causes recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis, including ischemic stroke in younger adults. Arterial thrombosis could contribute to carotid occlusion and scalp ischemia.

Scalp trauma with secondary skin necrosi.normalized_text: Scalp trauma with secondary skin necrosis related to recurrent falls
Scalp trauma with secondary skin necrosi.description: Repeated collapse can cause scalp injury; in a patient receiving dual antiplatelet therapy, trauma may lead to hematoma, skin breakdown, and delayed wound healing. This would not, however, explain the underlying major-vessel imaging abnormalities.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).description: A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites, transmitted by sandflies. It commonly affects immunosuppressed individuals and can cause prolonged fever, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and bone-marrow involvement. The image is consistent with Leishman-Donovan bodies (intracellular amastigotes) in macrophages.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause inflammatory arthritis, fever, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, and immune-complex vasculitic skin lesions.

Felty syndrome.description: A complication of long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually with splenomegaly, and increased susceptibility to infections.

Anti-TNF-associated disseminated leishma.description: Visceral leishmaniasis occurring or reactivating in a patient receiving tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibition, such as adalimumab. TNF-alpha blockade impairs macrophage-mediated control of intracellular Leishmania parasites.

Necrobiosis lipoidica.description: A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, typically causing slowly enlarging yellow-brown to reddish plaques on the shins with central atrophy, indentation, telangiectasia, and possible ulceration. Histology commonly shows layers of degenerated collagen (necrobiosis) with palisading granulomatous inflammation.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis characterized by dermal palisading granulomas surrounding degenerated collagen. It commonly presents as firm annular papules or plaques, often on the hands, feet, elbows, or ankles; generalized forms may be associated with diabetes.

Diabetic dermopathy.description: A common diabetes-associated microvascular skin finding consisting of small, round or oval, brown, slightly atrophic macules on the shins, often called diabetic shin spots.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous disorder that can involve the skin, producing red-brown papules, plaques, nodules, or scars. Skin biopsy typically demonstrates noncaseating granulomas.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B due to.normalized_text: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B due to paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q (GNAS methylation defect)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B due to.description: A disorder of parathyroid hormone resistance caused by abnormal imprinting/methylation at the GNAS locus, often due to paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone despite adequate hormone production. The methylation pattern shown, with increased NESP methylation and reduced methylation at other GNAS differentially methylated regions, is consistent with this mechanism.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A.description: A GNAS-related disorder causing resistance to parathyroid hormone and sometimes other hormones, including TSH. It is usually caused by an inactivating maternal GNAS mutation and is often associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy, including short stature, obesity, brachydactyly, and subcutaneous ossifications.

Hypocalcemic tetany with possible laryng.description: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability caused by low serum calcium. It may cause muscle stiffness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek sign, stridor, and laryngospasm.
