In this case, it is likely a manifestation of parathyroid hormone resistance rather than an isolated disease.

Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.normalized_text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), choking-related subtype
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorde.description: An eating or feeding disorder characterized by restricted intake due to fear of aversive consequences of eating, such as choking or vomiting. It can lead to dehydration, weight loss, nutritional compromise, and marked anxiety around swallowing.

Vitamin D deficiency or nutritional hypo.normalized_text: Vitamin D deficiency or nutritional hypocalcemia
Vitamin D deficiency or nutritional hypo.description: Insufficient vitamin D intake, absorption, or sun exposure can reduce calcium absorption and produce hypocalcemia with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone. It is a common cause of hypocalcemia in adolescents but usually produces low or normal phosphate because elevated parathyroid hormone increases renal phosphate excretion.

Dabrafenib-trametinib-associated pyrexia.description: A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, characterized by recurrent high fever, chills or diaphoresis, fatigue, nausea, and occasionally hypotension or organ dysfunction. Symptoms often improve after treatment interruption and recur with rechallenge.

Dabrafenib-trametinib-induced sarcoid-li.description: A drug-induced systemic inflammatory reaction that can resemble sarcoidosis, producing noncaseating granulomas and pulmonary, hepatic, splenic, lymph-node, or skin lesions during BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy.

Systemic sarcoidosis.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often affecting the lungs and lymph nodes but also potentially involving the liver and spleen.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that can produce fever, pulmonary disease, hepatosplenic involvement, granulomas, and yeast forms detectable with fungal stains in tissue.

Gallbladder metastasis from prostate ade.normalized_text: Gallbladder metastasis from prostate adenocarcinoma causing acute cholecystitis
Gallbladder metastasis from prostate ade.description: Rare metastatic involvement of the gallbladder by prostate cancer, potentially causing cystic-duct obstruction, gallbladder distention, and an acute cholecystitis-like presentation.

Acute calculous or acalculous cholecysti.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from cystic-duct obstruction by a gallstone, sludge, mass, or extrinsic compression; acalculous cholecystitis can occur without stones in severely ill or malignant patients.

Primary gallbladder adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the gallbladder that may obstruct the cystic duct or biliary tree and can present as cholecystitis, biliary pain, or cholestatic liver-enzyme elevation.

Acute biliary pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation caused by transient or persistent obstruction of the ampulla or common bile duct, most often from gallstones, sludge, or malignant biliary obstruction.

Allgrove syndrome (Triple-A syndrome; AA.description: An autosomal-recessive multisystem disorder caused by AAAS gene variants, classically characterized by alacrima, achalasia, and ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency; progressive neurologic dysfunction may produce the '4A' phenotype.

4A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with prog.normalized_text: 4A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with progressive neurologic dysfunction)
4A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with prog.description: A neurologic form of Allgrove syndrome in which alacrima, achalasia, adrenal insufficiency, and progressive autonomic, central, and peripheral neurologic abnormalities coexist.

Familial glucocorticoid deficiency (ACTH.description: A group of inherited disorders causing adrenal glucocorticoid failure with high ACTH but generally preserved mineralocorticoid production, often presenting in childhood with hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, and poor growth.

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 variants that can cause primary adrenal insufficiency in boys and progressive inflammatory cerebral or spinal-cord neurologic disease.

Syringomyelia due to cervical spinal cor.normalized_text: Syringomyelia due to cervical spinal cord syrinx
Syringomyelia due to cervical spinal cor.description: A fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord that may cause progressive weakness, muscle wasting, upper-motor-neuron signs, and gait disturbance. The cervical MRI appearance is compatible with a central intramedullary fluid signal/syrinx.

Cerebral fat embolism syndrome.description: Neurologic injury caused by fat emboli entering the cerebral circulation, usually after trauma or orthopedic procedures but occasionally associated with extensive bone metastases. MRI commonly shows multifocal punctate diffusion-restricted lesions ('starfield' pattern), edema, and microhemorrhages.

Cancer-associated multifocal embolic isc.normalized_text: Cancer-associated multifocal embolic ischemic stroke (malignancy-related hypercoagulability/Trousseau syndrome)
Cancer-associated multifocal embolic isc.description: Advanced malignancy can cause a hypercoagulable state, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or tumor-associated thrombosis, resulting in multiple acute embolic cerebral infarcts in different vascular territories.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy synd.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, commonly related to severe hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapy, or endothelial injury. It causes altered mental status, seizures, headache, and visual symptoms, usually with posterior-predominant MRI abnormalities.

Brain metastases from breast cancer with.normalized_text: Brain metastases from breast cancer with hemorrhagic or ischemic complications
Brain metastases from breast cancer with.description: Breast cancer can metastasize to the brain and cause focal deficits, seizures, headache, cognitive changes, edema, and occasionally hemorrhage. Metastases usually appear as enhancing mass lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema.

Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver meta.normalized_text: Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver metastases or hepatic failure
Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver meta.description: Hepatic dysfunction can lead to accumulation of neurotoxins, particularly ammonia, causing fluctuating confusion, impaired attention, altered consciousness, and coma.

Isolated intramedullary spinal cord sarc.description: Granulomatous inflammation of the spinal cord due to sarcoidosis, which may occur without pulmonary or other systemic involvement. MRI often shows an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion, and biopsy demonstrates noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.

Cervical spinal cord tumor (intramedulla.normalized_text: Cervical spinal cord tumor (intramedullary astrocytoma or ependymoma)
Cervical spinal cord tumor (intramedulla.description: Primary intramedullary tumors can expand and compress cervical spinal cord pathways, producing progressive myelopathy, sensory changes, weakness, and bladder dysfunction. However, granulomatous histology argues against a neoplasm.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder that commonly causes acute or subacute transverse myelitis, often involving long segments of the spinal cord and causing weakness, sensory loss, and sphincter dysfunction.

Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary.normalized_text: Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary tuberculoma or granulomatous myelitis)
Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary.description: Tuberculosis can cause granulomatous inflammation or a tuberculoma within the spinal cord, resulting in progressive myelopathy. Histology may show granulomas and giant cells, usually with caseous necrosis or microbiologic evidence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Pulmonary malakoplakia.description: A rare chronic granulomatous inflammatory disorder caused by impaired macrophage bacterial killing, most often associated with gram-negative infection. It can form a mass-like pulmonary consolidation and may show foamy histiocytes with characteristic Michaelis-Gutmann bodies on pathology.

Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.normalized_text: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess
Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lun.description: A severe bacterial infection causing pulmonary consolidation, tissue necrosis, and formation of one or more cavities or abscesses, commonly involving dependent portions of the lower lobes.

Pulmonary actinomycosis.description: A chronic suppurative infection caused by Actinomyces species that can produce mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and extension toward the pleura or chest wall. Diagnosis is usually made by pathology or microbiologic identification of sulfur granules.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lung, which may cause prolonged cough, sputum production, cavitary lesions, and focal consolidation; lower-lobe involvement can occur but is less classic than upper-lobe disease in reactivation tuberculosis.

Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an end.normalized_text: Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an endobronchial lesion
Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an end.description: Infection and collapse/consolidation distal to obstruction of a bronchus by a tumor, foreign body, mucus plug, or inflammatory lesion. Obstruction can lead to persistent localized pneumonia, bronchiectatic change, or abscess formation.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.normalized_text: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirof.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually involving dogs as reservoir hosts. In humans it commonly presents as a solitary painless subcutaneous nodule; histology may demonstrate a thick-cuticled nematode.

Subcutaneous gnathostomiasis.description: A tissue helminth infection caused by Gnathostoma larvae, classically producing intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings after ingestion of undercooked freshwater fish, eels, frogs, or other intermediate hosts in endemic regions.

Subcutaneous sparganosis.description: Infection by migrating larval Spirometra tapeworms, usually acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or raw amphibian/reptile meat. It can cause a slowly migrating subcutaneous mass.

Subcutaneous cysticercosis.description: Tissue infection with larval Taenia solium cysts that can form painless subcutaneous or intramuscular nodules, often in association with exposure to fecal contamination or undercooked pork in endemic settings.

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), Ri.description: A progressive tauopathy causing early postural instability and falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and midbrain atrophy.

Multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian ty.description: A synucleinopathy characterized by parkinsonism, autonomic failure, cerebellar dysfunction, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes abnormal eye movements.

Corticobasal syndrome (corticobasal dege.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually causes asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, dystonia, myoclonus, and sometimes supranuclear gaze palsy.

Dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson d.normalized_text: Dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson disease with dementia
Dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson d.description: Synucleinopathies causing parkinsonism with cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, fluctuating attention, REM sleep behavior disorder, and autonomic dysfunction; eye movement abnormalities can occur later.

Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.normalized_text: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset neurologic form
Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset.description: A lysosomal cholesterol-trafficking disorder that can present in adults with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and psychiatric or cognitive symptoms.

Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus ne.description: Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast, classically occurring in advanced HIV/AIDS. The images are consistent with encapsulated budding yeasts demonstrated by India ink staining.

Tuberculous meningitis.description: A subacute meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated opening pressure, and neurologic impairment. It is more likely in people with advanced HIV infection.

Viral meningitis or meningoencephalitis.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as herpesviruses or enteroviruses. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.

Acute ischemic infarction of the left me.normalized_text: Acute ischemic infarction of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) causing left internuclear ophthalmoplegia
Acute ischemic infarction of the left me.description: A small acute brainstem ischemic stroke affecting the left MLF, the pathway coordinating conjugate horizontal eye movements. This produces impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye. The diffusion-weighted MRI appearance is consistent with an acute small brainstem infarct.

Cardioembolic posterior-circulation isch.description: An acute ischemic stroke caused by embolization from the heart, particularly in atrial fibrillation. Small emboli can occlude perforating brainstem vessels and cause an isolated ocular-motor syndrome.

Multiple sclerosis causing internuclear.description: Multiple sclerosis can produce demyelinating lesions of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is a classic cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia, often with diplopia and abducting nystagmus.

Ocular myasthenia gravis.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disorder that may cause fluctuating diplopia and ophthalmoparesis, usually without pupillary abnormalities or other focal neurological deficits.

Congenital Plasmodium falciparum malaria.description: Malaria acquired transplacentally or during delivery, with symptomatic infection appearing in the first weeks of life. P. falciparum commonly causes high parasitemia, severe hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and life-threatening systemic illness.

Severe falciparum malaria with hemolysis.normalized_text: Severe falciparum malaria with hemolysis and shock
Severe falciparum malaria with hemolysis.description: Severe Plasmodium falciparum infection can cause massive red-cell destruction, hemoglobinuria, thrombocytopenia, metabolic stress, circulatory compromise, and respiratory distress. In a young infant, this may resemble bacterial sepsis.

Babesiosis.description: Babesiosis is an intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that can produce fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and hemoglobinuria. On blood smear it may resemble malaria, although Babesia classically may show tetrads forming a Maltese-cross pattern.

Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.normalized_text: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
Neonatal bacterial sepsis with dissemina.description: Neonatal sepsis can cause fever, lethargy, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, thrombocytopenia, coagulation abnormalities, and multiorgan dysfunction. It is an important clinical mimic of severe malaria in young infants.

Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.normalized_text: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal involvement
Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarci.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with locally recurrent pelvic disease involving or compressing the rectum and distant metastases to the lungs and liver.

Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with liver.normalized_text: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with liver and lung metastases
Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with liver.description: Cancer arising from the rectum that may cause local rectal pain and tenesmus, with hematogenous spread commonly involving the liver and lungs.

Rectal involvement by metastatic prostat.normalized_text: Rectal involvement by metastatic prostate cancer presenting as a rectal tumor
Rectal involvement by metastatic prostat.description: A specific manifestation of recurrent prostate cancer in which tumor extends into or infiltrates the rectal wall, potentially mimicking a primary rectal cancer and producing severe anorectal symptoms.

Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the b.normalized_text: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or urinary tract
Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the b.description: Urothelial cancer can invade pelvic structures and metastasize to lymph nodes, liver, and lungs, although the clinical history more strongly favors recurrent prostate cancer.

Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypoka.normalized_text: Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypoka.description: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism due to thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, often associated with diffuse thyroid enlargement and marked hypervascularity. In susceptible patients, thyrotoxicosis can cause intracellular potassium shifting and acute flaccid weakness.

Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysi.description: An acute neuromuscular complication of thyrotoxicosis in which thyroid hormone excess increases cellular potassium uptake, producing profound hypokalemia and sudden reversible muscle weakness or paralysis.

Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxico.normalized_text: Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm spectrum
Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxico.description: Thyrotoxicosis may be precipitated or worsened by supplements containing thyroid hormone, iodine, stimulants, or adulterants; it can exacerbate underlying Graves disease and trigger hypokalemic paralysis.

Distal renal tubular acidosis with hypok.normalized_text: Distal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemic paralysis
Distal renal tubular acidosis with hypok.description: A renal acidification disorder that causes non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, renal potassium wasting, and potentially severe hypokalemic muscle weakness; autoimmune thyroid disease can coexist with autoimmune renal tubular disorders.

Torus palatinus.description: A benign, non-neoplastic bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is often lobulated, slowly enlarges over time, and is usually asymptomatic.

Palatal exostosis.description: A benign localized overgrowth of mature bone on the palate. Torus palatinus is the most characteristic type of palatal exostosis.

Peripheral ossifying fibroma.description: A benign reactive gingival growth containing fibrous tissue and mineralized material, usually arising from the interdental gingiva rather than the palate.

Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor that may occur on the palate, usually presenting as a slow-growing, painless, firm submucosal mass.

Palatal malignant salivary-gland neoplas.normalized_text: Palatal malignant salivary-gland neoplasm (such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma)
Palatal malignant salivary-gland neoplas.description: A malignant tumor of minor salivary glands that can present as a palatal swelling, sometimes initially painless, but often with progressive enlargement, ulceration, pain, or tissue destruction.

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.icd11_title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.normalized_text: Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation with L4-L5 nerve-root compression
Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation wi.description: Displacement of degenerative disc material into the spinal canal or neural foramen, causing compression of a lumbar nerve root and radiculopathy. The MRI appearance is most consistent with a prominent lower-lumbar disc protrusion/extrusion, particularly at L4-L5.

Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to dege.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to degenerative disc disease
Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to dege.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal from disc bulging, facet-joint degeneration, and ligament thickening, potentially compressing the cauda equina or individual nerve roots.

Lumbar epidural synovial (facet) cyst.description: A fluid-containing cyst arising from a degenerative lumbar facet joint that can extend into the spinal canal and compress a nerve root, most commonly at L4-L5.

Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombos.normalized_text: Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombosed epidural varix
Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombos.description: Dilated or thrombosed epidural veins can form a mass-like lesion in the lumbar canal and mimic a disc herniation, producing acute radicular pain and neurological deficit.

Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.normalized_text: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with multisystem thromboembolic/vasculitic involvement
Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (H.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated injury to organs, particularly the heart, nervous system, lungs, skin, and blood vessels. Cardiac involvement can produce embolic cerebral infarctions.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.normalized_text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: A necrotizing small- to medium-vessel vasculitis associated with eosinophilia, asthma, chronic sinus disease, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, and possible cardiac or central nervous system involvement.

Eosinophilic myocarditis with cardioembo.normalized_text: Eosinophilic myocarditis with cardioembolic multifocal ischemic stroke
Eosinophilic myocarditis with cardioembo.description: Eosinophil-mediated inflammation of the myocardium, often associated with hypereosinophilic disorders, that can lead to myocardial injury, mural thrombus formation, embolic stroke, and heart failure.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous.normalized_text: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
Primary angiitis of the central nervous.description: An uncommon inflammatory vasculitis limited to the brain and spinal cord that causes multifocal ischemic infarctions, hemorrhage, encephalopathy, and angiographic segmental stenoses or beading.

Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic medium-vessel vasculitis
Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic.description: A systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause cerebral ischemia, cardiac ischemia, pulmonary or systemic vascular abnormalities, and constitutional symptoms.

Sarcoidosis.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and the lungs.

Breast cancer recurrence with mediastina.normalized_text: Breast cancer recurrence with mediastinal and hilar lymph-node metastases
Breast cancer recurrence with mediastina.description: Recurrent breast carcinoma can spread to intrathoracic lymph nodes, lungs, bone, liver, or other organs and may produce FDG-avid lesions on PET imaging.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis or pulmonary t.description: Tuberculosis is a granulomatous infection that can cause thoracic lymph-node enlargement and pulmonary abnormalities; granulomas are often caseating but may occasionally be noncaseating.

Lymphoma.description: Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas may cause FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy and constitutional or hematologic abnormalities.

IgG kappa multiple myeloma with osteoscl.normalized_text: IgG kappa multiple myeloma with osteosclerotic bone involvement
IgG kappa multiple myeloma with osteoscl.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin, associated with marrow infiltration, anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and bone disease. Rarely, myeloma may produce osteosclerotic rather than classic lytic skeletal lesions.

POEMS syndrome associated with osteoscle.normalized_text: POEMS syndrome associated with osteosclerotic plasma-cell neoplasm
POEMS syndrome associated with osteoscle.description: A rare plasma-cell disorder characterized by polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal protein, skin changes, and usually osteosclerotic bone lesions. The monoclonal protein is more often lambda restricted.

Smoldering multiple myeloma.description: An asymptomatic precursor plasma-cell neoplasm with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or marrow plasma-cell burden but without myeloma-defining organ damage or biomarkers requiring treatment.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined si.description: A common premalignant condition in older adults characterized by a small monoclonal protein without end-organ injury, substantial marrow plasma-cell infiltration, or myeloma-defining features.

Multifocal intracranial germinoma with s.normalized_text: Multifocal intracranial germinoma with suprasellar involvement
Multifocal intracranial germinoma with s.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor of the central nervous system that commonly involves the suprasellar/hypothalamic-pituitary region and may be multifocal, including basal ganglia or pineal-region lesions. It can cause diabetes insipidus, visual symptoms, hyperprolactinemia from stalk disruption, and panhypopituitarism.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving.normalized_text: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving.description: A histiocytic inflammatory/neoplastic disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, most often producing central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. CNS lesions can occur but multifocal enhancing brain lesions are less typical than in germinoma.

Craniopharyngioma.description: A benign but locally aggressive epithelial tumor arising near the pituitary stalk and suprasellar region. It commonly causes visual impairment, headaches, hyperprolactinemia, diabetes insipidus, and multiple anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.

Primary hypothalamic-pituitary lymphoma.normalized_text: Primary hypothalamic-pituitary lymphoma or secondary CNS lymphoma
Primary hypothalamic-pituitary lymphoma.description: Lymphomatous infiltration of the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, or suprasellar region can cause diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, visual symptoms, and panhypopituitarism. Multifocal enhancing CNS lesions may occur, although this is uncommon in an otherwise healthy young adult.

Neurosarcoidosis involving the hypothala.description: Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis can infiltrate the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, and meninges, leading to central diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, visual symptoms, and anterior pituitary failure. It can also produce enhancing CNS lesions.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.normalized_text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic-valve infective endocarditis
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aur.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, caused here by MRSA. Intravenous drug use, persistent fever, positive blood cultures, peripheral embolic signs, and echocardiographic valve lesions strongly support this diagnosis.

Aortic root/perivalvular abscess complic.normalized_text: Aortic root/perivalvular abscess complicating infective endocarditis
Aortic root/perivalvular abscess complic.description: A localized collection of infection adjacent to the aortic valve annulus or aortic root, usually caused by invasive infective endocarditis. It can damage the conduction system and cause new PR prolongation or atrioventricular block.

Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to in.normalized_text: Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to infective endocarditis
Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to in.description: Cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected valvular material from infective endocarditis into the cerebral circulation. It may produce focal neurological deficits, altered consciousness, and headache.

Acute or worsening aortic regurgitation.normalized_text: Acute or worsening aortic regurgitation secondary to infective endocarditis
Acute or worsening aortic regurgitation.description: Failure of the aortic valve to close properly because of infective destruction, perforation, or annular involvement. It produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur and may occur with aortic-valve endocarditis or peri-annular abscess.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, resulting in glycogen accumulation predominantly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile-onset disease commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, elevated muscle enzymes, hypotonia, and progressive respiratory muscle weakness.

Infantile-onset Pompe disease with early.normalized_text: Infantile-onset Pompe disease with early hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Infantile-onset Pompe disease with early.description: A cardiac-predominant presentation of infantile Pompe disease in which profound GAA deficiency causes glycogen deposition in the myocardium, producing cardiomegaly and often hypertrophic cardiomyopathy before major skeletal-muscle weakness becomes evident.

GAA pseudodeficiency.description: A benign genetic state in which certain GAA variants reduce activity in dried-blood-spot screening assays without causing clinically significant Pompe disease. It is an important cause of false-positive newborn screening results.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts in the bone marrow, often causing bone pain, fever, cytopenias, and extramedullary infiltration. The marrow morphology and flow cytometry showing blast cells expressing B-cell markers such as CD19 and CD10 support this diagnosis.

Neuroblastoma.description: A childhood embryonal tumor of sympathetic nervous-system tissue, commonly arising in the adrenal gland or paraspinal region. It can metastasize to bone and bone marrow and may cause periorbital ecchymoses, bone pain, limp, fever, and abdominal distention.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including.normalized_text: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including myeloid sarcoma
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including.description: A hematologic malignancy caused by proliferation of myeloid blasts in marrow and blood. AML can cause fever, bone pain, marrow failure, and extramedullary myeloid sarcomas involving bone, soft tissues, skin, or the orbit.

Ewing sarcoma with metastatic disease.description: An aggressive small round cell sarcoma of bone and soft tissue, usually affecting children and adolescents. It often causes localized bone pain, fever, limp, and can metastasize to lung, bone marrow, and other bones.

Acute bacterial cellulitis of the glutea.normalized_text: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the gluteal region
Acute bacterial cellulitis of the glutea.description: A diffuse bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, commonly caused by streptococci or staphylococci. Ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema with a cobblestoned appearance and no drainable abscess.

Erysipelas.description: A superficial form of bacterial cellulitis involving the upper dermis and lymphatic vessels, usually caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci. It produces rapidly developing painful red skin swelling, often with relatively defined borders.

Superficial thrombophlebitis of a glutea.normalized_text: Superficial thrombophlebitis of a gluteal superficial vein
Superficial thrombophlebitis of a glutea.description: Inflammation and thrombosis of a superficial vein, causing localized pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Ultrasound can demonstrate a noncompressible superficial venous structure with surrounding inflammatory change.

Early necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, potentially life-threatening infection of skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, or muscle. Early findings can resemble cellulitis, but pain is often severe and progression may be rapid; ultrasound may show edema, fascial fluid, or gas.

Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD.description: A late immune-mediated complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Skin involvement may be lichenoid, poikilodermatous, or sclerotic and can cause fascial tightening and joint contractures.

Dermatomyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive cutaneous eruptions; it may occur as an autoimmune syndrome after transplantation or overlap with chronic GVHD.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lu.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rash, fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, and positive antinuclear antibodies. Lupus-like syndromes can rarely develop after stem-cell transplantation.

Eosinophilic fasciitis.description: An inflammatory fibrosing disorder of the fascia that causes painful swelling followed by skin induration, restricted joint movement, and contractures. It may resemble scleroderma and can occur in association with immune dysregulation or chronic GVHD.

Generalized eruptive keratoacanthomas of.description: A rare form of eruptive keratoacanthoma characterized by the progressive appearance of numerous crateriform, keratin-filled papules and nodules, often on sun-exposed skin, with substantial pruritus.

Multiple keratoacanthomas associated wit.normalized_text: Multiple keratoacanthomas associated with chronic renal failure and dialysis
Multiple keratoacanthomas associated wit.description: Multiple keratoacanthomas may occur in patients with chronic renal failure, dialysis, prior transplantation, or altered immune function. They present as rapidly developing keratinizing crateriform papules or nodules and can resemble well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

Keratoacanthoma-type cutaneous squamous.description: Keratoacanthoma-type squamous cell carcinoma is a keratinocyte malignancy that can appear as a rapidly growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug. Multiple lesions may occur in patients with immunologic dysfunction or prior immunosuppression.

Acquired perforating dermatosis of renal.normalized_text: Acquired perforating dermatosis of renal failure
Acquired perforating dermatosis of renal.description: An intensely pruritic skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes and chronic kidney disease/dialysis, characterized by excoriated hyperkeratotic papules or nodules, usually on the extensor surfaces of the limbs.

Zika virus-associated acute transverse m.description: An inflammatory spinal cord syndrome caused by neuroinvasive Zika virus infection, producing motor weakness, sensory level, pain, and autonomic dysfunction. MRI may show focal or longitudinal intramedullary T2 hyperintensity.

Acute transverse myelitis, unspecified i.normalized_text: Acute transverse myelitis, unspecified infectious or post-infectious
Acute transverse myelitis, unspecified i.description: Acute inflammation of the spinal cord causing bilateral or asymmetric weakness, a defined sensory level, neuropathic pain, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. It may follow viral infection or occur as an isolated inflammatory syndrome.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder that can cause severe myelitis, often with longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesions, sensory deficits, weakness, and sphincter dysfunction. It is commonly associated with aquaporin-4 or MOG antibodies.

Multiple sclerosis presenting with parti.normalized_text: Multiple sclerosis presenting with partial transverse myelitis
Multiple sclerosis presenting with parti.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that may first present with a spinal cord lesion causing sensory symptoms, weakness, and bladder dysfunction.

Spinal cord infarction.description: Ischemic injury to the spinal cord, usually causing sudden severe back pain followed by weakness, dissociated sensory loss, and autonomic dysfunction. It is uncommon in adolescents without vascular risk factors or structural vascular disease.

T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.normalized_text: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), mature T-cell phenotype with t(X;14) involving TCRAD/IRS4
T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymp.description: An aggressive precursor T-cell neoplasm presenting with marrow and peripheral-blood blasts. The CD2+, CD3+, CD5+, and CD7+ phenotype supports T-lineage leukemia; the cytogenetic/FISH findings are consistent with a T-cell receptor alpha/delta locus rearrangement involving Xq22.3/IRS4.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL).description: A mature, aggressive T-cell leukemia characterized by marked lymphocytosis and expression of mature pan-T-cell markers, commonly CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It is usually a disease of older adults and often has splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).description: A mature peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). The leukemic form can cause high white-cell counts, circulating malignant T cells, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, skin lesions, and hypercalcemia.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with.normalized_text: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with.description: A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites that invade macrophages in the bone marrow, spleen, and liver. It can trigger secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), producing severe inflammation, cytopenias, coagulopathy, and multiorgan failure. Intracellular amastigotes in macrophages on marrow smears support this diagnosis.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with seconda.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Disseminated histoplasmosis with seconda.description: A disseminated fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species, in which small intracellular yeasts may be found within macrophages in bone marrow or tissue. Severe disseminated disease can cause fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse lung disease, and secondary HLH.

Talaromyces marneffei infection (talarom.normalized_text: Talaromyces marneffei infection (talaromycosis) with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Talaromyces marneffei infection (talarom.description: Talaromycosis is a disseminated dimorphic fungal infection endemic in parts of Southeast Asia and southern China. It commonly affects immunocompromised individuals but can occasionally occur in apparently immunocompetent patients. It may cause intracellular yeast-like organisms in macrophages, pulmonary infiltrates, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and HLH.

Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.normalized_text: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by severe infection
Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocyt.description: HLH is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by uncontrolled immune activation and macrophage-mediated blood-cell destruction. It may be triggered by parasitic, fungal, viral, or bacterial infection and causes fever, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, organ enlargement, and multiorgan failure.

Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with.normalized_text: Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with.description: Central nervous system infection/reactivation of varicella-zoster virus that can cause meningoencephalitis and inflammation of cerebral arteries, resulting in multifocal ischemic strokes.

Japanese encephalitis.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis acquired in endemic parts of Asia and the western Pacific, causing fever, encephalopathy, coma, and focal neurologic signs; deep gray-matter abnormalities are common on MRI.

West Nile virus neuroinvasive disease.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection that may cause meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, and occasionally rash, particularly in older adults.

Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated.normalized_text: Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated cerebral vasculopathy
Dengue encephalitis or dengue-associated.description: Neurologic dengue is an uncommon complication of dengue virus infection and can present with encephalitis, altered consciousness, seizures, stroke, or inflammatory vascular complications after travel to endemic tropical regions.

Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with.normalized_text: Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with infectious cerebral vasculitis
Acute bacterial meningoencephalitis with.description: Bacterial infection of the meninges and brain can cause fever, depressed consciousness, focal deficits, and secondary inflammatory narrowing or thrombosis of intracranial vessels, leading to cerebral infarctions.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, typically causing palpable purpura of the lower extremities, arthralgia or arthritis, abdominal symptoms, and possible kidney involvement. It often follows an upper respiratory infection.

Adalimumab-associated IgA vasculitis.description: A drug-associated form of IgA small-vessel vasculitis that can occur during treatment with TNF-alpha inhibitors such as adalimumab. It can present with palpable purpura and joint involvement, sometimes after prolonged exposure.

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis as.normalized_text: Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis associated with Crohn's disease
Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis as.description: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is inflammation of small dermal blood vessels causing palpable purpura. It may occur as an extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease or in association with infection or medication exposure.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing systemic small- and medium-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, skin, and peripheral nerves. It can cause purpura and sinonasal disease but usually has systemic organ involvement.

HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.normalized_text: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (tonsillar carcinoma) with cervical lymph-node metastasis
HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous ce.description: A squamous-cell cancer arising in the palatine tonsil or adjacent oropharynx, commonly associated with high-risk HPV in younger nonsmokers. It often presents with unilateral throat pain, referred ear pain, and an upper-neck metastatic lymph node. The imaging appearance is consistent with an oropharyngeal primary lesion and ipsilateral nodal disease.

Non-HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamou.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the oropharynx, including the tonsil and base of tongue, traditionally associated with tobacco and heavy alcohol exposure. It may invade locally and spread to upper cervical lymph nodes.

Oropharyngeal lymphoma involving the ton.normalized_text: Oropharyngeal lymphoma involving the tonsil with cervical lymphadenopathy
Oropharyngeal lymphoma involving the ton.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can involve Waldeyer's ring, including the tonsils, and may cause an oropharyngeal mass with cervical lymph-node enlargement.

Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma p.normalized_text: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma presenting as cervical lymphadenopathy
Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma p.description: Papillary thyroid carcinoma frequently spreads to cervical lymph nodes, sometimes before a thyroid primary is clinically apparent. Metastatic nodes may be cystic or solid and occur in the lateral neck.

Deep neck infection or suppurative cervi.normalized_text: Deep neck infection or suppurative cervical lymphadenitis
Deep neck infection or suppurative cervi.description: Bacterial infection of the pharynx, tonsil, or cervical lymph nodes can produce throat pain and enlarged neck nodes; abscesses may appear as fluid-containing masses on imaging.

Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.normalized_text: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in extranodal tissue, often associated with chronic antigenic stimulation. Primary bladder MALT lymphoma is rare and is associated with chronic/recurrent cystitis in older women.

Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of.normalized_text: Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can involve the urinary bladder, either as primary disease or as transformation of a pre-existing low-grade MALT lymphoma. It usually shows large atypical lymphoid cells and may present as a bladder mass.

Chronic follicular cystitis.description: A benign reactive inflammatory bladder condition characterized by lymphoid follicle formation, typically caused by chronic infection or irritation. It can mimic lymphoma clinically and cystoscopically.

Secondary urinary bladder involvement by.normalized_text: Secondary urinary bladder involvement by systemic extranodal marginal zone lymphoma
Secondary urinary bladder involvement by.description: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma can arise at another mucosal site and secondarily involve the bladder. Evaluation typically seeks disease in the stomach, salivary/ocular adnexal tissue, lymph nodes, marrow, and other extranodal sites.

Bilateral septic arthritis of the hips.normalized_text: Bilateral septic arthritis of the hips
Bilateral septic arthritis of the hips.description: Infection of one or both hip joints causing rapid cartilage loss, joint-space destruction, erosions, and possible subluxation. In frail older adults, presentation may be subtle and may occur from hematogenous spread or a urinary source.

Osteomyelitis involving the femoral head.normalized_text: Osteomyelitis involving the femoral heads/acetabula secondary to contiguous septic arthritis
Osteomyelitis involving the femoral head.description: Bone infection involving the proximal femur and/or acetabulum, often occurring together with septic arthritis and producing progressive erosions and bone destruction on radiographs.

Rapidly destructive osteoarthritis of th.normalized_text: Rapidly destructive osteoarthritis of the hip
Rapidly destructive osteoarthritis of th.description: An aggressive form of hip osteoarthritis characterized by rapid loss of the femoral head and acetabular bone, severe joint-space narrowing, and progressive deformity. It is more common in older women and can mimic septic arthritis radiographically.

Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy of the.description: Progressive joint destruction caused by loss of protective sensation and repetitive microtrauma. Diabetes is a major cause, although hip involvement is uncommon compared with foot and ankle involvement.

Osteochondritis dissecans of the medial.normalized_text: Osteochondritis dissecans of the medial femoral condyle
Osteochondritis dissecans of the medial.description: A focal osteochondral disorder in which subchondral bone and overlying cartilage of the femoral condyle become damaged and may partially or completely detach, producing an unstable fragment or loose body. It commonly affects athletic adolescents and young adults and can cause mechanical knee symptoms.

Intra-articular osteochondral loose body.normalized_text: Intra-articular osteochondral loose body secondary to an osteochondral lesion
Intra-articular osteochondral loose body.description: A free fragment of cartilage and bone within the knee joint, often arising from osteochondritis dissecans or prior osteochondral trauma. Loose bodies can intermittently obstruct joint motion and provoke synovitis and effusion.

Meniscal tear, particularly a displaced.normalized_text: Meniscal tear, particularly a displaced bucket-handle tear
Meniscal tear, particularly a displaced.description: A tear of the knee meniscus that may become displaced into the joint, causing locking, recurrent swelling, and pain. It is common in athletes and may follow twisting injury, although symptoms can occur after older injuries.

diagnoses.name: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma

Primary pancreatic follicular dendritic.normalized_text: Primary pancreatic follicular dendritic cell sarcoma
Primary pancreatic follicular dendritic.description: A rare malignant neoplasm of follicular dendritic cells that can arise extranodally, including in the pancreas. It may form a pancreatic head mass and cause biliary obstruction; histology commonly shows spindle to ovoid cells in whorled/storiform patterns with admixed lymphocytes and immunoreactivity for follicular dendritic-cell markers such as CD21, CD23, and CD35.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, usually arising in the pancreatic head and producing extrahepatic biliary obstruction. CA19-9 may be markedly elevated, especially in the setting of obstructive jaundice.

Primary pancreatic lymphoma.description: An uncommon extranodal lymphoma centered in the pancreas, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It can mimic pancreatic carcinoma and can cause jaundice when located in the pancreatic head.

Distal extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of the distal common bile duct that produces progressive extrahepatic biliary obstruction and may appear as, or be difficult to distinguish from, a pancreatic head lesion.

Uremic tumoral calcinosis (secondary tum.normalized_text: Uremic tumoral calcinosis (secondary tumoral calcinosis due to chronic renal failure)
Uremic tumoral calcinosis (secondary tum.description: Periarticular or subcutaneous deposition of lobulated calcium-phosphate material, most often occurring in patients on long-term dialysis with hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Calcinosis cutis secondary to chronic ki.normalized_text: Calcinosis cutis secondary to chronic kidney disease
Calcinosis cutis secondary to chronic ki.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin or subcutaneous tissue, often related to abnormal calcium-phosphate metabolism in renal failure.

Calcific uremic arteriolopathy (calciphy.description: A severe dialysis-associated disorder involving calcification and thrombosis of small dermal and subcutaneous vessels, usually causing painful ischemic skin lesions and necrosis.

Myositis ossificans / heterotopic ossifi.description: Formation of mature bone within soft tissue, often after trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or prolonged immobilization.

Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.normalized_text: Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-depression type, Schatzker II)
Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-d.description: An intra-articular fracture of the lateral upper tibia involving a vertical split and depression of the lateral tibial plateau, typically caused by high-energy valgus or axial loading trauma.

Bicondylar tibial plateau fracture (Scha.description: A high-energy intra-articular fracture involving both medial and lateral tibial plateaus, often associated with substantial swelling and potential ligamentous or neurovascular injury.

Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury.normalized_text: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury with hemarthrosis
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury.description: A tear of the anterior cruciate ligament caused by pivoting, hyperextension, or high-energy knee trauma; it can produce immediate swelling from bleeding into the joint and difficulty bearing weight.

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

Rectal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (G.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells, usually composed of spindle cells and often associated with KIT or PDGFRA mutations. Rectal GISTs commonly present as submucosal rectal masses.

Rectal leiomyoma.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that usually appears as a well-circumscribed submucosal mass composed of bland spindle cells. Larger lesions may cause obstructive symptoms.

Rectal leiomyosarcoma.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum that may form a large intramural or submucosal mass and produce obstructive bowel symptoms. Histology typically shows atypia, increased mitotic activity, and/or necrosis.

Rectal schwannoma.description: A rare mesenchymal tumor derived from peripheral nerve sheath cells. It can occur as a slow-growing, well-circumscribed submucosal colorectal mass and may cause pain or obstructive symptoms when large.

SHORT syndrome (PIK3R1-related disorder).description: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic PIK3R1 variants, characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, postnatal short stature, partial lipodystrophy, progeroid facial appearance, delayed dentition, and insulin-resistance risk.

Silver-Russell syndrome.description: A growth-restriction syndrome usually caused by abnormalities involving chromosome 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7, featuring prenatal and postnatal growth failure, triangular facies, prominent forehead, and feeding difficulties.

Neonatal progeroid syndrome (Wiedemann-R.description: A rare congenital progeroid disorder characterized by severe prenatal and postnatal growth failure, loss of subcutaneous fat, thin aged-appearing skin, sparse hair, and characteristic craniofacial features; it is typically associated with biallelic POLR3A variants.

Congenital generalized lipodystrophy (Be.description: A genetic lipodystrophy syndrome with near-complete absence of adipose tissue from birth or infancy, prominent musculature, metabolic complications including insulin resistance and hypertriglyceridemia, and accelerated growth in many patients.

Mandibuloacral dysplasia with lipodystro.description: A progeroid lipodystrophy disorder, most often caused by LMNA or ZMPSTE24 variants, characterized by growth retardation, craniofacial abnormalities including mandibular hypoplasia, skin changes, lipodystrophy, and skeletal abnormalities such as clavicular and acro-osteolysis changes.

Good syndrome (thymoma-associated immuno.description: A rare combined immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia, impaired B-cell and T-cell function, recurrent bacterial respiratory infections, and opportunistic infections.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A primary antibody deficiency disorder causing reduced immunoglobulin function, poor vaccine responses, recurrent bacterial respiratory infections, bronchiectasis, and sometimes gastrointestinal disease.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring in patients with impaired cellular immunity, typically causing fever, nonproductive cough, progressive dyspnea, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection that can cause constitutional symptoms, chronic cough, and cavitary pulmonary lesions, particularly in people from regions where tuberculosis is endemic or in immunocompromised patients.

Chronic suppurative airway disease with.normalized_text: Chronic suppurative airway disease with bronchiectasis secondary to immunodeficiency
Chronic suppurative airway disease with.description: Permanent bronchial dilation and airway damage caused by recurrent infections, resulting in chronic cough, recurrent bacterial exacerbations, dyspnea, fatigue, and persistent inflammatory lung abnormalities.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic ne.description: A benign, self-limited lymphadenitis usually affecting young adults, characterized by cervical lymphadenopathy and histology showing patchy necrosis, karyorrhectic debris, histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and absence of neutrophils.

Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.normalized_text: Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy)
Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytos.description: A non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder that commonly presents with painless bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and may involve mediastinal or extranodal sites; lymph nodes show abundant S100-positive histiocytes with emperipolesis.

Hodgkin lymphoma.description: A lymphoid malignancy that often affects young adults and commonly presents with painless cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; diagnosis requires identification of Reed-Sternberg cells in an appropriate inflammatory background.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis.description: Mycobacterial infection of lymph nodes, usually causing chronic cervical lymphadenopathy with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis; mediastinal lymphadenopathy may also occur.

Fulminant viral myocarditis.description: Acute inflammation of the heart muscle, often following a viral respiratory infection, causing severe ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and potentially sudden cardiac arrest.

Peripartum cardiomyopathy.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure occurring during the last month of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, characterized by reduced left-ventricular function, pulmonary congestion, edema, and arrhythmias.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by thrombus, commonly arising from deep venous thrombosis. Pregnancy, obesity, and reduced venous flow are major risk factors; massive embolism can cause shock and cardiac arrest.

Acute coronary syndrome due to pregnancy.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronary artery dissection
Acute coronary syndrome due to pregnancy.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma of a coronary artery that may occur during late pregnancy or the postpartum period, causing myocardial ischemia, infarction, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac arrest.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (H.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular malformation disorder characterized by recurrent spontaneous epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and arteriovenous malformations in organs such as the liver, lungs, brain, and gastrointestinal tract.

Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.normalized_text: Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due to hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hepatic arteriovenous malformations due.description: Abnormal direct connections between hepatic arteries, portal veins, and/or hepatic veins. In HHT, these can produce enlarged tortuous hepatic vessels, arterioportal shunting, portal hypertension, high-output cardiac failure, and less commonly hepatic encephalopathy.

Hepatic encephalopathy from portosystemi.normalized_text: Hepatic encephalopathy from portosystemic shunting associated with hepatic vascular malformations
Hepatic encephalopathy from portosystemi.description: A neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by impaired detoxification of gut-derived substances, often including ammonia, when blood bypasses functional hepatic metabolism through portosystemic shunts. Hepatic vascular malformations can create such shunting even without classic cirrhosis.

Maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (ur.description: A common pediatric form of mastocytosis caused by increased mast cells in the skin, producing tan, brown, or orange macules that may become red, swollen, or itchy after rubbing (Darier sign).

Juvenile xanthogranuloma.description: A benign non-Langerhans-cell histiocytic disorder of infancy and childhood that usually causes solitary or multiple yellow, orange, red-brown papules or nodules.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis, cutaneous.description: A clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells that can affect the skin alone or occur as part of multisystem disease; skin lesions may be red-brown papules, crusted lesions, or seborrheic dermatitis-like eruptions.

Café-au-lait macules.description: Benign, sharply bordered hyperpigmented macules caused by increased melanin; multiple lesions can occur in neurocutaneous syndromes such as neurofibromatosis type 1.

Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation.description: Residual darkening of the skin after inflammation, trauma, insect bites, dermatitis, or other skin injury; pigmentation may persist after the original eruption resolves.

Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (Wil.description: Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, usually after marked loss of retroperitoneal fat from severe weight loss. The CT measurements show a markedly narrowed aortomesenteric angle and distance with proximal gastric/duodenal dilatation, supporting this diagnosis.

Anorexia nervosa or severe restrictive e.normalized_text: Anorexia nervosa or severe restrictive eating disorder
Anorexia nervosa or severe restrictive e.description: A psychiatric eating disorder characterized by inadequate caloric intake, low body weight, and endocrine consequences of malnutrition. Severe weight loss can precipitate superior mesenteric artery syndrome by reducing the mesenteric fat cushion.

Mechanical proximal small-bowel obstruct.description: Partial or complete blockage of the upper small bowel causing retained gastric contents, postprandial vomiting, and reduced bowel movements. In this case, the likely mechanical cause is superior mesenteric artery compression of the duodenum.

Gastrocolic fistula involving the Roux-e.normalized_text: Gastrocolic fistula involving the Roux-en-Y gastric pouch and transverse colon
Gastrocolic fistula involving the Roux-e.description: An abnormal communication between the gastric pouch and colon, allowing ingested food to pass directly into the colon. This is a rare late complication of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and can result from marginal ulceration, chronic inflammation, or surgical complications. The contrast study demonstrates a fistulous tract from the gastric pouch to the transverse/descending colon.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.normalized_text: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (S.description: Excessive bacterial colonization of the small intestine, often promoted by altered anatomy or intestinal stasis after bariatric surgery. It can cause malabsorption, diarrhea, gas, and nutritional deficiencies.

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.description: Insufficient pancreatic digestive enzyme secretion causing fat malabsorption, steatorrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. It can produce pale, floating, foul-smelling stools but does not explain the demonstrated gastric-colonic connection.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum (Hamman sy.description: Air leaks into the mediastinum, usually after increased intrathoracic pressure from coughing, wheezing, or an asthma exacerbation. It commonly causes acute pleuritic chest pain with pain radiating to the neck.

Acute asthma exacerbation.description: An episode of worsening bronchospasm and airway inflammation causing wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, often precipitated by poor adherence to inhaled therapy or respiratory infection.

Viral bronchitis or lower respiratory tr.normalized_text: Viral bronchitis or lower respiratory tract infection
Viral bronchitis or lower respiratory tr.description: Inflammation of the bronchi, usually viral, causing cough, sputum production, wheeze, and sometimes triggering an asthma exacerbation.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial blood flow by a thrombus, typically causing sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and occasionally cough.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, often presenting with sudden unilateral pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. It can occur in patients with underlying lung disease, including asthma.

Pellagra (niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency).description: A nutritional deficiency syndrome caused by inadequate niacin or tryptophan intake, classically producing photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhea, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and peripheral neuropathy. The images are suggestive of pellagrous dermatitis, including a Casal necklace-like rash on the neck and symmetric acral dermatitis.

Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.normalized_text: Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobulinemia with peripheral neuropathy
Hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobuli.description: An immune-complex vasculitic disorder associated with chronic hepatitis C infection that can cause painful distal sensory neuropathy, purpura, arthralgia, renal disease, and systemic symptoms.

Nutritional peripheral neuropathy due to.normalized_text: Nutritional peripheral neuropathy due to thiamine deficiency (dry beriberi)
Nutritional peripheral neuropathy due to.description: Thiamine deficiency, often related to poor nutrition, can cause a painful symmetric distal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, gait impairment, weakness, and reduced reflexes.

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency-relat.description: Vitamin B6 deficiency can occur with malnutrition and may cause a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy with distal numbness, burning pain, and paresthesias; dermatitis and mucosal changes can also occur.

Heroin-associated toxic or nutritional l.normalized_text: Heroin-associated toxic or nutritional length-dependent peripheral neuropathy
Heroin-associated toxic or nutritional l.description: Chronic heroin use may be associated with peripheral neuropathy through toxic exposure, adulterants, repeated hypoxic injury, infections, or severe nutritional deficiency. It commonly presents with distal symmetric sensory complaints.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA, Bruton.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked BTK gene, resulting in failure of B-cell maturation, markedly reduced immunoglobulins, and susceptibility to recurrent bacterial respiratory infections after maternal antibodies decline.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).description: A group of severe inherited immunodeficiencies characterized by profound T-cell dysfunction, often with impaired B-cell and/or natural killer-cell function, leading to severe and recurrent infections in infancy.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID).description: A predominantly antibody-deficiency disorder causing low immunoglobulin levels, impaired antibody production, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections; it usually presents later in childhood or adulthood.

Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infan.description: A temporary delay in maturation of immunoglobulin production during infancy that may cause low IgG and recurrent respiratory infections but generally improves spontaneously.

Penile fracture (rupture of the right co.normalized_text: Penile fracture (rupture of the right corpus cavernosum/tunica albuginea)
Penile fracture (rupture of the right co.description: Acute tear of the tunica albuginea surrounding an erect corpus cavernosum, usually during sexual intercourse. The MRI demonstrates a defect in the right corpus cavernosum tunica albuginea near the penile base with associated soft-tissue hematoma extending into the scrotum.

Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/pe.normalized_text: Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/perineal hematoma
Proximal penile fracture with scrotal/pe.description: A subtype of penile fracture in which a tear near the root of the penis allows blood to track into the perineum and scrotum, potentially producing marked scrotal bruising with relatively little visible penile shaft swelling.

Rupture of the superficial dorsal penile.normalized_text: Rupture of the superficial dorsal penile vein
Rupture of the superficial dorsal penile.description: Traumatic tearing of the superficial dorsal vein during intercourse can cause penile or scrotal bruising and swelling and may clinically resemble penile fracture, although the tunica albuginea remains intact.

Testicular rupture or traumatic testicul.normalized_text: Testicular rupture or traumatic testicular hematoma
Testicular rupture or traumatic testicul.description: Testicular trauma may produce acute scrotal pain, swelling, and hematoma, often after blunt trauma. It is an important emergency differential diagnosis in patients with an acute swollen bruised scrotum.

Muscle-eye-brain disease (MEB disease; P.description: An autosomal-recessive congenital muscular dystrophy caused by abnormal alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation. It combines severe hypotonia and muscle weakness with elevated CK, major developmental impairment, structural brain abnormalities, and ocular involvement.

Walker-Warburg syndrome.description: A severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy characterized by profound developmental delay, congenital muscle weakness, markedly abnormal brain development such as cobblestone lissencephaly and hydrocephalus, and eye abnormalities.

Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy.description: An alpha-dystroglycanopathy causing congenital muscular dystrophy with hypotonia, elevated CK, severe intellectual disability, brain malformations, and sometimes ocular abnormalities. Severity varies, with some affected children surviving into later childhood.

Urachal adenocarcinoma.description: A rare gland-forming malignancy arising from urachal remnants, usually located at the bladder dome or midline anterior pelvis and often presenting late as a lower abdominal or suprapubic mass.

Primary urinary bladder adenocarcinoma.description: An uncommon bladder cancer composed of malignant glandular epithelial cells, usually arising from the bladder mucosa and potentially forming an invasive pelvic mass.

Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic ex.normalized_text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic extension or metastasis
Colorectal adenocarcinoma with pelvic ex.description: A malignant glandular tumor of the colon or rectum that can present as a lower abdominal mass and may invade adjacent pelvic structures, including the bladder.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion, often intentional, that causes high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, increased osmolal gap early after ingestion, lactic-acidosis-like laboratory findings, and central nervous system depression.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion that produces an elevated osmolal gap followed by severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and neurologic depression; visual toxicity is a characteristic later finding.

Propylene glycol toxicity.description: Propylene glycol is a solvent in some medications, particularly intravenous sedatives and certain liquid formulations. Accumulation or overdose can cause somnolence, increased osmolal gap, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and lactic acidosis.

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis due.normalized_text: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis due to metformin overdose
Metformin-associated lactic acidosis due.description: Metformin overdose can cause profound lactic acidosis, altered mental status, and gastrointestinal symptoms, particularly after intentional ingestion or in the presence of renal impairment. An elevated osmolal gap is not usually a primary feature.

Isopropyl alcohol poisoning.description: Isopropyl alcohol ingestion causes central nervous system depression and an elevated osmolal gap, often with ketosis. Unlike other toxic alcohols, it generally does not cause severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

diagnoses.name: Juvenile granulosa-cell tumor
diagnoses.icd11_title: Juvenile granulosa cell tumour unknown behaviour of unspecified site

Ovarian yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus.normalized_text: Ovarian yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor)
Ovarian yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus.description: A highly malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor that typically occurs in children and adolescents and can grow rapidly, often producing a large unilateral pelvic mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. Histology commonly shows reticular/microcystic patterns, Schiller-Duval bodies, and hyaline globules; serum alpha-fetoprotein is usually markedly elevated.

Ovarian torsion associated with a large.normalized_text: Ovarian torsion associated with a large ovarian neoplasm
Ovarian torsion associated with a large.description: Twisting of the ovarian vascular pedicle causes venous congestion, edema, hemorrhage, infarction, and abdominal pain. Torsion frequently occurs in an enlarged ovary, including one enlarged by a benign or malignant ovarian tumor.

Ovarian dysgerminoma.description: A malignant ovarian germ-cell tumor composed of primitive germ cells, most often affecting adolescents and young women. It usually presents as a unilateral solid pelvic mass with abdominal pain or distension and may be associated with elevated lactate dehydrogenase.

Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.normalized_text: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ovary
Juvenile granulosa cell tumor of the ova.description: A sex cord-stromal ovarian tumor that occurs predominantly in children and adolescents. It may become large and can cause abdominal pain, distension, torsion, or hemorrhage; many tumors secrete estrogen and cause precocious puberty or abnormal uterine bleeding.

Ovarian immature teratoma.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor containing immature embryonal tissue, most commonly diagnosed in the first two decades of life. It may present with a rapidly enlarging unilateral adnexal mass, abdominal pain, torsion, rupture, or abdominal distension.

diagnoses.name: X-linked alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome
diagnoses.icd11_title: X-linked alpha thalassaemia with mental retardation

Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual.normalized_text: Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual disability syndrome (ATR-X syndrome)
Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual.description: A rare X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATRX. It is characterized by severe developmental delay/intellectual disability, infantile hypotonia, distinctive facial appearance, skeletal or digital abnormalities, seizures in some patients, and alpha-thalassemia with hemoglobin H inclusions on supravital blood smear.

ATR-16 syndrome (alpha-thalassemia intel.normalized_text: ATR-16 syndrome (alpha-thalassemia intellectual disability syndrome due to 16p13.3 deletion)
ATR-16 syndrome (alpha-thalassemia intel.description: A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome involving the alpha-globin gene cluster on chromosome 16p13.3. It causes alpha-thalassemia, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, and variable craniofacial dysmorphism.

Hemoglobin H disease (alpha-thalassemia.normalized_text: Hemoglobin H disease (alpha-thalassemia with three affected alpha-globin genes)
Hemoglobin H disease (alpha-thalassemia.description: A form of alpha-thalassemia caused by loss or inactivation of three alpha-globin genes. It produces excess beta-globin tetramers (hemoglobin H), which can appear as multiple punctate inclusions in red cells with supravital staining, often called golf-ball inclusions.

Smith-Magenis syndrome.description: A neurodevelopmental disorder usually caused by a deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 or pathogenic variants in RAI1. It features developmental delay, hypotonia, distinctive facial features, behavioral dysregulation, repetitive behaviors, and self-injurious behavior.

Pyogenic iliopsoas abscess.description: A bacterial infection causing pus collection within the iliopsoas muscle, often presenting with fever, back or flank pain, and marked inflammatory laboratory abnormalities. CT appearance is compatible with inflammatory enlargement/collection involving the left psoas region.

Pyogenic spondylodiscitis with secondary.normalized_text: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis with secondary psoas abscess
Pyogenic spondylodiscitis with secondary.description: Bacterial infection of an intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral endplates that can extend into the psoas muscle and form an abscess. Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause.

Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with me.normalized_text: Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with metastatic infection
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with me.description: Bloodstream infection with Staphylococcus aureus can seed distant sites, causing vertebral osteomyelitis, psoas abscess, septic thrombophlebitis, pneumonia, or other deep abscesses.

Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis or iliac.normalized_text: Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis or iliac vein thrombosis secondary to psoas infection
Septic pelvic thrombophlebitis or iliac.description: Inflammation and thrombosis of pelvic or iliac veins can occur adjacent to an iliopsoas abscess or other deep pelvic infection. It may cause bilateral lower-extremity edema and persistent fever.

Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.normalized_text: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disease) with psoas abscess
Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disea.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine can cause chronic back pain, constitutional symptoms, vertebral destruction, and cold psoas abscesses. It is generally more indolent than pyogenic infection.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema.description: Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema that can occur after rapid drainage of a large pleural effusion or pneumothorax, causing edema in the re-expanded lung.

Hepatic hydrothorax.description: A typically right-sided transudative pleural effusion caused by passage of ascitic fluid through diaphragmatic defects in patients with advanced cirrhosis.

Aspiration pneumonitis.description: Acute chemical lung injury caused by aspiration of gastric or oropharyngeal contents, often producing cough, hypoxemia, and dependent pulmonary infiltrates.
