Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.description: Pulmonary fluid accumulation due to elevated cardiac filling pressures, usually causing dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia, and bilateral perihilar or diffuse infiltrates.

Pneumonia.description: Infection of the lung parenchyma that can cause cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, crackles, and focal or multifocal pulmonary consolidation.

Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia invo.normalized_text: Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia involving the renal and right iliac arteries
Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia invo.description: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disease, most often affecting middle-aged women. It can produce a characteristic alternating stenosis and dilation ('string-of-beads') appearance and may involve renal, carotid, and less commonly iliac arteries.

External iliac artery endofibrosis.description: External iliac artery endofibrosis is a nonatherosclerotic narrowing of the external iliac artery, classically occurring in highly active endurance athletes. It causes exercise-induced buttock, hip, or thigh claudication with normal or near-normal resting pulses and ABI.

Atherosclerotic aortoiliac peripheral ar.description: Atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease can cause stenosis of the aortoiliac arteries, producing buttock or thigh claudication that is reproducibly triggered by exertion and relieved by rest.

Torsades de pointes.description: A form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QT-interval prolongation, often caused by QT-prolonging medications such as sotalol. It can cause transient episodes of hemodynamic instability and may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation.

Acquired long QT syndrome due to sotalol.normalized_text: Acquired long QT syndrome due to sotalol
Acquired long QT syndrome due to sotalol.description: QT-interval prolongation caused by medication exposure, particularly class III antiarrhythmic drugs such as sotalol. Acquired long QT syndrome predisposes to torsades de pointes and syncope.

Drug-induced proarrhythmia from combined.normalized_text: Drug-induced proarrhythmia from combined antiarrhythmic therapy
Drug-induced proarrhythmia from combined.description: A clinically significant new or worsened arrhythmia caused by antiarrhythmic medication. Sotalol can prolong repolarization and provoke polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; concomitant verapamil may contribute to bradycardia or conduction effects that increase susceptibility to QT-related arrhythmia.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.description: A rapid ventricular rhythm with changing QRS morphology. When associated with prolonged QT interval it is termed torsades de pointes; it commonly presents with palpitations, presyncope, syncope, or sudden cardiac arrest.

Sarcoidosis (acute sarcoid arthritis wit.normalized_text: Sarcoidosis (acute sarcoid arthritis with cutaneous sarcoidosis)
Sarcoidosis (acute sarcoid arthritis wit.description: A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving intrathoracic lymph nodes, lungs, skin, joints, liver, and lymph nodes. Acute presentations can include fever, erythematous skin lesions, and inflammatory arthritis.

Tuberculosis with Poncet disease (tuberc.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with Poncet disease (tuberculosis-associated reactive polyarthritis)
Tuberculosis with Poncet disease (tuberc.description: Poncet disease is a sterile reactive polyarthritis occurring in association with active tuberculosis elsewhere in the body. Tuberculosis may also produce lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, skin lesions, and hilar or mediastinal lymph node enlargement.

Lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma.description: Hodgkin lymphoma can cause prolonged fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, elevated inflammatory markers, and mediastinal or hilar lymph node enlargement. Paraneoplastic inflammatory manifestations, including arthritis and skin eruptions, can occur but are uncommon.

Disseminated fungal infection, such as h.normalized_text: Disseminated fungal infection, such as histoplasmosis
Disseminated fungal infection, such as h.description: Disseminated histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection that can involve lymph nodes, liver, lungs, skin, and bone marrow. It may produce fever, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, inflammatory markers, and granulomatous histology.

Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis with r.normalized_text: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nodules
Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis with r.description: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune arthritis that usually affects small joints symmetrically but can occasionally present atypically. Rheumatoid nodules are firm subcutaneous lesions with palisading granulomatous inflammation and central fibrinoid necrosis.

Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of th.normalized_text: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the distal radial epiphysis, likely treatment-associated
Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of th.description: Ischemic death of bone marrow and trabecular bone caused by impaired blood supply. The MRI appearance of a subchondral/epiphyseal low-signal band in the distal radius is concerning for osteonecrosis. Antineoplastic therapy, including antiangiogenic agents, can rarely contribute even without corticosteroid exposure.

Stress injury or insufficiency fracture.normalized_text: Stress injury or insufficiency fracture of the distal radius
Stress injury or insufficiency fracture.description: A stress or insufficiency fracture is a small fracture caused by repetitive loading or weakened bone rather than a major traumatic event. It can cause focal pain and may appear as a linear low-signal band on MRI.

Kienböck disease (osteonecrosis of the l.description: Kienböck disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate carpal bone, causing progressive dorsal wrist pain, stiffness, and impaired wrist motion. It is a consideration for dorsal wrist pain but is less consistent with an abnormality centered in the distal radius.

Menkes disease.description: An X-linked ATP7A-related disorder of copper transport causing systemic copper deficiency, low ceruloplasmin, neurodegeneration, characteristic sparse kinky hair (pili torti), connective-tissue abnormalities, and tortuous cerebral arteries.

Occipital horn syndrome.description: A milder allelic ATP7A-related copper transport disorder characterized primarily by connective-tissue abnormalities, bladder diverticula, hernias, joint laxity, and occipital bone exostoses; neurologic impairment is generally less severe than in classic Menkes disease.

Nutritional or acquired copper deficienc.description: Copper deficiency due to inadequate intake, malabsorption, excessive zinc exposure, or prolonged parenteral nutrition can cause low serum copper and ceruloplasmin, anemia, poor growth, hypotonia, and neurologic dysfunction.

Mitochondrial encephalopathy with stroke.normalized_text: Mitochondrial encephalopathy with stroke-like or ischemic brain lesions
Mitochondrial encephalopathy with stroke.description: Mitochondrial disorders can present in infancy with failure to thrive, hypotonia, developmental delay, recurrent illness, and multifocal brain lesions, although they do not usually cause profound copper deficiency or pili torti.

Adrenal oncocytoma.description: A rare, usually benign adrenal cortical tumor composed of large eosinophilic oncocytic cells. It is commonly nonfunctioning and discovered incidentally, but may enlarge substantially.

Adrenocortical adenoma.description: A common benign tumor of the adrenal cortex. Many adenomas are nonfunctioning and found incidentally, although some produce cortisol or aldosterone.

Adrenocortical carcinoma.description: A rare malignant tumor of the adrenal cortex that often presents as a large enlarging adrenal mass and may be hormonally functional or nonfunctioning.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-producing tumor of the adrenal medulla that may be discovered incidentally; some lesions are clinically silent or minimally functional.

Adrenal cavernous hemangioma.description: A rare benign vascular lesion of the adrenal gland that is often nonfunctioning, asymptomatic, and detected incidentally; it can enlarge and become heterogeneous because of hemorrhage, thrombosis, or calcification.

Linear morphea (linear scleroderma) of t.normalized_text: Linear morphea (linear scleroderma) of the forehead/scalp, "en coup de sabre"
Linear morphea (linear scleroderma) of t.description: A localized autoimmune sclerosing disorder causing a linear band of induration, atrophy, pigment change, and sometimes scarring alopecia on the forehead and scalp. The "en coup de sabre" subtype resembles a saber-cut depression and commonly affects the frontoparietal scalp.

Deep morphea (morphea profunda).description: A deeper variant of localized scleroderma involving the deep dermis, subcutaneous fat, fascia, and sometimes muscle, producing marked induration and tethering of the skin.

Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus.description: A form of cutaneous lupus in which inflammation of subcutaneous fat causes firm plaques followed by lipoatrophy and sometimes scarring alopecia when the scalp is involved.

Discoid lupus erythematosus.description: A chronic cutaneous lupus variant that produces well-demarcated inflammatory plaques with scale, dyspigmentation, scarring, and permanent alopecia on the scalp.

Lichen planopilaris.description: A lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia in which inflammation around hair follicles causes progressive permanent scalp hair loss, often with perifollicular erythema and scale.

ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.normalized_text: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis (mesenteric vasculitis)
ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosu.description: Systemic lupus erythematosus can rarely occur despite repeatedly negative ANA testing. Immune-complex vasculitis of mesenteric vessels may cause bowel-wall edema, intestinal pseudo-obstruction or ileus, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and CT features such as bowel-wall thickening/target appearance and mesenteric vascular engorgement.

Lupus mesenteric vasculitis / lupus ente.description: A gastrointestinal manifestation of active SLE caused by inflammation of small mesenteric vessels, producing bowel ischemia, submucosal edema, ascites, bowel dilation, and potentially perforation if untreated.

Behçet disease with gastrointestinal vas.description: Behçet disease is a multisystem inflammatory vasculitis classically characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, eye inflammation, skin lesions, and sometimes gastrointestinal ulceration or vascular involvement causing abdominal pain.

Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic medium-vessel vasculitis
Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic.description: Medium-vessel vasculitides can involve mesenteric arteries and cause acute abdominal pain, bowel ischemia, vomiting, and renal vascular abnormalities. Polyarteritis nodosa generally does not cause glomerulonephritis.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (.description: A nonatherosclerotic tear or intramural hematoma within a coronary artery wall that narrows the true lumen and causes acute coronary syndrome. The angiogram is consistent with dissection involving the left anterior descending coronary artery.

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) with assoc.description: A noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic arterial disease causing stenosis, aneurysm, dissection, or a characteristic beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries. It is strongly associated with SCAD; the renal artery imaging appears consistent with multifocal FMD.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) secondary to SCAD
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Myocardial infarction without persistent ST-segment elevation, caused here by reduced coronary blood flow from spontaneous coronary artery dissection rather than plaque rupture.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS).description: A heritable connective-tissue disorder, usually caused by pathogenic COL3A1 variants, characterized by arterial dissection or rupture, organ fragility, and pregnancy-related complications. It is an important consideration in patients with spontaneous arterial dissections and a relevant family history.

Atherosclerotic acute coronary syndrome.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by atherosclerotic plaque rupture or erosion with coronary thrombosis. This is a common cause of acute chest pain but is less favored than SCAD because of the angiographic appearance and absence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

Congenital duodenal stenosis or duodenal.normalized_text: Congenital duodenal stenosis or duodenal web
Congenital duodenal stenosis or duodenal.description: Partial congenital obstruction of the duodenum caused by narrowing or an intraluminal mucosal web. Unlike complete duodenal atresia, it may present later with chronic feeding intolerance and poor growth.

Intestinal malrotation with intermittent.normalized_text: Intestinal malrotation with intermittent midgut volvulus
Intestinal malrotation with intermittent.description: Abnormal embryologic positioning of the bowel that can predispose to twisting of the mesentery and intermittent or acute obstruction. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study is commonly performed to evaluate this condition.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.description: Progressive hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction, typically in young male infants between 2 and 8 weeks of age.

Annular pancreas causing partial duodena.normalized_text: Annular pancreas causing partial duodenal obstruction
Annular pancreas causing partial duodena.description: A congenital pancreatic anomaly in which pancreatic tissue encircles the duodenum, producing variable narrowing and delayed gastric emptying. Partial obstruction may present with chronic feeding intolerance and poor weight gain.

Dermatomyositis with prominent facial an.normalized_text: Dermatomyositis with prominent facial and upper-airway edema
Dermatomyositis with prominent facial an.description: An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness, elevated muscle enzymes, characteristic cutaneous findings, and possible dysphagia from pharyngeal muscle involvement. Severe periorbital, facial, subcutaneous, and pharyngeal edema can rarely be a presenting manifestation.

Polymyositis.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing symmetric proximal muscle weakness, muscle pain, elevated CK, and possible dysphagia due to involvement of bulbar and pharyngeal muscles. Unlike dermatomyositis, it does not produce characteristic skin findings.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.description: A severe autoimmune myopathy characterized by marked CK elevation and rapidly progressive proximal weakness. It may be associated with statin exposure, anti-HMGCR antibodies, anti-SRP antibodies, malignancy, or other autoimmune disease.

Bradykinin-mediated angioedema, includin.normalized_text: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema, including ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema
Bradykinin-mediated angioedema, includin.description: Angioedema is localized swelling of subcutaneous and submucosal tissues, often involving the lips, tongue, face, and upper airway. Bradykinin-mediated forms typically lack urticaria and pruritus and can be associated with ACE inhibitor use.

Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phen.normalized_text: Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine (PPD) in black henna tattoo
Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phen.description: A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction caused by PPD, a common additive in black henna tattoos. It often produces an intensely itchy, eczematous or blistering rash precisely following the tattoo pattern several days after exposure.

Impetiginized allergic contact dermatiti.description: Allergic contact dermatitis complicated by superficial bacterial infection, usually Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes. Damaged, scratched eczematous skin can develop honey-colored or golden crusts and drainage.

Bullous impetigo.description: A superficial Staphylococcus aureus skin infection characterized by fragile blisters, erosions, yellow drainage, and crusting. It may occur secondarily on disrupted skin such as dermatitis or a tattoo reaction.

Irritant contact dermatitis from henna t.normalized_text: Irritant contact dermatitis from henna tattoo chemicals
Irritant contact dermatitis from henna t.description: An inflammatory skin reaction caused by direct chemical injury from tattoo ingredients or solvents. It can cause redness, burning, blistering, and weeping at sites of exposure, though it usually occurs sooner than allergic dermatitis.

Chronic tophaceous gout.description: Advanced gout caused by longstanding deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and soft tissues, producing large tophi, erosive arthritis, and joint deformity.

Rheumatoid arthritis with rheumatoid nod.description: A chronic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis that can cause symmetric hand deformities and firm subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, usually over pressure points.

Calcinosis cutis / tumoral calcinosis.description: Deposition of calcium salts in skin and periarticular soft tissues, causing firm calcified nodules near large joints and sometimes restricting joint movement.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.normalized_text: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular scle.description: A subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells in an inflammatory background, often with collagen fibrosis and frequent mediastinal involvement in young adults. Tumor cells are typically CD15-positive, CD30-positive, and CD45-negative.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that commonly arises as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass in young adults and can cause dyspnea and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. It usually expresses B-cell markers such as CD20, PAX5, and CD45 rather than the classic Hodgkin immunophenotype.

Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoma with overlapping clinical, morphologic, and immunophenotypic features of classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma. It often presents with a mediastinal mass in young adults.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma.description: A CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma that can present with systemic symptoms and lymphadenopathy. Depending on subtype, it may express ALK and usually retains CD45 and expresses T-cell-associated markers.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP/PC.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia in people with advanced HIV infection, typically causing subacute hypoxemic respiratory illness with bilateral diffuse or perihilar interstitial/ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lungs, which is more frequent in people with HIV and may produce atypical diffuse, lower-zone, or miliary radiographic infiltrates in immunosuppressed patients.

Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis.description: An opportunistic viral pneumonia occurring mainly in severely immunocompromised patients with HIV, causing dyspnea, cough, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral interstitial or ground-glass infiltrates.

HIV-associated bacterial pneumonia.description: Acute bacterial infection of the lung, commonly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae or other bacteria, which occurs more often and may be more severe in people with HIV.

HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma with.normalized_text: HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma with pulmonary involvement
HIV-associated non-Hodgkin lymphoma with.description: Aggressive lymphoma can occur in advanced HIV infection and may involve the lungs, producing diffuse infiltrates, nodules, lymphadenopathy, cough, and dyspnea.

Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis fr.normalized_text: Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis from bronchogenic carcinoma
Pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis fr.description: Tumour spread through pulmonary lymphatic vessels, commonly from lung adenocarcinoma or another malignancy, causing interlobular septal thickening and asymmetric interstitial lung abnormalities.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial vessels by thrombus, typically causing acute or subacute breathlessness, chest pain, syncope, and an elevated D-dimer level. Pulmonary embolism may occasionally be associated with unilateral pulmonary oedema or pleural effusion.

Unilateral pulmonary oedema due to pulmo.normalized_text: Unilateral pulmonary oedema due to pulmonary venous obstruction
Unilateral pulmonary oedema due to pulmo.description: Pulmonary oedema confined predominantly to one lung can occur when pulmonary venous drainage is obstructed, for example by a hilar malignancy, pulmonary vein thrombosis, or severe asymmetric mitral regurgitation. CT may show smooth septal thickening, ground-glass opacity, and pleural effusion.

Primary lung cancer with right hilar/med.normalized_text: Primary lung cancer with right hilar/mediastinal vascular or lymphatic involvement
Primary lung cancer with right hilar/med.description: A central bronchogenic malignancy may cause progressive dyspnoea and chest discomfort by obstructing bronchi, pulmonary vessels, or lymphatic drainage. Smoking is a major risk factor, and secondary lymphatic congestion can produce unilateral interstitial abnormalities and pleural fluid.

Atypical pneumonia or pneumonitis.description: Infectious or inflammatory pneumonitis can cause breathlessness and unilateral interstitial or ground-glass pulmonary opacities, sometimes with a small pleural effusion.

Right hemidiaphragm paralysis (phrenic n.description: Loss of right diaphragmatic motor function causing elevation of the right hemidiaphragm, reduced lung expansion, and basal compressive atelectasis. It can cause marked dyspnea and hypoxemia, particularly in people with obesity or underlying lung disease.

Diaphragmatic eventration.description: A congenital or acquired abnormal elevation of an intact but thinned or weakened diaphragm. It may compress the adjacent lung and cause dyspnea, recurrent basal atelectasis, and reduced oxygenation.

Right lower-lobe and/or middle-lobe comp.normalized_text: Right lower-lobe and/or middle-lobe compressive atelectasis secondary to elevated right hemidiaphragm
Right lower-lobe and/or middle-lobe comp.description: Partial collapse of lung tissue caused by external compression and reduced ventilation from a markedly elevated diaphragm. Atelectasis can produce basal reduced breath sounds, aegophony, dyspnea, and impaired oxygenation.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (C.description: An acute worsening of airflow limitation in a smoker, often presenting with dyspnea, wheeze, and hypoxemia. COPD may coexist with diaphragmatic dysfunction and make respiratory compromise more severe.

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.normalized_text: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the maxilla/oral cavity
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that may arise at extranodal sites such as the maxilla, gingiva, palate, or extraction sockets. It can present as a rapidly enlarging oral mass with bone destruction and delayed healing after dental extraction.

Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse larg.normalized_text: Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse larg.description: A subtype of aggressive B-cell lymphoma often occurring in older adults or people with impaired immunity. It can involve extranodal sites, including the oral cavity, and may present as a destructive mass or nonhealing extraction wound.

Plasmablastic lymphoma.description: A highly aggressive lymphoma with plasmablastic cell morphology, most often affecting the oral cavity in immunocompromised individuals. It can cause rapidly enlarging oral soft-tissue masses, ulceration, bone involvement, and delayed healing after extraction.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.normalized_text: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw with secondary infection
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Jawbone necrosis associated with antiresorptive or antiangiogenic cancer therapies, often triggered by tooth extraction. It commonly presents with nonhealing extraction wounds, exposed necrotic bone, swelling, pain, and secondary inflammation or infection.

Odontogenic infection or maxillary osteo.description: A bacterial infection of the maxillary alveolar bone and surrounding tissues, often following dental extraction. It may produce swelling, pain, delayed socket healing, inflammatory laboratory abnormalities, and bone destruction.

Tinea corporis and tinea cruris (steroid.normalized_text: Tinea corporis and tinea cruris (steroid-modified tinea incognito)
Tinea corporis and tinea cruris (steroid.description: A dermatophyte fungal infection of the body and groin producing annular, enlarging, scaly plaques. Prior potent topical corticosteroid use can suppress classic scale and inflammation while allowing extensive spread, termed tinea incognito.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory eruption characterized by slowly expanding annular plaques, often with trailing scale inside the advancing border. It may be triggered by infections, medications, or other systemic factors.

Annular psoriasis.description: A variant of psoriasis in which red, scaly plaques develop ring-like or polycyclic borders. It may involve the groin and other body sites but usually has a chronic relapsing course.

Nummular dermatitis.description: An eczematous dermatitis causing pruritic coin-shaped erythematous, scaly plaques, commonly on the limbs. Lesions can become widespread but are usually not truly annular with an active raised edge.

Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.normalized_text: Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (linitis plastica, including signet-ring cell carcinoma)
Diffuse-type gastric adenocarcinoma (lin.description: An infiltrative gastric cancer that spreads diffusely through the stomach wall, often sparing the mucosal surface early and causing rigid wall thickening, gastric outlet obstruction, and marked gastric dilatation.

Gastric outlet obstruction from pancreat.normalized_text: Gastric outlet obstruction from pancreatic adenocarcinoma
Gastric outlet obstruction from pancreat.description: Cancer of the pancreatic head or adjacent pancreas can externally compress or invade the duodenum or distal stomach, producing progressive gastric outlet obstruction.

Peptic-ulcer-related benign pyloric or d.normalized_text: Peptic-ulcer-related benign pyloric or duodenal stricture
Peptic-ulcer-related benign pyloric or d.description: Chronic acid-peptic ulcer disease can scar and narrow the pylorus or proximal duodenum, causing mechanical gastric outlet obstruction.

Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (.description: A mesenchymal tumor arising from the gastric wall that may grow intramurally or exophytically and cause obstruction when located near the antrum or pylorus.

Gastric lymphoma.description: Primary gastric lymphoma can infiltrate and thicken the gastric wall, occasionally causing outlet obstruction and systemic nutritional decline.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.description: An X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the WAS gene, classically characterized by thrombocytopenia with bleeding manifestations, eczema, and immune dysfunction. In neonates, bruising and petechiae from thrombocytopenia may be the first finding; the maternal carrier pattern in the sequencing image supports an X-linked inherited disorder.

X-linked thrombocytopenia.description: A milder phenotypic form of WAS gene-related disease characterized predominantly by congenital thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding, often without the severe eczema and immunodeficiency of classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia.description: A condition in which maternal antibodies against fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal or neonatal platelets, causing severe thrombocytopenia, petechiae, bruising, and risk of intracranial hemorrhage in an otherwise well newborn.

Inherited thrombocytopenia due to a plat.normalized_text: Inherited thrombocytopenia due to a platelet-production or platelet-function disorder
Inherited thrombocytopenia due to a plat.description: Inherited platelet disorders can cause congenital or neonatal thrombocytopenia and impaired primary hemostasis, producing petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, and disproportionate bleeding after minor trauma or injections.

Hemophilia A or hemophilia B.description: X-linked deficiencies of factor VIII or factor IX that cause impaired secondary coagulation and bleeding in male infants, particularly after trauma, procedures, or injections. Severe disease may present in the neonatal period.

Acute subdural hematoma due to headbangi.normalized_text: Acute subdural hematoma due to headbanging
Acute subdural hematoma due to headbangi.description: Bleeding between the dura mater and arachnoid membrane, typically caused by tearing of bridging veins after acceleration-deceleration head movement. CT commonly shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection with mass effect.

Chronic or subacute subdural hematoma.description: A slowly accumulating subdural blood collection that may occur after minor or unrecognized trauma and can present primarily with headache, cognitive change, or focal neurological deficits weeks later.

Traumatic intracranial contusion.description: A focal bruise of brain tissue caused by traumatic acceleration-deceleration forces, most often involving the frontal or temporal lobes and potentially associated with headache and cerebral edema.

Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.normalized_text: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor (pPNET) of the omentum
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma / peripheral.description: A malignant small round-cell sarcoma occurring in soft tissue rather than bone. It commonly harbors an EWSR1 gene rearrangement and may show neural/neuroendocrine differentiation with synaptophysin and PGP9.5 positivity.

Desmoplastic small round cell tumor (DSR.description: An aggressive small round-cell sarcoma that usually arises in the peritoneal cavity and may present as an abdominal or omental mass. It often carries an EWSR1-WT1 fusion, although its typical immunophenotype includes desmin and cytokeratin expression rather than predominantly neural markers.

Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine car.description: A high-grade malignant epithelial tumor with neuroendocrine differentiation, often positive for synaptophysin and other neuroendocrine markers. It can arise in or metastasize to the abdomen and peritoneum.

Neuroblastoma or peripheral neuroblastic.description: A malignant tumor of primitive sympathetic nervous system cells that can express synaptophysin and other neural markers. It is predominantly a childhood malignancy and is uncommon as a primary omental tumor in adults.

Drug-induced hemophagocytic lymphohistio.normalized_text: Drug-induced hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) caused by dabrafenib plus trametinib
Drug-induced hemophagocytic lymphohistio.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells, often causing fever, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, hyperferritinemia, and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow. In this case it is temporally associated with initiation of BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy.

Pembrolizumab-associated immune-related.description: HLH can rarely occur as an immune-related adverse event from immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab, due to excessive immune activation. It may occur during therapy or, less commonly, after treatment exposure.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.normalized_text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) due to dabrafenib/trametinib
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and syst.description: DRESS is a severe delayed drug hypersensitivity reaction that can cause fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, hematologic abnormalities, and internal-organ involvement. BRAF/MEK inhibitors can cause significant drug eruptions and systemic inflammatory toxicity.

Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to pene.normalized_text: Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to penetrating sellar/pituitary injury
Traumatic panhypopituitarism due to pene.description: Loss of multiple anterior pituitary hormone functions following direct traumatic injury to the pituitary gland or hypothalamic-pituitary region. The imaging suggests a retained projectile in the sellar region, making direct pituitary destruction highly likely.

Traumatic pituitary stalk injury or hypo.normalized_text: Traumatic pituitary stalk injury or hypothalamic-pituitary disconnection
Traumatic pituitary stalk injury or hypo.description: Damage to the pituitary stalk or hypothalamus can interrupt hypothalamic releasing hormones and reduce anterior pituitary hormone secretion. In a complete stalk injury, prolactin is often elevated because dopamine inhibition is lost; however, direct pituitary damage can instead cause low prolactin.

Central adrenal insufficiency secondary.normalized_text: Central adrenal insufficiency secondary to traumatic ACTH deficiency
Central adrenal insufficiency secondary.description: Central adrenal insufficiency occurs when inadequate ACTH secretion from the pituitary or hypothalamus causes deficient cortisol production. It can be life-threatening during acute illness or trauma despite initially stable vital signs.

Central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism wi.normalized_text: Central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with delayed puberty
Central hypogonadotropic hypogonadism wi.description: Reduced hypothalamic GnRH or pituitary gonadotropin secretion leads to low LH/FSH and low testosterone, resulting in delayed or arrested pubertal development. In this case it is likely part of broader traumatic hypopituitarism.

Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing o.normalized_text: Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Congenital aqueductal stenosis causing o.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct blocks cerebrospinal fluid flow from the third to fourth ventricle, producing marked enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles with a relatively normal fourth ventricle. It may present in infancy with progressive macrocephaly and signs of raised intracranial pressure.

Obstructive hydrocephalus due to a tecta.normalized_text: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to a tectal glioma
Obstructive hydrocephalus due to a tecta.description: A low-grade tumor of the tectal plate can compress the cerebral aqueduct and cause progressive obstructive hydrocephalus. Children may initially present primarily with symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure rather than focal neurologic signs.

Hydrocephalus due to an intraventricular.normalized_text: Hydrocephalus due to an intraventricular cyst or aqueductal web
Hydrocephalus due to an intraventricular.description: A congenital membrane, web, or cyst near the cerebral aqueduct can intermittently or progressively obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow, leading to triventricular hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure.

Choroid plexus papilloma causing hydroce.description: A choroid plexus papilloma is a benign intraventricular tumor that can cause hydrocephalus through cerebrospinal fluid overproduction, obstruction, or both. It often presents in young children with macrocephaly and increased intracranial pressure.

Dandy-Walker malformation or other poste.normalized_text: Dandy-Walker malformation or other posterior fossa cerebrospinal fluid-flow malformation
Dandy-Walker malformation or other poste.description: Dandy-Walker spectrum disorders involve abnormal development of the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle and may lead to hydrocephalus, developmental delay, and progressive macrocephaly in infancy.

Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome).description: A cause of secondary hypertension due to inappropriate aldosterone activity, usually from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, producing sodium retention and suppression of renin.

Low-renin essential hypertension associa.normalized_text: Low-renin essential hypertension associated with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea
Low-renin essential hypertension associa.description: Primary hypertension can be associated with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea; these conditions increase sympathetic activity and may suppress renin through relative volume expansion.

Cushing syndrome.description: Cushing syndrome is chronic excess cortisol production, which can cause hypertension, obesity, fatigue, glucose intolerance, and characteristic physical changes.

Apparent mineralocorticoid excess or ano.normalized_text: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess or another low-renin mineralocorticoid hypertension syndrome
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess or ano.description: These disorders cause hypertension through mineralocorticoid receptor activation independent of aldosterone, leading to low renin and often low or normal aldosterone. Causes include inherited enzyme defects, licorice ingestion, or other mineralocorticoid-like states.

Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) w.normalized_text: Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) with coronary artery spasm
Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal angina) w.description: Transient constriction of an epicardial coronary artery causing myocardial ischemia, often with transient ST-segment elevation and potentially malignant ventricular arrhythmias or cardiac arrest.

Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.normalized_text: Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction due to coronary vasospasm
Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.description: Acute myocardial infarction caused by prolonged coronary vasospasm leading to sustained ischemia and myocardial necrosis, even in the absence of fixed obstructive coronary artery disease.

Sumatriptan-induced coronary vasospasm a.normalized_text: Sumatriptan-induced coronary vasospasm and myocardial ischemia
Sumatriptan-induced coronary vasospasm a.description: A medication-associated coronary vasospasm syndrome in which triptan-induced serotonergic vasoconstriction triggers myocardial ischemia, ST-segment elevation, infarction, or rarely cardiac arrest.

Myocardial infarction with non-obstructi.normalized_text: Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Myocardial infarction with non-obstructi.description: Myocardial infarction meeting biomarker and clinical criteria for acute ischemia without obstructive coronary artery disease on angiography; possible mechanisms include coronary vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, embolism, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and plaque disruption.

Sigmoid volvulus with acute large-bowel.normalized_text: Sigmoid volvulus with acute large-bowel obstruction
Sigmoid volvulus with acute large-bowel.description: Twisting of the sigmoid colon around its mesentery, causing a closed-loop large-bowel obstruction. It is strongly associated with chronic constipation, neurologic disease, and institutionalized or immobile patients. The imaging appearance is consistent with a markedly dilated, obstructed colon.

Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvi.description: Functional obstruction with massive colonic dilatation in the absence of a fixed mechanical blockage. It commonly occurs in patients with severe neurologic disease, immobility, metabolic illness, or medications affecting intestinal motility.

Stercoral colitis with fecal impaction.description: Inflammation and pressure injury of the colon caused by impacted stool, usually in patients with severe chronic constipation, neurologic impairment, dehydration, or limited mobility. It can progress to ischemia, ulceration, perforation, and sepsis.

Ischemic colitis or impending colonic is.normalized_text: Ischemic colitis or impending colonic ischemia secondary to obstructive megacolon
Ischemic colitis or impending colonic is.description: Compromised blood flow to the colon due to severe distension or a closed-loop obstruction, such as volvulus. This can cause bowel-wall ischemia, pneumatosis, necrosis, perforation, and systemic deterioration.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP).description: Opportunistic fungal pneumonia, usually in patients with impaired cellular immunity such as undiagnosed HIV infection, hematologic malignancy, or immunosuppressive therapy. CT commonly shows diffuse ground-glass opacities and may show small nodules; direct fluorescent staining of respiratory specimens can demonstrate characteristic cysts.

Disseminated cryptococcosis with cryptoc.normalized_text: Disseminated cryptococcosis with cryptococcal meningitis and pulmonary cryptococcosis
Disseminated cryptococcosis with cryptoc.description: Infection caused by Cryptococcus neoformans or Cryptococcus gattii, often affecting immunocompromised individuals. It may cause subacute pulmonary disease with nodules or infiltrates and can disseminate to the central nervous system, producing subacute meningitis with headache, fever, and neck stiffness.

Tuberculosis with pulmonary and tubercul.normalized_text: Tuberculosis with pulmonary and tuberculous meningitis involvement
Tuberculosis with pulmonary and tubercul.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause chronic cough, constitutional symptoms, pulmonary nodules or tree-in-bud opacities, and subacute meningitis. Healthcare exposure and travel may increase exposure risk.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: Legionella pneumophila causes an atypical pneumonia associated with fever, cough, dyspnea, headache, myalgias, and gastrointestinal or neurologic manifestations. Exposure to contaminated water systems, including those in healthcare facilities or hotels during travel, is a risk factor.

Disseminated histoplasmosis with central.normalized_text: Disseminated histoplasmosis with central nervous system involvement
Disseminated histoplasmosis with central.description: Histoplasma capsulatum infection is acquired by inhalation and can produce pulmonary nodules, diffuse infiltrates, constitutional symptoms, and, especially in immunocompromised patients, disseminated infection including chronic meningitis.

Renal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA).description: A kidney vascular injury pattern caused by endothelial damage and microvascular thrombosis, producing glomerular ischemia, arteriolar intimal thickening, and renal dysfunction. The biopsy appearance is compatible with TMA.

Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.normalized_text: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome)
Complement-mediated thrombotic microangi.description: A form of thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway. It may be kidney-predominant and can occur without diarrhea or severe hypertension.

Renal-limited thrombotic microangiopathy.description: A kidney-predominant form of thrombotic microangiopathy in which biopsy shows TMA lesions but systemic manifestations such as thrombocytopenia and overt hemolytic anemia may be absent or mild.

Malignant hypertension-associated thromb.description: Severe hypertension can damage renal arterioles and glomerular capillaries, causing a thrombotic microangiopathy pattern with renal failure, hematuria, proteinuria, and anemia.

Uterine arteriovenous malformation (uter.description: An abnormal high-flow connection between uterine arteries and veins, often acquired after pregnancy-related events such as miscarriage, curettage, or uterine trauma. It can cause sudden, recurrent, life-threatening uterine bleeding.

Retained products of conception.description: Persistence of placental or fetal tissue within the uterus after miscarriage or pregnancy termination, causing continued or delayed vaginal bleeding and sometimes infection.

Gestational trophoblastic disease (persi.normalized_text: Gestational trophoblastic disease (persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia)
Gestational trophoblastic disease (persi.description: Abnormal persistent proliferation of pregnancy-related trophoblastic tissue after a pregnancy event, including miscarriage; it may produce irregular or heavy uterine bleeding and can be highly vascular.

Submucosal uterine leiomyoma (fibroid).description: A benign smooth-muscle tumour of the uterus. Fibroids projecting into the uterine cavity commonly cause heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia.

Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infec.description: C. difficile infection is antibiotic-associated colitis caused by toxin-producing C. difficile, often presenting with watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Recurrence can occur weeks after apparent resolution of an initial episode.

Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome.description: Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome is a functional bowel disorder that can develop after an episode of infectious or antibiotic-associated diarrhea, causing persistent or recurrent abdominal discomfort with altered bowel habits.

Antibiotic-associated diarrhea.description: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea is diarrhea occurring during or shortly after antibiotic use due to disruption of the normal intestinal microbiota. It may be mild and noninfectious or may reflect C. difficile infection.

Clostridioides difficile colonization wi.normalized_text: Clostridioides difficile colonization with another cause of diarrhea
Clostridioides difficile colonization wi.description: C. difficile colonization refers to detection of C. difficile by PCR without active toxin-mediated disease. PCR can remain positive after prior infection or identify asymptomatic carriage, while diarrhea may be due to another condition such as post-infectious bowel dysfunction.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often occurring in advanced HIV/AIDS; it can involve the lungs, reticuloendothelial system, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, and bone marrow.

Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary pulmonary tuberculosis
Disseminated tuberculosis with miliary p.description: Hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, particularly likely in severe immunosuppression, producing diffuse tiny pulmonary nodules and potentially involving lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract.

Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex.description: Opportunistic disseminated infection caused by nontuberculous mycobacteria, usually occurring in patients with advanced AIDS and very low CD4 counts; it commonly causes constitutional, hematologic, lymph node, liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal manifestations.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia in advanced HIV/AIDS, classically causing subacute fever, dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral ground-glass pulmonary opacities.

AIDS-related non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: Aggressive B-cell lymphoma associated with advanced HIV infection that may involve lymph nodes, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and bone marrow, causing systemic symptoms and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) wi.normalized_text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) with cutaneous involvement
Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) wi.description: An aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1 infection, often occurring in people from HTLV-1-endemic regions. It may present with pruritic, polymorphic skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, blood involvement, hypercalcemia, and systemic organ disease.

Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymp.description: Mycosis fungoides is the most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and typically causes slowly progressive, pruritic patches, plaques, or tumors with epidermotropic atypical T lymphocytes on biopsy.

Secondary syphilis.description: Secondary syphilis is a disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection that can cause a generalized papulosquamous eruption, classically involving the palms and soles, along with generalized lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms.

Scabies.description: Scabies is an infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei that causes intense pruritus and papules, excoriations, burrows, or eczematous plaques, often affecting finger webs, wrists, axillae, genital areas, and sometimes palms and soles.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized histologically by myocardial inflammation, necrosis, and multinucleated giant cells. It commonly causes ventricular arrhythmias, conduction disease, heart failure, and sudden cardiac death.

Cardiac sarcoidosis.description: Granulomatous inflammation involving the myocardium that can produce ventricular arrhythmias, atrioventricular block, heart failure, and scar-related cardiomyopathy. Histology usually demonstrates noncaseating granulomas, sometimes with giant cells.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.description: An inherited myocardial disorder characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, fibrosis, exertional symptoms, and increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death.

Coronary artery disease with exertional.normalized_text: Coronary artery disease with exertional angina
Coronary artery disease with exertional.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries causes myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch, typically producing exertional chest pressure and dyspnea. It may also predispose to ventricular arrhythmias when ischemia or scar is present.

Postoperative pyoderma gangrenosum.description: A rare neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis causing rapidly progressive, painful ulceration after trauma or surgery (pathergy). Surgical debridement can worsen the wound.

Postpartum wound infection / cesarean su.normalized_text: Postpartum wound infection / cesarean surgical-site infection
Postpartum wound infection / cesarean su.description: A bacterial infection involving the cesarean incision, ranging from superficial cellulitis to deep incisional infection, often causing fever, leukocytosis, wound drainage, and delayed healing.

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of fascia and soft tissue that may occur after surgery and causes systemic toxicity, severe pain, tissue necrosis, and wound breakdown.

Chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infecti.description: An infection and inflammation of the amniotic fluid, placenta, membranes, or uterus, usually presenting during labor with maternal fever, leukocytosis, uterine tenderness, contractions, and fetal tachycardia.

Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.normalized_text: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), including postoperative pathergy
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophil.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory disorder characterized by fever, neutrophilia, elevated inflammatory markers, and painful erythematous plaques or pseudovesicular lesions; trauma or surgery may trigger lesions.

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.normalized_text: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) with large anterior cervical osteophytes
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis.description: A disorder characterized by flowing calcification and ossification along spinal ligaments, often producing large anterior cervical osteophytes that can mechanically compress the pharynx or esophagus.

Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervi.normalized_text: Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervical osteophyte-related dysphagia
Cervical spondylosis with anterior cervi.description: Degenerative disease of the cervical spine that can form anterior osteophytes; when large, these bony spurs may compress the hypopharynx or cervical esophagus and cause dysphagia and aspiration.

Retropharyngeal or cervical esophageal m.description: A benign or malignant mass arising in the retropharyngeal space, hypopharynx, thyroid region, cervical esophagus, or adjacent tissues can externally compress the swallowing passage and lead to progressive dysphagia and aspiration.

Zenker diverticulum.description: A pharyngoesophageal pouch that can retain food and secretions, producing dysphagia, regurgitation, coughing, choking, and aspiration, particularly in older adults.

NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma) of.normalized_text: NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma) of the mediastinum
NUT carcinoma (NUT midline carcinoma) of.description: A rare, highly aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma driven by NUTM1 gene rearrangement, often arising in the midline thorax/mediastinum of children and young adults and frequently initially misdiagnosed as thymic carcinoma.

Thymic carcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising from the thymus, typically presenting as an anterior mediastinal mass and capable of causing respiratory symptoms through compression of adjacent lung or airways.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphom.description: An aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that commonly affects young women and presents with a bulky anterior mediastinal mass causing cough, dyspnea, pleural effusion, or compression of mediastinal structures.

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclero.normalized_text: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis subtype
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclero.description: A lymphoma frequently affecting adolescents and young adults, especially women, that commonly causes mediastinal lymph-node enlargement and respiratory symptoms from a bulky mediastinal mass.

Primary mediastinal germ cell tumor.description: A germ cell neoplasm arising in the mediastinum, usually presenting as a large anterior mediastinal mass with cough, dyspnea, chest discomfort, or pleural effusion. Teratoma, seminoma, and nonseminomatous tumors are major subtypes.

Primary bilateral macronodular adrenal h.description: A cause of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome in which both adrenal glands become enlarged and nodular, producing excess cortisol. It often presents later in adulthood with subtle or gradual hypercortisolism.

Cushing syndrome due to adrenal cortisol.normalized_text: Cushing syndrome due to adrenal cortisol excess
Cushing syndrome due to adrenal cortisol.description: Cushing syndrome is chronic exposure to excessive cortisol. When due to an adrenal source, cortisol production is relatively autonomous and ACTH is usually suppressed; causes include adrenal adenoma, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, or rarely adrenal carcinoma.

Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical.description: A rare ACTH-independent cause of Cushing syndrome caused by multiple small cortisol-producing adrenal nodules. It may occur alone or as part of Carney complex and can produce mild or cyclic hypercortisolism.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.icd11_title: Glomerular disease associated with thin basement membrane nephropathy

Chronic inferior vena cava thrombosis (i.normalized_text: Chronic inferior vena cava thrombosis (inferior vena cava syndrome)
Chronic inferior vena cava thrombosis (i.description: Obstruction of the inferior vena cava by thrombus causes impaired venous return from the legs and pelvis, often producing bilateral leg edema, abdominal wall collateral veins, and flank or abdominal pain.

Congenital absence or atresia of the inf.normalized_text: Congenital absence or atresia of the inferior vena cava
Congenital absence or atresia of the inf.description: A developmental abnormality in which part or all of the inferior vena cava is absent or severely narrowed. Venous blood is redirected through collateral abdominal, pelvic, paravertebral, and superficial veins; symptoms may develop in adulthood due to venous insufficiency or thrombosis.

Retroperitoneal fibrosis causing inferio.normalized_text: Retroperitoneal fibrosis causing inferior vena cava and iliac venous obstruction
Retroperitoneal fibrosis causing inferio.description: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is inflammatory fibrous tissue in the retroperitoneum that can encase the aorta, inferior vena cava, iliac vessels, and ureters, leading to venous obstruction, leg edema, and abdominal or flank pain.

Bilateral iliocaval deep venous thrombos.description: Thrombosis involving the iliac veins and/or inferior vena cava causes severe obstruction of venous drainage from both lower limbs and may produce pelvic, abdominal, and flank collateral veins.

Chronic venous insufficiency due to cent.normalized_text: Chronic venous insufficiency due to central venous outflow obstruction
Chronic venous insufficiency due to cent.description: Chronic impairment of venous return causes dependent leg edema, aching, and swelling that worsens after prolonged standing. In this case, central obstruction of the iliac veins or inferior vena cava would explain the severity and bilateral extent.

Epstein-Barr virus-associated acute acal.description: Acute inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, occurring as an uncommon complication of primary Epstein-Barr virus infection. Imaging may show gallbladder wall thickening, edema, and pericholecystic fluid without calculi.

Acute infectious mononucleosis with chol.normalized_text: Acute infectious mononucleosis with cholestatic hepatitis due to Epstein-Barr virus
Acute infectious mononucleosis with chol.description: Primary Epstein-Barr virus infection commonly causes fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and mild hepatitis. In rare cases, it causes marked cholestasis with jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools.

Acute cholangitis from biliary obstructi.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree, usually caused by obstruction such as a common bile duct stone. It classically presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, often with cholestatic liver abnormalities.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal ar.normalized_text: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal artery involvement and bilateral renal infarction
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) with renal ar.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that causes segmental arterial stenoses, microaneurysms, thrombosis, and organ ischemia. Renal involvement commonly causes severe hypertension, renal infarcts, impaired kidney function, and elevated inflammatory markers. The imaging appearance of multifocal renal arterial abnormalities with bilateral wedge-shaped renal infarcts is highly suggestive.

Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia wit.normalized_text: Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia with renal infarction
Renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia wit.description: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder that can produce alternating renal artery stenoses and aneurysmal dilatations, often described as a 'string-of-beads' appearance. It can cause renovascular hypertension, renal artery dissection, thrombosis, or renal infarction.

Acute renal infarction due to renal arte.normalized_text: Acute renal infarction due to renal arterial thromboembolism or in-situ thrombosis
Acute renal infarction due to renal arte.description: Renal infarction results from abrupt interruption of renal arterial blood flow, commonly from cardiac emboli, renal artery thrombosis, arterial dissection, or hypercoagulable states. It produces acute flank or abdominal pain, elevated LDH, hypertension, and kidney dysfunction, often with a relatively bland urinalysis.

Segmental arterial mediolysis (SAM).description: Segmental arterial mediolysis is a rare noninflammatory arteriopathy involving medium-sized visceral arteries. It can cause arterial dissections, aneurysms, stenoses, thrombosis, and renal or abdominal organ infarction. Its angiographic appearance can resemble polyarteritis nodosa.

Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.normalized_text: Disseminated tuberculosis with intestinal tuberculosis and tuberculous aortitis
Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving multiple sites, potentially including the ileocecal bowel, lungs, lymph nodes, and aorta. Tuberculous aortitis can cause a mycotic aortic aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm.

Intestinal tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis affecting the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly the ileocecal region, producing ulceration, bowel-wall thickening, abdominal pain, diarrhea, anorexia, and weight loss.

Mycotic abdominal aortic aneurysm due to.normalized_text: Mycotic abdominal aortic aneurysm due to Salmonella infection
Mycotic abdominal aortic aneurysm due to.description: An infected aortic aneurysm caused by bacteremia, frequently due to nontyphoidal Salmonella in older adults with diabetes and severe atherosclerotic vascular disease. It may cause abdominal pain and constitutional symptoms and can enlarge rapidly.

Ileocecal adenocarcinoma with possible m.normalized_text: Ileocecal adenocarcinoma with possible metastatic disease
Ileocecal adenocarcinoma with possible m.description: Colorectal adenocarcinoma involving the cecum or terminal ileum can cause progressive weight loss, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, altered bowel habits, and an ulcerated mass lesion.

Pancreatic panniculitis secondary to acu.normalized_text: Pancreatic panniculitis secondary to acute pancreatitis
Pancreatic panniculitis secondary to acu.description: A rare form of lobular panniculitis caused by release of pancreatic enzymes into the circulation during pancreatic disease, producing enzymatic fat necrosis. Histology characteristically shows necrotic adipocytes ('ghost cells') with inflammation.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas, commonly associated with alcohol use, gallstones, medications, hypertriglyceridemia, or other pancreatic injury. Severe disease can cause pancreatic necrosis and systemic complications, including pancreatic panniculitis.

Erythema nodosum.description: An inflammatory septal panniculitis that produces tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules, most often on the anterior lower legs. It may occur with infections, inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, medications, or systemic inflammatory conditions.

Multiple myeloma with extramedullary pla.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with extramedullary plasmacytoma involving the skull
Multiple myeloma with extramedullary pla.description: A malignant clonal plasma-cell disorder causing monoclonal light-chain production, marrow involvement, osteolytic bone disease, and end-organ damage. The skull mass represents a plasmacytoma, an aggregate of neoplastic plasma cells.

Macro-focal multiple myeloma.description: A variant of multiple myeloma characterized by multiple bone or soft-tissue plasmacytomas with relatively limited bone marrow plasma-cell infiltration, but often with myeloma-defining organ damage or monoclonal protein production.

Solitary plasmacytoma of bone.description: A localized clonal plasma-cell tumor arising in bone, commonly involving the axial skeleton, with little or no marrow involvement and without systemic myeloma-related organ damage.

Primary systemic AL amyloidosis associat.normalized_text: Primary systemic AL amyloidosis associated with a plasma-cell dyscrasia
Primary systemic AL amyloidosis associat.description: A disorder in which monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains form amyloid deposits in organs, often occurring with an underlying plasma-cell clone and causing renal, cardiac, neurologic, or gastrointestinal dysfunction.

Metastatic carcinoma to the skull and sp.normalized_text: Metastatic carcinoma to the skull and spine
Metastatic carcinoma to the skull and sp.description: Cancer spread from a solid-organ primary tumor to bone can cause skull masses, spinal pain, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, and renal dysfunction, particularly when there is widespread skeletal involvement.

Hepatic tuberculosis (macronodular hepat.description: Localized hepatic infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can form a solitary or conglomerate mass-like tuberculoma, sometimes with satellite nodules or calcification. It may occur as recurrent or residual disease after prior abdominal tuberculosis.

Hepatic inflammatory pseudotumor (inflam.description: A benign-to-intermediate inflammatory spindle-cell lesion of the liver that can appear as a solitary hepatic mass and may be associated with prior infection or inflammation.

Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A rare primary liver cancer that typically affects adolescents and young adults without cirrhosis. Imaging may show a large heterogeneous hepatic mass with a central scar and calcification.

Hepatic abscess, including tuberculous o.normalized_text: Hepatic abscess, including tuberculous or pyogenic abscess
Hepatic abscess, including tuberculous o.description: A localized collection of infection in the liver that can cause upper abdominal pain and anorexia. Tuberculous abscesses may be relatively indolent and can lack high fever.

Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrom.normalized_text: Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrome (atheroembolic renal disease)
Cholesterol crystal embolization syndrom.description: Systemic embolization of cholesterol crystals from disrupted atherosclerotic plaques, often occurring days to weeks after angiography, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation. It commonly causes renal failure, eosinophilia, livedo reticularis, and painful blue or dusky toes.

Polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis that can cause renal ischemia, hypertension, peripheral neuropathy, skin nodules, livedo reticularis, and digital ischemia. It generally does not cause glomerulonephritis.

ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatos.normalized_text: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis)
ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatos.description: Small-vessel autoimmune vasculitis that can produce rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, constitutional symptoms, pulmonary disease, neuropathy, and purpuric skin lesions.

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury.description: Acute kidney injury following iodinated contrast exposure, usually caused by renal vasoconstriction and tubular injury. Creatinine typically rises within 24 to 72 hours after contrast administration and improves over days to weeks.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with th.description: An immune-mediated prothrombotic reaction to heparin exposure, usually occurring 5 to 10 days after exposure, causing thrombocytopenia and arterial or venous thrombosis that may produce limb ischemia.

Severe accidental hypothermia.description: A dangerous reduction in core body temperature, often causing depressed consciousness, hypotension, marked bradycardia, and characteristic Osborn (J) waves on ECG.

Myxedema coma.description: Life-threatening decompensated severe hypothyroidism characterized by hypothermia, altered mental status, bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoventilation.

Sepsis with hypothermia.description: Severe systemic infection can produce shock and altered consciousness; elderly patients may become hypothermic rather than febrile.

Adrenal crisis.description: Acute adrenal insufficiency causing circulatory collapse, weakness, altered mental status, and sometimes hypothermia or hypoglycemia.

Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.normalized_text: Seronegative anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (atypical Goodpasture syndrome)
Seronegative anti-glomerular basement me.description: An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome caused by antibodies or immune reactivity directed at basement membranes, producing diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. Some patients have negative circulating anti-GBM antibody tests despite tissue evidence of basement-membrane IgG deposition.

Goodpasture syndrome with central nervou.normalized_text: Goodpasture syndrome with central nervous system involvement
Goodpasture syndrome with central nervou.description: Goodpasture syndrome is the clinical combination of anti-GBM-mediated diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis. Rarely, neurologic manifestations such as seizures or focal deficits may occur through cerebral vascular or immune-mediated involvement.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, and occasionally the nervous system. It can cause pulmonary hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (lupus pneumonitis/capillaritis)
Systemic lupus erythematosus with diffus.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, pulmonary capillaritis with alveolar hemorrhage, anemia, and neurologic complications including seizures.

IgA vasculitis or IgA nephropathy with p.normalized_text: IgA vasculitis or IgA nephropathy with pulmonary hemorrhage
IgA vasculitis or IgA nephropathy with p.description: IgA-mediated immune-complex disease usually affecting the kidneys and sometimes small vessels in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and lungs. Rare severe cases can cause diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular ge.normalized_text: Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumor (mixed germ cell tumor, likely with yolk sac tumor component)
Metastatic nonseminomatous testicular ge.description: A malignant testicular germ cell tumor that may contain mixed histologic elements such as yolk sac tumor, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, and teratoma. Markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein strongly supports a nonseminomatous component. These tumors can metastasize to retroperitoneal lymph nodes and, less commonly, the gastrointestinal tract, causing ulceration and bleeding.

Testicular yolk sac tumor with gastroint.normalized_text: Testicular yolk sac tumor with gastrointestinal metastasis
Testicular yolk sac tumor with gastroint.description: Yolk sac tumor is a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor characterized by substantial alpha-fetoprotein production. In adults it often occurs as part of a mixed germ cell tumor and can spread through retroperitoneal lymphatics and hematogenously, occasionally involving the gastrointestinal tract.

Testicular embryonal carcinoma as part o.normalized_text: Testicular embryonal carcinoma as part of a mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor
Testicular embryonal carcinoma as part o.description: Embryonal carcinoma is an aggressive nonseminomatous testicular germ cell tumor that commonly occurs in mixed tumors. It can elevate alpha-fetoprotein and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin and has an early tendency toward lymphatic and hematogenous metastasis, including rare gastrointestinal metastases.

NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease wi.normalized_text: NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease with upper gastrointestinal bleeding
NSAID-associated peptic ulcer disease wi.description: Frequent NSAID use can damage gastric and duodenal mucosa, causing erosions or peptic ulcers that produce abdominal pain, melena, and chronic or acute blood-loss anemia.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma of gastric origin

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens.description: A severe form of massive proximal deep-vein thrombosis causing near-total venous outflow obstruction, profound limb edema, cyanosis, and threatened limb ischemia.

Extensive iliofemoral deep venous thromb.description: A thrombus involving the deep veins of the thigh and pelvis, often producing severe unilateral leg pain and swelling; extensive disease may progress to phlegmasia cerulea dolens.

Acute limb ischemia due to arterial occl.normalized_text: Acute limb ischemia due to arterial occlusion
Acute limb ischemia due to arterial occl.description: Sudden reduction or interruption of arterial blood flow to a limb, commonly caused by embolism or thrombosis, resulting in pain, coolness, cyanosis, and reduced pulses.

Gastric adenocarcinoma with malignancy-a.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the stomach. Advanced gastric adenocarcinoma can create a hypercoagulable state and predispose to extensive venous thromboembolism, including iliofemoral thrombosis and phlegmasia.

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVL.normalized_text: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL) involving the penis
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVL.description: A rare aggressive extranodal B-cell lymphoma in which malignant large B cells proliferate predominantly within small blood vessels, often without lymphadenopathy or a detectable mass. Penile vascular involvement can cause ischemic priapism.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the penis
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can rarely arise in or infiltrate the penis, producing painful swelling, erectile dysfunction, or priapism. Most cases form a mass rather than being confined to vessels.

Primary penile lymphoma.description: A rare lymphoma localized initially to penile tissue, most commonly of diffuse large B-cell type. It may present with penile enlargement, pain, induration, nodules, ulceration, urinary symptoms, or priapism.

Ischemic priapism secondary to malignant.normalized_text: Ischemic priapism secondary to malignant corporal infiltration or venous obstruction
Ischemic priapism secondary to malignant.description: Low-flow ischemic priapism is a painful prolonged erection caused by impaired venous drainage from the corpora cavernosa. Malignancy, including hematologic cancer, can produce this through infiltration, thrombosis, or vascular obstruction.

Struma ovarii with pseudo-Meigs syndrome.description: A rare monodermal ovarian teratoma composed predominantly of thyroid tissue. It can produce ascites and pleural effusion (pseudo-Meigs syndrome), markedly elevate CA-125, and demonstrate radioiodine uptake despite normal thyroid function.

Epithelial ovarian carcinoma.description: A malignant ovarian neoplasm, commonly high-grade serous carcinoma, that often presents after menopause with an adnexal mass, ascites, abdominal symptoms, and elevated CA-125.

Ovarian fibroma/thecoma with Meigs syndr.description: A benign sex-cord stromal ovarian tumor that may cause the Meigs triad of ovarian fibroma, ascites, and pleural effusion; CA-125 can be elevated because of peritoneal irritation.

Mature cystic teratoma containing thyroi.normalized_text: Mature cystic teratoma containing thyroid tissue
Mature cystic teratoma containing thyroi.description: A benign germ-cell tumor that can contain multiple mature tissue types, including thyroid tissue. When thyroid tissue predominates, it is classified as struma ovarii.

Cervical spinal epidural abscess / verte.normalized_text: Cervical spinal epidural abscess / vertebral osteomyelitis
Cervical spinal epidural abscess / verte.description: Infection involving the vertebrae, intervertebral disc spaces, and/or epidural space that can produce inflammatory soft-tissue or epidural collections and spinal canal narrowing. MRI is substantially more sensitive than plain radiographs early in the disease.

Primary spinal epidural lymphoma.description: Lymphoma may involve the cervical epidural space and vertebral marrow, producing an infiltrative soft-tissue mass with pain and possible spinal cord compression. Early radiographs may be normal.

Cervical spinal tuberculosis (tuberculou.description: Mycobacterial infection of the cervical spine can cause slowly progressive neck pain, marrow abnormalities, paraspinal soft-tissue inflammation or abscess, and epidural extension. Radiographs may be unrevealing early.

Cervical spinal epidural tumor, such as.normalized_text: Cervical spinal epidural tumor, such as metastatic disease
Cervical spinal epidural tumor, such as.description: Epidural tumor involving vertebral marrow or the spinal canal may cause persistent pain before neurologic compression symptoms occur. MRI can detect marrow and epidural disease not visible on initial radiographs.

Cervical spinal epidural venous malforma.normalized_text: Cervical spinal epidural venous malformation/epidural hemangioma
Cervical spinal epidural venous malforma.description: A vascular lesion in the epidural space or vertebra can cause neck pain and may appear as an enhancing epidural or paravertebral soft-tissue lesion on MRI; plain radiographs may be normal.

Fibrous hamartoma of infancy.description: A benign congenital or early-childhood soft-tissue hamartoma composed of fibrous tissue, immature mesenchyme, and fat. It typically presents before age 2 years as a painless, slowly enlarging, firm subcutaneous mass or plaque.

Eccrine angiomatous hamartoma.description: A rare benign hamartoma involving eccrine sweat glands and vascular structures, often present at birth or arising in childhood. It may appear as a plaque or nodule and can cause focal hyperhidrosis, pain, or increased hair growth.

Eccrine nevus.description: A benign localized overgrowth of eccrine sweat glands that presents as a circumscribed plaque, most often in childhood, with focal excessive sweating as the principal clinical feature.

Congenital smooth muscle hamartoma.description: A benign developmental proliferation of arrector pili smooth muscle, usually recognized at birth or in early childhood as a skin-colored or hyperpigmented plaque, often on the trunk or lumbosacral region. The lesion may become more prominent over time.

Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosi.description: A clonal inflammatory disorder involving Langerhans cells that can affect skin, bone, lungs, liver, and other organs. In children, a persistent crusted scalp eruption, lytic bone lesions, and cystic/nodular lung disease are characteristic.

Cystic fibrosis with bronchiectasis.description: An inherited CFTR-related disorder causing chronic airway infection, bronchiectasis, systemic inflammation, poor weight gain, and occasionally hepatobiliary disease.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with skeletal and.normalized_text: Pulmonary tuberculosis with skeletal and cutaneous involvement
Pulmonary tuberculosis with skeletal and.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause constitutional symptoms and pulmonary infiltrates or cavitation; disseminated disease may involve bone and skin.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis.description: A necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis that can affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, kidneys, skin, and other organs; pulmonary nodules may cavitate.
