Sarcoidosis.description: A granulomatous inflammatory disease that most commonly affects the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, eyes, and occasionally liver or bone.

Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.normalized_text: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (NST), grade 2
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special.description: The most common form of invasive breast cancer, historically termed invasive ductal carcinoma. Malignant epithelial cells invade beyond the breast ducts into surrounding breast tissue.

Locally extensive or multifocal invasive.normalized_text: Locally extensive or multifocal invasive breast carcinoma
Locally extensive or multifocal invasive.description: Invasive breast carcinoma may have a larger extent on MRI than is evident on mammography or ultrasound, including additional adjacent foci or non-mass enhancement that can influence selection of mastectomy rather than breast-conserving surgery.

Regional lymph node metastasis from left.normalized_text: Regional lymph node metastasis from left breast carcinoma
Regional lymph node metastasis from left.description: Breast cancer can spread to regional lymph nodes, including axillary, intramammary, or internal mammary chain nodes. Suspicious enhancing nodal findings on staging MRI warrant correlation with dedicated nodal imaging or pathology.

Hydroxychloroquine-induced retinopathy (.description: A toxic retinopathy caused by long-term hydroxychloroquine exposure, characterized by parafoveal retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptor damage that can progress to bull's-eye maculopathy and irreversible central visual loss.

Age-related macular degeneration.description: A degenerative disorder of the macula in older adults that causes central visual impairment, often associated with drusen, retinal pigment epithelial change, geographic atrophy, or choroidal neovascularization.

Retinitis pigmentosa or retinal dystroph.normalized_text: Retinitis pigmentosa or retinal dystrophy with ring scotoma
Retinitis pigmentosa or retinal dystroph.description: A group of inherited retinal degenerations causing progressive photoreceptor dysfunction, commonly with night blindness, peripheral field constriction, pigmentary retinal changes, and sometimes a ring scotoma.

Autoimmune retinopathy.description: An immune-mediated retinal degeneration that may occur alone or in association with systemic autoimmune disease or malignancy, producing photopsias, visual-field loss, dyschromatopsia, and progressive retinal dysfunction.

Primary extranodal classical Hodgkin lym.normalized_text: Primary extranodal classical Hodgkin lymphoma of the nasopharynx, lymphocyte-rich subtype
Primary extranodal classical Hodgkin lym.description: A rare localized form of classical Hodgkin lymphoma arising in extranodal tissue of the nasopharynx. The lymphocyte-rich subtype can show a nodular background of small lymphocytes with scattered Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells that express CD30 and often CD15.

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin l.description: An indolent Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by nodular aggregates of small B lymphocytes and scattered large lymphocyte-predominant cells. It usually involves lymph nodes and typically has CD20-positive, CD45-positive large cells that are negative for CD15 and CD30.

Reactive atypical lymphoid hyperplasia o.normalized_text: Reactive atypical lymphoid hyperplasia of the adenoids/nasopharynx
Reactive atypical lymphoid hyperplasia o.description: A benign reactive proliferation of lymphoid tissue that may occur with infection, chronic inflammation, or immune stimulation and can produce adenoidal enlargement and nasal obstruction.

Ipilimumab-induced immune checkpoint inh.description: Immune-mediated inflammation of the heart muscle caused by ipilimumab, a CTLA-4 immune checkpoint inhibitor. It can present with chest pain, ST-segment elevation, elevated troponin, arrhythmias, and nonobstructive coronary arteries.

Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopath.normalized_text: Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopathy), potentially triggered by immunotherapy-associated inflammation
Takotsubo syndrome (stress cardiomyopath.description: A transient stress-induced cardiomyopathy that mimics acute myocardial infarction, often with chest pain, ST elevation, troponin elevation, and unobstructed coronary arteries. It may be triggered by severe illness, emotional stress, malignancy, or immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation involving both the myocardium and pericardium, causing chest pain, ST-segment changes, and troponin elevation. In this setting, it could be immune-mediated from ipilimumab.

Myocardial infarction with nonobstructiv.normalized_text: Myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA)
Myocardial infarction with nonobstructiv.description: A clinical syndrome of myocardial infarction with elevated cardiac biomarkers and ischemic ECG changes but no obstructive coronary lesion on angiography. Potential mechanisms include coronary vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, embolism, myocarditis, or stress cardiomyopathy.

Cardiac metastatic melanoma.description: Melanoma can metastasize to the heart, including the myocardium or pericardium, and may cause chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmias, myocardial injury, or pericardial disease. Cardiac imaging is needed to identify a focal infiltrative mass.

Syphilitic proctitis (anorectal syphilis.normalized_text: Syphilitic proctitis (anorectal syphilis due to Treponema pallidum)
Syphilitic proctitis (anorectal syphilis.description: Sexually transmitted rectal infection caused by Treponema pallidum, which can cause painful proctitis, rectal bleeding, fissures, and a plasma cell-rich inflammatory infiltrate. The immunohistochemical image is consistent with spirochetes in the rectal tissue.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) proctitis.description: An invasive sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3 that can produce severe proctitis in men who have sex with men, including rectal pain, bleeding, and inflammatory mucosal changes.

Herpes simplex virus proctitis.description: Sexually acquired HSV infection of the anorectum that may cause severe anorectal pain, tenesmus, bleeding, ulceration, and proctitis, particularly after receptive anal sexual exposure.

Inflammatory bowel disease, especially C.normalized_text: Inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn disease with perianal involvement
Inflammatory bowel disease, especially C.description: Crohn disease can involve the rectum and anus, causing chronic proctitis, rectal bleeding, fissures, skin tags, and perianal pain. Ulcerative proctitis is another inflammatory bowel disease consideration but is less associated with fissures and perianal skin tags.

Hemorrhoids with anal fissures.description: Hemorrhoids are dilated anal vascular cushions that commonly cause painless bright red blood on toilet paper, while anal fissures cause sharp pain during defecation and may produce small-volume bleeding.

Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria.description: The presence of blood detected on urine testing without visible blood in the urine or urinary symptoms; dipstick blood should be confirmed with microscopic urinalysis.

Urinary tract malignancy (bladder, kidne.normalized_text: Urinary tract malignancy (bladder, kidney, or upper tract urothelial cancer)
Urinary tract malignancy (bladder, kidne.description: Cancers of the urinary tract can present with painless microscopic or gross hematuria, particularly in older adults, although risk is lower in never-smokers.

Prostate cancer.description: A malignant growth of the prostate that may be asymptomatic early and is more likely with increasing age and a first-degree family history.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia.description: Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate that commonly occurs in older men and can occasionally be associated with hematuria from prostatic vascularity.

Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones).description: Urinary stones can cause microscopic hematuria, sometimes without symptoms, although they more commonly cause sudden flank pain or renal colic.

Congenital dysfibrinogenemia (FGG-relate.description: An inherited disorder in which fibrinogen antigen concentration is normal or near normal but the fibrinogen molecule functions poorly, causing reduced Clauss fibrinogen activity and prolonged clotting times. It may result from a de novo FGG mutation.

Congenital hypodysfibrinogenemia.description: A hereditary fibrinogen disorder with both reduced fibrinogen function and, in many cases, reduced fibrinogen quantity. Some variants may have near-normal antigen values despite markedly impaired clot-based fibrinogen activity.

Congenital afibrinogenemia or severe hyp.description: A severe inherited quantitative fibrinogen deficiency that can cause neonatal bleeding and marked prolongation of clotting studies. It is usually caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in fibrinogen genes and produces very low or absent fibrinogen antigen.

diagnoses.name: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung
diagnoses.normalized_text: Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the lung

Non-small cell lung cancer (poorly diffe.normalized_text: Non-small cell lung cancer (poorly differentiated carcinoma, likely squamous cell carcinoma)
Non-small cell lung cancer (poorly diffe.description: A malignant epithelial lung tumor strongly associated with heavy tobacco exposure. A central right hilar or mediastinal tumor can obstruct the right main bronchus and compress or invade the superior vena cava, producing superior vena cava syndrome.

Small cell lung carcinoma.description: An aggressive, smoking-associated neuroendocrine lung cancer that commonly arises centrally in the hilum or mediastinum. It frequently presents with bulky mediastinal disease, bronchial obstruction, early metastasis, and superior vena cava syndrome.

Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of t.normalized_text: Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung
Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of t.description: A high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma that occurs predominantly in older heavy smokers. It can form a large central lung or mediastinal mass, cause airway and superior vena cava compression, and metastasize early.

Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcoma.normalized_text: Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcomatoid non-small cell lung carcinoma)
Pulmonary pleomorphic carcinoma (sarcoma.description: A rare, poorly differentiated and highly aggressive non-small cell lung cancer composed of pleomorphic large malignant cells, sometimes with spindle-cell or giant-cell features. It is strongly associated with smoking and may present as a bulky invasive thoracic mass.

Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to.normalized_text: Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to an intrathoracic malignancy
Superior vena cava syndrome secondary to.description: A clinical syndrome caused by obstruction of the superior vena cava, most often from lung cancer or mediastinal tumor compression, invasion, or thrombosis. It produces impaired venous drainage from the head, neck, upper chest, and arms.

BCL11B-related severe combined immunodef.normalized_text: BCL11B-related severe combined immunodeficiency with neurodevelopmental abnormalities
BCL11B-related severe combined immunodef.description: A rare genetic disorder caused by pathogenic BCL11B variants that can impair thymic T-cell development and cause profound T-cell lymphopenia, along with craniofacial, neurologic, skin, and developmental abnormalities.

PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndro.normalized_text: PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 with severe T-cell immunodeficiency)
PAX1 deficiency (otofaciocervical syndro.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder caused by PAX1 deficiency, characterized by defective thymic development causing severe T-cell immunodeficiency, often with craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities.

22q11.2 deletion syndrome with congenita.normalized_text: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome with congenital athymia (complete DiGeorge syndrome)
22q11.2 deletion syndrome with congenita.description: A chromosomal deletion syndrome that may cause thymic aplasia or hypoplasia, resulting in severe T-cell lymphopenia, together with congenital heart defects, hypocalcemia, and characteristic craniofacial findings.

PGM3-congenital disorder of glycosylatio.normalized_text: PGM3-congenital disorder of glycosylation with immunodeficiency
PGM3-congenital disorder of glycosylatio.description: A congenital glycosylation disorder that can cause combined immunodeficiency, eczema or dermatitis, hypotonia, developmental abnormalities, and skeletal or craniofacial findings.

NEMO/IKBKG-related ectodermal dysplasia.description: A disorder of NF-kappa-B signaling that can produce combined immunodeficiency and ectodermal abnormalities involving the skin, teeth, hair, and sweat glands. Severe forms in males may present in infancy.

Primary rectal extranodal marginal zone.normalized_text: Primary rectal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma)
Primary rectal extranodal marginal zone.description: An indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. In the rectum it can appear as submucosal nodules, erosions, or polypoid lesions and histology commonly shows dense lymphoid infiltration with lymphoepithelial lesions.

Rectal adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the rectum that may cause altered bowel habits, mucus discharge, rectal urgency, tenesmus, bleeding, or obstructive symptoms.

Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis.normalized_text: Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum)
Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease confined to the rectum, typically causing continuous mucosal inflammation, urgency, tenesmus, rectal bleeding, and mucus discharge.

Intestinal tuberculosis involving the co.normalized_text: Intestinal tuberculosis involving the colon or rectum
Intestinal tuberculosis involving the co.description: Gastrointestinal infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually affecting the ileocecal region but occasionally involving the colon. It may produce ulceration, strictures, nodules, abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, or bowel obstruction.

Acute left iliofemoral deep venous throm.normalized_text: Acute left iliofemoral deep venous thrombosis with pulmonary embolism
Acute left iliofemoral deep venous throm.description: Acute clot formation in the deep veins of the left lower extremity/pelvis with embolization to pulmonary arteries. The CT images are consistent with pulmonary arterial filling defects and pelvic venous thrombosis.

May-Thurner syndrome (iliac vein compres.description: Compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery, causing impaired venous drainage and predisposing young women to extensive left-sided iliofemoral DVT and pulmonary embolism.

Acute pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arterial branches by embolized venous thrombus, most commonly originating from a lower-extremity or pelvic DVT. The chest CT demonstrates pulmonary arterial filling defects.

Cellulitis of the left lower extremity.normalized_text: Cellulitis of the left lower extremity
Cellulitis of the left lower extremity.description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues that typically causes localized erythema, warmth, tenderness, and swelling.

Superficial thrombophlebitis.description: Inflammation and thrombosis of superficial veins, usually causing a painful, warm, erythematous, cord-like area along the course of a superficial vein.

X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (.description: A primary immunodeficiency caused by defective NADPH oxidase activity in phagocytes, resulting in impaired oxidative burst and susceptibility to recurrent severe bacterial and fungal infections. The flow-cytometry pattern is consistent with absent oxidative burst, and sequencing suggests a CYBB-related defect.

Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatou.description: A form of CGD caused by defects in other NADPH oxidase components, such as NCF1, NCF2, NCF4, or CYBA. It produces impaired neutrophil oxidative burst and recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms.

Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome).description: A primary immunodeficiency, commonly due to STAT3-related disease, characterized by recurrent staphylococcal skin and lung infections, eczema, markedly elevated IgE, and possible lung structural damage such as pneumatoceles.

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.description: A primary adenocarcinoma arising from bile ducts within the liver. It commonly produces a desmoplastic gland-forming tumor on pathology, may present as multifocal liver masses, and can elevate CA 19-9.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with li.normalized_text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with liver metastases
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with li.description: An aggressive pancreatic exocrine adenocarcinoma that often causes abdominal pain radiating to the back, elevated CA 19-9, and liver metastases. Histology typically shows infiltrative malignant glands in dense desmoplastic stroma.

Metastatic upper gastrointestinal or pan.normalized_text: Metastatic upper gastrointestinal or pancreatobiliary adenocarcinoma of occult primary
Metastatic upper gastrointestinal or pan.description: Adenocarcinomas originating in the stomach, pancreas, biliary tract, or ampullary region may metastasize to the liver and produce glandular tumors with fibrosis. CA 19-9 can be elevated in pancreatobiliary and some upper gastrointestinal cancers.

Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.normalized_text: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the liver
Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to.description: Colorectal cancer frequently metastasizes to the liver and can form glandular lesions. It may be considered given the family history of colorectal cancer, although the normal CEA and elevated CA 19-9 are less characteristic.

Parotid gland leiomyoma (vascular leiomy.description: A rare benign smooth-muscle tumor arising from vascular smooth muscle within or adjacent to the parotid gland. It often forms a well-circumscribed mobile mass and may be painful because of vascular contraction or nerve irritation.

Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.normalized_text: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland
Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.description: The most common benign salivary-gland tumor, usually presenting as a slowly growing, mobile, well-defined parotid mass. Histology generally contains epithelial and myoepithelial elements in a chondromyxoid stroma rather than pure smooth-muscle spindle cells.

Warthin tumor.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor composed of papillary cystic epithelial structures and lymphoid stroma, usually occurring in the parotid gland of older adults, especially male smokers.

Parotid schwannoma.description: A benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumor that may arise from intraparotid branches of the facial nerve or other nerves in the parotid region. It is usually slow growing and may cause pain from nerve compression.

Parotid gland carcinoma, including carci.normalized_text: Parotid gland carcinoma, including carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma or other salivary malignancy
Parotid gland carcinoma, including carci.description: Malignant salivary-gland tumors can present with a painful parotid mass and may invade surrounding tissues, regional lymph nodes, or the facial nerve. Imaging and pathology are needed to establish the specific subtype.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter sy.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, leading to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans. Severe forms cause progressive neurodevelopmental decline, coarse facies, hearing impairment, macroglossia, spasticity, and characteristic brain white-matter/perivascular-space abnormalities.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (Hurler syn.description: A lysosomal storage disease caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency. The severe Hurler phenotype produces developmental regression, coarse facial features, macroglossia, hearing loss, progressive motor disability, and white-matter abnormalities with ventricular enlargement on brain MRI.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (Sanfilip.description: A group of lysosomal disorders involving impaired heparan-sulfate degradation. It is characterized primarily by progressive neurocognitive decline, severe language impairment, behavioral changes, hearing problems, mild coarse facies, and progressive brain atrophy or white-matter abnormalities.

Mucolipidosis type II (I-cell disease).description: A severe autosomal-recessive lysosomal trafficking disorder caused by deficient mannose-6-phosphate targeting of multiple lysosomal enzymes. It causes coarse facies, gingival/mucosal enlargement, developmental delay, severe skeletal disease, growth failure, and progressive neurologic impairment.

Alpha-mannosidosis.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency. It can cause intellectual disability, speech delay, hearing loss, immune dysfunction, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, ataxia, and progressive motor impairment.

diagnoses.name: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis
diagnoses.icd11_title: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx[Bilateral]

Congenital bilateral vocal fold paralysi.description: Impaired movement of both vocal folds, typically leaving them in a paramedian or near-midline position and causing a critically narrowed glottic airway. It is an important cause of neonatal stridor.

Acquired bilateral vocal fold paralysis.normalized_text: Acquired bilateral vocal fold paralysis secondary to hypoxic-ischemic neurologic injury
Acquired bilateral vocal fold paralysis.description: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction or central neurologic injury after severe hypoxia can cause immobility of both vocal folds and upper-airway obstruction after extubation.

Posterior glottic stenosis with bilatera.normalized_text: Posterior glottic stenosis with bilateral cricoarytenoid fixation
Posterior glottic stenosis with bilatera.description: Scarring or fixation of the posterior glottis and cricoarytenoid joints can prevent vocal-fold abduction, producing a clinical picture similar to bilateral vocal fold paralysis. It may occur after prolonged or traumatic intubation.

Post-intubation subglottic stenosis.description: Narrowing of the subglottic airway due to edema, scar formation, or cartilage injury after endotracheal intubation. It commonly causes persistent or recurrent stridor after extubation.

Laryngomalacia.description: A common congenital cause of neonatal stridor caused by dynamic collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration. Symptoms often worsen with feeding, crying, or supine positioning.

Fourth branchial pouch sinus (pyriform s.normalized_text: Fourth branchial pouch sinus (pyriform sinus fistula) with recurrent left neck abscess
Fourth branchial pouch sinus (pyriform s.description: A congenital tract arising from the apex of the pyriform sinus that commonly causes recurrent infections or abscesses in the left lower anterior neck, often near or involving the thyroid gland.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis due to a p.normalized_text: Acute suppurative thyroiditis due to a pyriform sinus fistula
Acute suppurative thyroiditis due to a p.description: A bacterial infection of the thyroid gland, frequently caused in young patients by an underlying congenital pyriform sinus tract that permits contamination from the pharynx.

Second branchial cleft cyst with recurre.normalized_text: Second branchial cleft cyst with recurrent infection
Second branchial cleft cyst with recurre.description: A congenital epithelial cyst in the lateral neck that may become infected, enlarge rapidly, and form an abscess.

Cervical lymphadenitis with abscess form.description: Infection and suppuration of cervical lymph nodes, usually from bacterial infection of the upper aerodigestive tract, skin, or dental sources.

Drug-induced urticarial vasculitis.description: A small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis presenting with urticarial-appearing lesions that are painful or burning, persist for about 24 hours or longer, and may leave bruising or hyperpigmentation. Medications and supplements can trigger it.

Serum sickness-like reaction due to diet.normalized_text: Serum sickness-like reaction due to dietary supplement or medication
Serum sickness-like reaction due to diet.description: A delayed drug-related hypersensitivity reaction, usually occurring days to several weeks after exposure, characterized by rash or urticaria, fever, joint pain, muscle pain, and edema. Unlike classic serum sickness, complement levels are often normal and major immune-complex organ disease is uncommon.

Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis.description: A systemic form of urticarial vasculitis in which recurrent painful urticarial lesions persist longer than ordinary hives and may be accompanied by fever, arthralgia, angioedema, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities. It is often associated with low complement levels and sometimes renal, pulmonary, ocular, or gastrointestinal disease.

Acute drug-induced urticaria with angioe.description: A mast-cell-mediated medication or supplement reaction causing transient pruritic wheals and deeper swelling of the skin or soft tissues. Lesions usually resolve within hours and do not leave pigmentation or bruising.

Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar.normalized_text: Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar with intestinal extension)
Rapunzel syndrome (gastric trichobezoar.description: A large mass of swallowed hair (trichobezoar) filling the stomach with a tail extending into the small intestine, causing gastric outlet or intermittent intestinal obstruction. It is most common in adolescent girls and may be associated with trichotillomania, trichophagia, pica, or psychiatric conditions.

Gastric trichobezoar.description: A compact accumulation of ingested hair within the stomach. It can cause abdominal pain, vomiting, early satiety, anemia, and gastric outlet obstruction; when it extends into the small bowel it is termed Rapunzel syndrome.

Peptic ulcer disease.description: Ulceration of the stomach or duodenal lining, commonly related to Helicobacter pylori infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug exposure. It can cause epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and iron-deficiency anemia from occult bleeding.

Gastric outlet obstruction.description: Mechanical blockage at the distal stomach or proximal duodenum, causing impaired gastric emptying. In this case, the obstruction would be caused by the large trichobezoar rather than a tumor or ulcer-related stricture.

NSAID-associated gastritis.description: Inflammation and injury of the gastric mucosa caused or worsened by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen. It commonly causes epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally bleeding.

Disseminated tuberculosis with intestina.description: Systemic infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis involving the lungs, ileum, and kidney. Ileal tuberculous ulcers can undergo transmural necrosis and perforation, causing fatal purulent peritonitis.

Disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria.description: Systemic infection with environmental mycobacteria, particularly Mycobacterium avium complex, which may occur in immunocompromised individuals and can produce pulmonary and gastrointestinal disease with acid-fast organisms.

Crohn disease with perforating ileitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that commonly affects the terminal ileum and can cause deep ulceration, transmural inflammation, fistulation, obstruction, or bowel perforation. Noncaseating granulomas may be present.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that may involve lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs, particularly in immunocompromised patients. It can produce granulomatous inflammation and intestinal ulceration.

Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (neur.normalized_text: Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (neurally mediated syncope with sinus arrest)
Cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope (neur.description: A reflex-mediated autonomic event causing abrupt increased vagal tone, hypotension, bradycardia, and sometimes transient sinus arrest or asystole. It is often triggered by pain, nausea, vomiting, emotional stress, or medical procedures.

Brugada syndrome.description: An inherited cardiac sodium-channel disorder that predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. ECG findings may include right precordial ST-segment elevation with a coved or saddleback morphology, and the pattern may be unmasked by fever or acute illness.

Acute myopericarditis.description: Inflammation of the myocardium and/or pericardium, often following a viral illness. It can cause chest pain, ECG ST-segment changes, arrhythmias, and occasionally impaired cardiac function.

Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal vasospastic angina)
Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary.description: Transient coronary artery spasm can cause episodic chest pain and temporary ST-segment elevation, often resolving when the spasm ends. Significant ischemia can occasionally provoke bradyarrhythmias or other rhythm disturbances.

Hyperventilation syndrome associated wit.normalized_text: Hyperventilation syndrome associated with panic or acute autonomic distress
Hyperventilation syndrome associated wit.description: Hyperventilation during acute anxiety, pain, or autonomic distress can produce dyspnea, dizziness, chest discomfort, sweating, and distal paresthesias through respiratory alkalosis.

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum.description: Free air within the mediastinum occurring without trauma or an invasive procedure, often due to rupture of small alveoli with air tracking along bronchovascular sheaths. It can occur in otherwise healthy young adults.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, commonly presenting in young adults with sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.

Esophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndro.description: A full-thickness tear of the esophagus that can release air and gastrointestinal contents into the mediastinum, producing pneumomediastinum and potentially severe mediastinitis.

Acute pericarditis.description: Inflammation of the pericardium that typically causes sharp chest pain, often worsened by inspiration or lying flat and relieved by sitting forward.

Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.normalized_text: Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis
Erythema migrans due to Lyme borreliosis.description: The characteristic expanding annular skin lesion of early Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia infection transmitted by Ixodes ticks. Serology may be negative early in infection, and many patients do not recall a tick bite.

Tinea corporis (ringworm).description: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection causing an itchy, enlarging ring-shaped rash, often with a more active red edge and relative central clearing.

Erythema annulare centrifugum.description: A reactive inflammatory skin eruption characterized by slowly enlarging annular red patches or plaques with central clearing; a trailing inner scale may occur.

Granuloma annulare.description: A benign inflammatory skin condition producing annular plaques, usually without scale, often on the hands or feet but occasionally elsewhere on the body.

Vasospastic angina (Prinzmetal/variant a.description: Transient epicardial coronary artery spasm causing episodic myocardial ischemia, often occurring at rest during the night or early morning. Smoking and alcohol exposure are recognized triggers.

Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.normalized_text: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) due to coronary vasospasm
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (.description: Acute myocardial infarction without persistent ST-segment elevation, caused here potentially by prolonged coronary vasospasm producing myocardial injury despite no fixed obstructive coronary lesion.

Acute coronary syndrome from nonobstruct.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome from nonobstructive coronary artery disease (MINOCA)
Acute coronary syndrome from nonobstruct.description: Myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries, which may result from coronary vasospasm, plaque disruption, embolism, spontaneous coronary dissection, or microvascular dysfunction.

Unstable angina due to transient coronar.normalized_text: Unstable angina due to transient coronary vasomotor dysfunction
Unstable angina due to transient coronar.description: New or worsening ischemic chest discomfort occurring at rest due to transient reduction in coronary blood flow, including episodes caused by dynamic coronary spasm.

Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM), als.description: A congenital limb-malformation disorder characterized by absence or hypoplasia of central fingers and/or toes, producing cleft or lobster-claw-like hands and feet. Dental agenesis and enamel abnormalities can occur in some forms.

Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefti.description: A TP63-associated ectodermal dysplasia syndrome characterized by split-hand/split-foot malformations, ectodermal abnormalities, dental agenesis or enamel defects, and frequently cleft lip and/or palate.

Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic f.normalized_text: Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic fetal exposure to acetazolamide)
Acetazolamide embryopathy (teratogenic f.description: A congenital malformation pattern attributed to prenatal exposure to acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Reported fetal effects include growth restriction and limb/digital abnormalities; dental developmental abnormalities may be associated with disrupted fetal development.

Ectodermal dysplasia with hypodontia and.normalized_text: Ectodermal dysplasia with hypodontia and limb anomalies
Ectodermal dysplasia with hypodontia and.description: A heterogeneous group of genetic disorders affecting ectoderm-derived tissues, often causing hypodontia, enamel hypoplasia, delayed eruption, and sometimes digital malformations such as ectrodactyly or syndactyly.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.description: An intermittent supraventricular arrhythmia characterized by episodic, irregular atrial electrical activity that starts and stops spontaneously. Holter monitoring directly documented two episodes.

Frequent premature atrial contractions (.description: Premature atrial contractions are early beats originating in the atria. They can cause skipped beats, fluttering, or brief palpitations and may trigger atrial fibrillation.

Alcohol-triggered atrial arrhythmia (hol.description: Alcohol-associated atrial arrhythmia, most commonly atrial fibrillation, occurring after alcohol intake even in people without severe structural heart disease.

Intestinal T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.normalized_text: Intestinal T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (ITCL-NOS)
Intestinal T-cell lymphoma, not otherwis.description: A rare aggressive peripheral T-cell lymphoma involving the gastrointestinal tract, often presenting with ulcerative colitis-like colonic lesions, abdominal symptoms, weight loss, and destructive lymphoid infiltration on biopsy.

Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell.normalized_text: Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary colorectal diffuse large B-cell.description: An aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that can arise in the colon and produce abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, ulcerated mucosal lesions, and inflammatory-appearing colonoscopic findings.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, causing diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, weight loss, erythema, edema, loss of vascular pattern, friability, and ulceration.

Crohn colitis.description: A form of Crohn disease confined predominantly to the colon, characterized by patchy transmural inflammation, irregular ulcers, abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and possible extraintestinal complications.

Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst with sec.normalized_text: Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst with secondary hydropneumothorax
Ruptured pulmonary hydatid cyst with sec.description: Pulmonary echinococcosis caused by Echinococcus larvae can form a lung cyst. Rupture into a bronchus or pleural space may produce an air-fluid level, detached internal membranes (water-lily/camellia sign), pneumothorax, and pleural effusion.

Spontaneous hydropneumothorax.description: Hydropneumothorax is the simultaneous presence of air and fluid in the pleural space, causing partial lung collapse. It may occur spontaneously or secondary to infection, trauma, a ruptured cyst, or an underlying lung lesion.

Spontaneous pneumothorax.description: A spontaneous pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space, leading to partial or complete lung collapse. It classically causes sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and reduced breath sounds.

Pleural empyema with bronchopleural fist.description: Empyema is infected pleural fluid, usually following pneumonia. If a bronchopleural fistula develops, air enters the pleural collection and produces a pyopneumothorax or hydropneumothorax.

diagnoses.name: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver
diagnoses.normalized_text: Solitary extramedullary plasmacytoma of the liver

Primary hepatic extramedullary plasmacyt.description: A rare localized plasma-cell neoplasm arising outside the bone marrow, in this case involving the liver, without evidence of systemic multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma with hepatic plasmacyto.normalized_text: Multiple myeloma with hepatic plasmacytoma involvement
Multiple myeloma with hepatic plasmacyto.description: A systemic malignant plasma-cell disorder that typically involves bone marrow and may rarely produce extramedullary masses in the liver.

Primary hepatic lymphoma.description: A lymphoma predominantly involving the liver, often presenting as a solitary or multifocal hepatic mass and potentially showing lymphoid-appearing cells on biopsy.

Hepatocellular carcinoma.description: A primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes, usually occurring in patients with chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or other chronic liver disease.

Chlamydial cervicitis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis that commonly causes cervicitis and may be asymptomatic or present with abnormal vaginal discharge.

Gonococcal cervicitis.description: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae that can infect the cervix and cause increased, mucopurulent vaginal discharge.

Trichomoniasis.description: A sexually transmitted vaginal infection caused by the protozoan Trichomonas vaginalis, often causing discharge, vaginal irritation, and sometimes a characteristic frothy or malodorous discharge.

Bacterial vaginosis.description: An imbalance of normal vaginal bacteria that can cause thin vaginal discharge with a fishy odor, sometimes more noticeable after intercourse.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis.description: A yeast infection of the vagina, usually caused by Candida species, which commonly causes itching and thick white discharge.

Mycoplasma genitalium cervicitis.description: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection that can cause cervicitis, abnormal vaginal discharge, dysuria, or postcoital bleeding and may be asymptomatic.

Giant bullous emphysema (vanishing lung.description: A severe form of bullous emphysema characterized by very large air-filled bullae, often affecting the upper lobes and compressing adjacent functioning lung. It is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and cannabis use and can mimic pneumothorax on chest radiography.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wi.normalized_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with emphysema
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wi.description: A progressive obstructive lung disease, usually caused by smoking, in which destruction of alveolar walls causes air trapping, hyperinflation, and impaired airflow. Bullae may develop in advanced emphysema.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.normalized_text: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to bullous emphysema
Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due t.description: A pneumothorax caused by rupture of a bulla or bleb in a person with underlying lung disease, such as emphysema. It typically presents suddenly with pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, reduced breath sounds, and hyper-resonance.

Cannabis-associated bullous lung disease.description: Bullous emphysema occurring in association with chronic cannabis smoking, often in relatively young adults and frequently involving large upper-lobe or paraseptal bullae. Concurrent tobacco use increases risk.

Sporadic Burkitt lymphoma.description: An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by very rapid proliferation, frequent bulky abdominal disease, a high risk of spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome, and possible bone marrow and renal involvement.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.description: The most common aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma in adults; it can produce bulky nodal or extranodal abdominal masses, constitutional symptoms, marrow infiltration, renal dysfunction, and tumor lysis syndrome.

Plasma cell myeloma (multiple myeloma).description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder causing excess monoclonal immunoglobulin production, anemia, renal impairment, hypercalcemia, and marrow replacement; it may occasionally form extramedullary plasmacytomas.

Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.normalized_text: Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneous PAN) with mononeuritis multiplex
Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (cutaneou.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of small-to-medium muscular arteries limited predominantly to the skin, sometimes associated with peripheral nerve involvement. Skin biopsy typically shows necrotizing inflammation of a medium-sized vessel.

Systemic polyarteritis nodosa.description: A necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can affect skin, peripheral nerves, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Mononeuritis multiplex and livedo-like skin lesions are characteristic manifestations.

ANCA-associated vasculitic neuropathy.description: Small-vessel vasculitis, including microscopic polyangiitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, can cause painful asymmetric peripheral neuropathy and skin purpura, often with systemic renal, pulmonary, or constitutional features.

Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis, often associated with hepatitis C or autoimmune disease, that may cause palpable purpura, arthralgia, weakness, renal disease, and peripheral neuropathy.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyang.description: An ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis characterized by asthma, eosinophilia, sinus disease, pulmonary involvement, skin lesions, and frequently mononeuritis multiplex.

Classic homocystinuria due to cystathion.normalized_text: Classic homocystinuria due to cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency
Classic homocystinuria due to cystathion.description: An autosomal-recessive disorder of methionine metabolism causing markedly elevated homocysteine and methionine. It commonly produces ectopia lentis, severe myopia, marfanoid skeletal features, osteoporosis, and increased thromboembolic risk.

Marfan syndrome.description: An autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder caused most often by pathogenic variants in FBN1. It is characterized by skeletal overgrowth, pectus deformity, scoliosis, ectopia lentis, myopia, and cardiovascular disease such as aortic-root dilation and mitral-valve prolapse.

Homocystinuria due to a remethylation de.normalized_text: Homocystinuria due to a remethylation defect, such as methionine synthase or methionine synthase reductase deficiency
Homocystinuria due to a remethylation de.description: These inherited disorders impair remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, causing hyperhomocysteinemia and often neurologic, developmental, hematologic, and ophthalmologic manifestations. Unlike CBS deficiency, methionine is usually low or normal rather than elevated.

Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing.normalized_text: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing acquired hyperhomocysteinemia
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing.description: Deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate can impair homocysteine remethylation and elevate plasma homocysteine. It commonly causes macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia and, in vitamin B12 deficiency, elevated methylmalonic acid and neurologic symptoms.

Pontine cavernous malformation (brainste.normalized_text: Pontine cavernous malformation (brainstem cavernoma) with recent hemorrhage
Pontine cavernous malformation (brainste.description: A cerebral cavernous malformation is a cluster of fragile, low-flow vascular channels that can bleed repeatedly. In the pons, even a small hemorrhage can cause prominent long-tract, cranial-nerve, and cerebellar symptoms. The hyperdense pontine lesion on CT and mixed-signal brainstem lesion on MRI are compatible with a hemorrhagic cavernoma.

Primary pontine hemorrhage.description: Pontine hemorrhage is bleeding within the pons that can produce contralateral weakness and sensory loss, ataxia, tremor, diplopia, and obstructive hydrocephalus. In a young patient without hypertension, an underlying vascular lesion such as a cavernoma is more likely than spontaneous hypertensive hemorrhage.

Brainstem glioma (pontine tumor), possib.normalized_text: Brainstem glioma (pontine tumor), possibly with intratumoral hemorrhage
Brainstem glioma (pontine tumor), possib.description: A brainstem glioma is a tumor arising within the pons or adjacent brainstem structures. It may cause progressive cranial-nerve symptoms, corticospinal tract signs, sensory deficits, cerebellar dysfunction, and hydrocephalus when it obstructs the fourth ventricle or cerebral aqueduct. Hemorrhage within a tumor can create a hyperdense CT focus.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: Systemic infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, often acquired by inhalation of fungal spores and capable of disseminating through macrophages to bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and other tissues. Bone-marrow histology may show intracellular small yeasts within macrophages.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania species and transmitted by sandflies. It can cause prolonged fever, constitutional symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone-marrow macrophages containing intracellular amastigotes.

Acute bacterial pyelonephritis with uros.description: A bacterial infection of the kidney and upper urinary tract, usually caused by enteric gram-negative organisms such as Escherichia coli. Severe disease can cause systemic inflammatory response or sepsis.

Acute bacterial prostatitis.description: An acute bacterial infection of the prostate, commonly caused by urinary gram-negative bacteria. It can produce fever, systemic toxicity, dysuria, pelvic or lower abdominal pain, and pain radiating to the groin, scrotum, or low back.

Iliopsoas pyomyositis or psoas abscess.description: A deep bacterial infection of the iliopsoas or adjacent pelvic musculature, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or enteric organisms. It may cause fever, systemic illness, abdominal pain, groin pain, hip-region pain, and low back pain; CT or MRI may demonstrate muscle enlargement, inflammation, or abscess.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.normalized_text: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), likely bisphosphonate- or denosumab-associated
Medication-related osteonecrosis of the.description: Progressive exposed, nonhealing necrotic jaw bone in a patient receiving or previously exposed to antiresorptive therapy, commonly used for skeletal metastases. It may occur in native mandibular bone or in vascularized bone grafts.

Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.normalized_text: Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstructed mandible
Chronic osteomyelitis of the reconstruct.description: A persistent inflammatory or infectious process involving mandibular bone that can cause devitalized bone, sequestrum formation, mucosal breakdown, and exposed bone after major oral surgery or reconstruction.

Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.normalized_text: Recurrent or progressive metastatic clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma involving the mandible or fibular graft
Recurrent or progressive metastatic clea.description: Clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma can metastasize to bone and produce destructive osteolytic lesions. Local recurrence or metastatic involvement of the reconstructed mandible could contribute to bone destruction and mucosal breakdown.

Ischemic necrosis or failure of the fibu.normalized_text: Ischemic necrosis or failure of the fibular free-flap bone graft
Ischemic necrosis or failure of the fibu.description: Compromised vascular supply to a vascularized fibular bone flap can lead to graft nonunion, bone devitalization, mucosal dehiscence, and eventual exposure of necrotic graft bone.

Osteoradionecrosis of the mandible.description: Radiation-induced hypovascular, hypocellular bone injury causing chronic nonhealing exposed bone and necrosis, typically after therapeutic radiation to the head and neck.

Giant cell myocarditis.description: A rare, rapidly progressive inflammatory myocarditis characterized histologically by multinucleated giant cells, myocyte necrosis, and mixed inflammatory infiltrates. It can mimic acute myocardial infarction and rapidly cause severe heart failure, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and mitral regurgitation.

Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis.description: An acute inflammatory injury to the myocardium, often following a viral or other systemic illness, which can produce chest pain, acute systolic heart failure, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic shock. Unlike giant cell myocarditis, typical biopsy findings are predominantly lymphocytic inflammation without characteristic multinucleated giant cells.

Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.normalized_text: Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock
Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial i.description: Acute myocardial necrosis caused by abrupt coronary artery occlusion, commonly due to plaque rupture and thrombosis. A large anterior infarction can cause severe left-ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary edema, acute ischemic mitral regurgitation, and cardiogenic shock.

Acute decompensated systolic heart failu.normalized_text: Acute decompensated systolic heart failure with cardiogenic shock
Acute decompensated systolic heart failu.description: A syndrome of severe pump failure in which inadequate cardiac output and elevated filling pressures cause pulmonary congestion, systemic venous congestion, tissue hypoperfusion, and shock. In this case, myocarditis or acute myocardial infarction could be the underlying cause.

Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related c.normalized_text: Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related channelopathy; Long QT syndrome type 7)
Andersen-Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2-related c.description: A rare autosomal-dominant potassium-channel disorder caused most often by KCNJ2 variants, characterized by ventricular arrhythmias, prominent U waves/QU prolongation, periodic paralysis, and distinctive craniofacial and skeletal features.

Congenital long QT syndrome, especially.normalized_text: Congenital long QT syndrome, especially LQT1
Congenital long QT syndrome, especially.description: An inherited cardiac repolarization disorder that predisposes to torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, syncope, and sudden cardiac arrest, often triggered by adrenergic stimulation, stress, exercise, or some anesthetic medications.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricula.description: An inherited arrhythmia syndrome in which adrenergic stress triggers bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia despite a structurally normal heart and often a normal resting ECG.

Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.normalized_text: Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long QT syndrome type 8)
Timothy syndrome (CACNA1C-related long Q.description: A severe multisystem calcium-channel disorder associated with marked QT prolongation, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, syndactyly, characteristic facial features, and frequently developmental delay or autism-spectrum features.

Strongyloidiasis.description: Infection with the intestinal nematode Strongyloides stercoralis, acquired through contaminated soil in tropical and subtropical regions. It can cause chronic diarrhea, rash, weight loss, and prominent eosinophilia.

Hookworm infection.description: Intestinal infection with Ancylostoma or Necator species acquired through skin contact with contaminated soil. It can produce eosinophilia, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash at the site of penetration, and fatigue from iron-deficiency anemia.

Schistosomiasis.description: Parasitic infection caused by Schistosoma species, acquired from freshwater exposure in endemic areas. Intestinal schistosomiasis can cause diarrhea, weight loss, eosinophilia, rash, and hepatosplenic disease.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis or eosinoph.description: An eosinophil-predominant inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract that can cause diarrhea, abdominal bloating, weight loss, and peripheral eosinophilia. It may be triggered by allergy, medications, or parasitic infection.

Ulcerative colitis flare.description: A relapse of chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colonic mucosa. Typical flares cause frequent diarrhea, urgency, rectal bleeding, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, and weight loss.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia that can infiltrate and damage multiple organs, including the skin, gastrointestinal tract, lungs, heart, and spleen. Secondary causes such as parasitic infection must be excluded first.

Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (hemorrhagic.normalized_text: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (hemorrhagic high-grade diffuse astrocytic glioma)
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (hemorrhagic.description: An aggressive primary glial brain tumor that commonly shows central necrosis, irregular ring enhancement, extensive vasogenic edema, and occasionally intratumoral hemorrhage. The imaging and immunohistochemical pattern of GFAP and Olig2 positivity with retained ATRX and absent/low IDH1 staining favors a high-grade astrocytic glioma.

Anaplastic oligodendroglioma.description: A WHO grade 3 diffuse glioma, classically occurring in young to middle-aged adults and often presenting with seizures. It is defined molecularly by IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion; imaging may show calcification, enhancement, necrosis, and hemorrhage in higher-grade tumors.

Cerebral abscess.description: A focal intracranial infection producing a pus-filled lesion with a smooth ring-enhancing capsule and surrounding edema. It can cause seizures, reduced consciousness, and mass effect, but usually has clinical or laboratory evidence of infection.

Hemorrhagic cerebral metastasis.description: Metastatic tumors to the brain can present as well-circumscribed enhancing lesions with extensive edema and intralesional bleeding. Common hemorrhagic metastases include melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, and some lung cancers.

Disseminated blastomycosis with vertebra.description: Blastomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by Blastomyces species, usually acquired by inhalation. It can cause pulmonary disease and disseminate hematogenously to bone, including the spine, producing destructive vertebral osteomyelitis and paraspinal soft-tissue masses. Tissue may show broad-based budding yeast.

Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis due to.normalized_text: Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis due to bacterial infection
Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis due to.description: Vertebral osteomyelitis is infection of vertebral bone, often with involvement of the adjacent intervertebral disc and possible epidural or paraspinal extension. Common causes include Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative bacteria, but fungal causes should be considered when the course is indolent.

Spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease).description: Spinal tuberculosis is a chronic granulomatous infection of the vertebrae caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It commonly produces slowly progressive back pain, vertebral destruction, disc-space involvement, paraspinal abscesses, and constitutional symptoms.

Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.normalized_text: Metastatic malignancy involving the lumbar spine
Metastatic malignancy involving the lumb.description: Metastatic cancer can involve the vertebrae and cause progressive mechanical or nocturnal back pain, weight loss, vertebral destruction, and occasionally neurologic compromise. In an older adult, lung, prostate, renal, gastrointestinal, and hematologic malignancies are important considerations.

Disseminated cryptococcosis.description: Systemic infection caused by Cryptococcus species, usually involving the lungs and potentially spreading to skin, lymph nodes, soft tissue, and the central nervous system. Histology may show encapsulated yeast with prominent clear halos.

Disseminated talaromycosis (Talaromyces.description: A systemic dimorphic fungal infection that can cause fever, weight loss, pulmonary disease, lymphadenopathy, and skin or subcutaneous lesions, particularly in immunocompromised patients.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that may produce constitutional symptoms, diffuse lung abnormalities, lymph-node enlargement, and skin or soft-tissue involvement.

Pulmonary tuberculosis with extrapulmona.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause chronic constitutional symptoms, cough, pulmonary infiltrates or nodules, and peripheral lymphadenopathy; less commonly, it can involve the eyelid or other soft tissues.

Lymphoma with pulmonary and extranodal i.normalized_text: Lymphoma with pulmonary and extranodal involvement
Lymphoma with pulmonary and extranodal i.description: Lymphoma is a malignancy of lymphoid cells that may produce fever, weight loss, painless lymph-node enlargement, lung lesions, and occasionally orbital or eyelid involvement.

Congenital Zika syndrome due to maternal.normalized_text: Congenital Zika syndrome due to maternal Zika virus infection
Congenital Zika syndrome due to maternal.description: Fetal neurologic injury caused by in-utero Zika virus infection, often following maternal infection with fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and headache. Prenatal imaging may show ventriculomegaly, cortical malformations, calcifications, corpus callosum abnormalities, and microcephaly, although microcephaly is not always present.

Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstru.normalized_text: Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstructive hydrocephalus
Fetal aqueductal stenosis causing obstru.description: Narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct impairs cerebrospinal fluid flow from the third to fourth ventricle, producing enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles. It may be isolated or associated with infection, hemorrhage, or genetic conditions.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection.description: In-utero cytomegalovirus infection can cause fetal ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcifications, cortical developmental abnormalities, growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, and hearing loss. Maternal infection is often asymptomatic but may resemble a nonspecific viral illness.

Congenital toxoplasmosis.description: Transplacental infection with Toxoplasma gondii may cause hydrocephalus or ventriculomegaly, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, and neurologic impairment. Maternal infection may be asymptomatic or produce a mild influenza-like syndrome.

diagnoses.name: Complex hereditary spastic paraplegia
diagnoses.icd11_title: Autosomal recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegia

SPG11-associated hereditary spastic para.normalized_text: SPG11-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia (spatacsin-related complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia)
SPG11-associated hereditary spastic para.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG11 variants. It commonly produces progressive lower-limb spasticity, gait impairment, cognitive decline, dysphagia, white-matter abnormalities, and thinning of the corpus callosum.

SPG15-associated hereditary spastic para.normalized_text: SPG15-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia (ZFYVE26-related spastic paraplegia)
SPG15-associated hereditary spastic para.description: A rare autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia that resembles SPG11, often causing progressive spastic paraparesis, intellectual decline, dysphagia, peripheral neuropathy, and thinning of the corpus callosum.

SPG47-associated hereditary spastic para.normalized_text: SPG47-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia (AP4B1-related AP-4 deficiency syndrome)
SPG47-associated hereditary spastic para.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia due to AP4B1 deficiency, characterized by spastic paraplegia, intellectual disability, speech impairment, microcephaly, and sometimes a thin corpus callosum.

SPG21-associated hereditary spastic para.description: An autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic SPG21 variants. It may include progressive spastic paraparesis, intellectual disability or dementia, dysarthria, extrapyramidal manifestations, and brain atrophy.

Adult-onset leukodystrophy with axonal s.normalized_text: Adult-onset leukodystrophy with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia (CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy)
Adult-onset leukodystrophy with axonal s.description: A progressive white-matter neurodegenerative disorder that often presents in adulthood with cognitive or psychiatric decline followed by gait dysfunction, spasticity, and motor impairment. It is usually autosomal dominant but can occasionally appear sporadic.

Functional mediastinal paraganglioma (th.description: A catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumor arising from sympathetic paraganglia in the mediastinum, often near the great vessels or heart. These tumors commonly produce norepinephrine and normetanephrine rather than epinephrine.

Cardiac paraganglioma.description: A rare functional paraganglioma located adjacent to the heart, commonly near the left atrium, aortic root, pulmonary artery, or atrioventricular groove. It may cause severe catecholamine-mediated hypertension and can be detected as an intensely avid mediastinal mass.

Pheochromocytoma.description: A catecholamine-secreting tumor of adrenal medullary chromaffin cells that classically causes episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, and hypertension. Most pheochromocytomas are adrenal, whereas paragangliomas occur outside the adrenal glands.

Preeclampsia.description: A pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder occurring after 20 weeks of gestation, typically characterized by new-onset hypertension with proteinuria and/or maternal organ dysfunction. Severe disease may cause headache and marked hypertension.

Cerebral nocardiosis (Nocardia brain abs.description: An opportunistic bacterial infection caused by Nocardia species that can produce suppurative, ring-enhancing brain abscesses, particularly in patients receiving chronic immunosuppressive therapy. The imaging and histology are most consistent with a cerebral Nocardia abscess.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis.description: Toxoplasma gondii reactivation is an opportunistic parasitic infection that commonly causes multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions with edema in severely immunocompromised patients.

Primary central nervous system lymphoma.description: A lymphoma confined to the brain, meninges, spinal cord, or eyes. It is more frequent in immunosuppressed patients and may cause focal neurologic deficits and enhancing brain lesions.

Glioblastoma.description: A high-grade primary glial tumor that commonly occurs in older adults and can produce an irregular enhancing mass with central necrosis, edema, headache, cognitive changes, and focal deficits.

Legionnaires' disease (Legionella pneumo.description: A potentially severe atypical bacterial pneumonia caused by Legionella species, often associated with exposure to aerosolized freshwater or contaminated water systems and capable of rapidly progressing to multilobar pneumonia.

Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia,.normalized_text: Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, likely pneumococcal pneumonia
Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia,.description: An acute bacterial infection of the lung parenchyma, commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, producing fever, productive cough, pleuritic pain, and lobar consolidation.

Aspiration pneumonia.description: Pneumonia caused by inhalation of oropharyngeal or gastric contents, typically involving dependent lung regions such as the right lower lobe and sometimes causing bilateral lower-lobe infiltrates.

Pulmonary tuberculosis.description: A chronic granulomatous lung infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually presenting with prolonged cough, constitutional symptoms, and often upper-lobe infiltrates or cavitation in reactivation disease.

Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.description: A rare viral zoonotic illness acquired through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, initially causing fever and myalgias and potentially progressing rapidly to pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, and shock.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS), po.normalized_text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS), postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor deficiency
Congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS), po.description: A genetic neuromuscular-junction disorder causing impaired transmission of acetylcholine signals to muscle, often due to variants in CHRNE, CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND, or RAPSN. It produces fatigable ocular, facial, bulbar, respiratory, and limb weakness from infancy.

RAPSN-related congenital myasthenic synd.description: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by rapsyn deficiency, which impairs clustering and stabilization of acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate. Severe neonatal respiratory crises and episodic respiratory decompensation are characteristic.

CHAT-related congenital myasthenic syndr.normalized_text: CHAT-related congenital myasthenic syndrome (choline acetyltransferase deficiency)
CHAT-related congenital myasthenic syndr.description: A presynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by deficient acetylcholine synthesis. It commonly presents in infancy with episodic apnea or respiratory failure, hypotonia, ptosis, and a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.

Ethylene glycol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolal gap, acute kidney injury, and calcium oxalate crystal deposition in urine.

Methanol poisoning.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion that produces formic acid, causing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated osmolal gap, neurologic symptoms, and potentially visual toxicity.

Diabetic ketoacidosis.description: A metabolic emergency caused by insulin deficiency, characterized by hyperglycemia, ketone production, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, dehydration, and Kussmaul respirations.

Salicylate poisoning.description: Aspirin or salicylate toxicity causes respiratory alkalosis with concurrent high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, tachypnea, altered mental status, and sometimes elevated lactate.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Q.description: A self-limited inflammatory thyroid disorder, often following a viral upper respiratory illness, causing thyroid enlargement, fever, systemic symptoms, and sometimes transient thyrotoxicosis. CT may show diffuse thyroid enlargement with heterogeneous low attenuation.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis.description: A rare bacterial infection of the thyroid that can cause fever, neck swelling, painful thyroid enlargement, and occasionally thyroid abscess formation. It is more likely in patients with anatomic fistulas, immunocompromise, or preexisting thyroid disease.

Graves disease.description: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies cause diffuse thyroid enlargement and hyperthyroidism. It commonly presents with tachycardia, heat intolerance, tremor, weight loss, and sometimes eye disease.

Hashimoto thyroiditis.description: A chronic autoimmune thyroiditis that causes gradual thyroid enlargement and commonly leads to hypothyroidism; an early transient inflammatory phase may occasionally cause thyrotoxic symptoms.

Thyroid lymphoma.description: A rare malignancy, usually arising in the setting of longstanding Hashimoto thyroiditis, that presents with rapidly enlarging thyroid mass and compressive neck symptoms.

Acute pancreatitis.description: Acute inflammatory injury of the pancreas, commonly causing sudden upper abdominal pain and elevation of pancreatic enzymes. The CT appearance is consistent with pancreatic inflammation and peripancreatic fat stranding.

Drug-induced acute pancreatitis.description: Acute pancreatitis caused by an adverse medication reaction. Lipid-lowering agents, including some statins and other cholesterol-lowering medications, have rarely been associated with pancreatitis and gastrointestinal adverse effects.

Lymphocytic colitis (microscopic colitis.description: A form of microscopic colitis characterized by chronic nonbloody watery diarrhea, colonic mucosal inflammation, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes on biopsy. Colonoscopy may appear grossly normal despite abnormal histology.

Pancreatic adenocarcinoma.description: A malignant tumor of the pancreas that can produce abdominal or back pain, early satiety, weight loss, and occasionally pancreatitis due to pancreatic duct obstruction. A pancreatic mass or obstructive jaundice is often present but is not described here.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possibl.normalized_text: Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possible acute exacerbation
Chronic mesenteric ischemia with possibl.description: Reduced intestinal blood flow caused by mesenteric arterial atherosclerosis. It is more likely in patients with coronary artery disease and can cause postprandial pain, food avoidance, early satiety, diarrhea, and weight loss; acute ischemia usually causes more severe pain and systemic illness.

Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.normalized_text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with gonococcal septic arthritis
Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.description: Hematogenous spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae causing migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, dermatitis, or purulent arthritis. Synovial-fluid culture and Gram stain may show gram-negative diplococci, and growth can occur on chocolate agar.

Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis.description: Bacterial infection of a joint, most commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus, producing acute painful swelling, warmth, restricted movement, and joint effusion. It may involve more than one joint, particularly in patients with bacteremia or immunosuppression.

Reactive arthritis due to sexually trans.normalized_text: Reactive arthritis due to sexually transmitted infection
Reactive arthritis due to sexually trans.description: A sterile inflammatory arthritis that can occur after genitourinary infection, classically Chlamydia trachomatis and less often gonorrhea. It usually causes asymmetric lower-extremity oligoarthritis and may include urethritis, conjunctivitis, enthesitis, or skin findings.

Lyme arthritis.description: Inflammatory arthritis caused by Borrelia burgdorferi infection, often occurring weeks to months after tick exposure. It most commonly causes intermittent or persistent swelling of one or a few large joints, especially the knee.

Rheumatoid arthritis.description: A chronic systemic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that typically causes symmetric small-joint synovitis, prolonged morning stiffness, and gradual joint damage if untreated.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.description: Crystal-induced inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals. It commonly affects knees and wrists but can affect ankles and small joints, producing abrupt pain, warmth, swelling, and effusion.

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.normalized_text: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type

Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma.description: A rare aggressive extranodal B-cell lymphoma in which malignant lymphoid cells proliferate mainly within small blood vessels. It often presents with fever, markedly elevated LDH, cytopenias, and no detectable lymphadenopathy; adrenal, liver, lung, skin, neurologic, and bone marrow involvement can occur.

Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic d.normalized_text: Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic dissemination
Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic d.description: An aggressive lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, involving one or both adrenal glands. It may cause fever, constitutional symptoms, elevated LDH, cytopenias, and adrenal insufficiency when both glands are affected.

Disseminated histoplasmosis.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Disseminated disease can involve the reticuloendothelial system, liver, bone marrow, lungs, and adrenal glands, causing fever, cytopenias, transaminitis, and adrenal enlargement.

Disseminated tuberculosis with adrenal i.description: Systemic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs, liver, bone marrow, and adrenal glands. Adrenal tuberculosis may produce bilateral enlargement and eventually adrenal insufficiency.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secon.normalized_text: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secondary to occult lymphoma or infection
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secon.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, high LDH, and often very high ferritin. It can be triggered by lymphoma, viral infection, fungal infection, or tuberculosis.

Patent ductus arteriosus (large adult PD.description: A congenital persistent communication between the descending thoracic aorta and the pulmonary artery, causing a left-to-right shunt, pulmonary arterial enlargement, and a characteristic continuous murmur or bruit.

Ductus arteriosus aneurysm associated wi.normalized_text: Ductus arteriosus aneurysm associated with patent ductus arteriosus
Ductus arteriosus aneurysm associated wi.description: An aneurysmal dilation of the ductus arteriosus or its aortic/pulmonary arterial connection. In adults it may cause chest discomfort, dyspnea, compression of adjacent structures, or turbulent flow producing a bruit.

Aortopulmonary window.description: A rare congenital defect consisting of an abnormal direct communication between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery, resulting in a left-to-right shunt and possible pulmonary overcirculation or pulmonary hypertension.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation.description: An abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that bypasses the capillary bed. Larger lesions can produce dyspnea, chest bruit, hypoxemia, and paradoxical embolic complications.

IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis.description: An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder in which IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration causes a retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass, often encasing major vessels and ureters. Venous compression can cause marked bilateral leg edema.

Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Orm.description: A fibroinflammatory condition characterized by plaque-like retroperitoneal tissue, commonly surrounding the aorta, iliac vessels, and ureters. It may obstruct venous or lymphatic drainage and produce lower-limb edema.

Retroperitoneal lymphoma.description: Lymphoma can present as retroperitoneal nodal or infiltrative soft-tissue disease that compresses the inferior vena cava, iliac veins, or lymphatic channels, resulting in bilateral lower-extremity edema.

Malignant retroperitoneal mass causing i.normalized_text: Malignant retroperitoneal mass causing inferior vena cava or iliac venous compression
Malignant retroperitoneal mass causing i.description: Primary retroperitoneal tumors or metastatic malignancy may produce an infiltrative or mass-like retroperitoneal lesion that obstructs venous return from both legs, causing severe bilateral edema.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax.description: Air in the pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of the lung, occurring without trauma or known underlying lung disease; it is most common in young men. The radiograph shows a large left pneumothorax with absent peripheral lung markings and a collapsed left lung medially.

Large left pneumothorax.description: A large collection of air in the left pleural cavity causing substantial collapse of the left lung. This is a radiographic diagnosis and may be primary spontaneous, secondary spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic depending on the clinical cause.

Tension pneumothorax.description: A life-threatening form of pneumothorax in which pleural air accumulates under pressure, potentially shifting mediastinal structures and impairing venous return and cardiac output. It is primarily a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment when suspected.

Pulmonary embolism.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries, usually by thrombus, which can cause acute pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia. However, it would not explain the visible large pleural air collection on this radiograph.

Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.normalized_text: Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic carditis and mitral regurgitation
Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic car.description: An immune-mediated complication of group A streptococcal streptococcal infection, characterized by migratory polyarthritis, fever, and carditis. Valvulitis commonly affects the mitral valve and can cause severe mitral regurgitation and heart failure.

Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.normalized_text: Infective endocarditis with mitral valve regurgitation
Infective endocarditis with mitral valve.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, that can produce fever, a new or worsening regurgitant murmur, systemic inflammation, embolic phenomena, and heart failure.

Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.normalized_text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory arthritis and possible valvular involvement
