Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflam.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that commonly affects young women and may cause fatigue, fever, inflammatory polyarthritis, serositis, and occasionally nonbacterial valvular disease such as Libman-Sacks endocarditis.

Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.normalized_text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with gonococcal arthritis
Disseminated gonococcal infection with g.description: Hematogenous spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and septic monoarthritis, most often affecting young sexually active adults.

Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtaf.normalized_text: Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtafacet cyst) causing radiculopathy
Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtaf.description: A fluid-containing degenerative cyst arising near a lumbar facet joint that can extend into the spinal canal or neural foramen and compress a nerve root. The MRI appearance of a focal posterior-lateral epidural cystic lesion adjacent to a degenerated facet joint is most consistent with this diagnosis.

Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.normalized_text: Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerative facet arthropathy and ligamentous hypertrophy
Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerati.description: Degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal or lateral recess caused by facet-joint osteoarthritis, disc degeneration, and thickening of supporting ligaments. It may produce nerve-root compression and radicular leg pain.

Lumbar disc herniation or degenerative d.normalized_text: Lumbar disc herniation or degenerative disc disease with left-sided radiculopathy
Lumbar disc herniation or degenerative d.description: Degeneration or protrusion of a lumbar intervertebral disc may narrow the lateral recess or neural foramen and irritate or compress a lumbar nerve root, producing sciatica-like pain.

Lumbar epidural schwannoma.description: A benign nerve-sheath tumor arising from a spinal nerve root that can produce a focal epidural mass and slowly progressive radicular pain. It is a differential consideration for an enhancing epidural lesion, although the apparent facet-adjacent cystic morphology is less typical.

Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infec.description: HIV infection can impair cellular immunity, causing persistent or unusually severe herpes simplex lesions, recurrent infections, fatigue, and generalized or cervical lymphadenopathy.

Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV.normalized_text: Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection with possible immunosuppression
Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV.description: HSV-1 commonly causes recurrent painful vesicles and crusted ulcers at the lip margin. Persistence for months or unusually large ulceration raises concern for underlying immune dysfunction.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral.normalized_text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral cavity
Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral.description: Squamous cell carcinoma can present as a persistent nonhealing ulcer or crusted lesion on the lip and may spread to submandibular or cervical lymph nodes.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma may cause fatigue, recurrent infections from immune dysfunction, and painless cervical lymphadenopathy; immunosuppression can also predispose to persistent HSV lesions.

Hematologic malignancy causing immunosup.normalized_text: Hematologic malignancy causing immunosuppression, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Hematologic malignancy causing immunosup.description: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and related blood cancers can present with fatigue, recurrent upper-respiratory infections, lymphadenopathy, and prolonged mucocutaneous herpesvirus infections.

Crohn disease.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, commonly causing transmural bowel inflammation, ulceration, strictures, anemia, malnutrition, and extraintestinal joint manifestations.

Ulcerative colitis.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease limited primarily to the colon and rectum, producing continuous mucosal inflammation, bloody diarrhea, anemia, protein loss, and sometimes peripheral arthritis.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.description: An inherited hamartomatous polyposis syndrome characterized by gastrointestinal polyps, recurrent bleeding and anemia, abdominal symptoms, and a risk of bowel intussusception and malignancy.

Juvenile polyposis syndrome.description: A hereditary hamartomatous polyposis disorder causing multiple gastrointestinal juvenile polyps, rectal bleeding, chronic anemia, diarrhea, and occasionally protein-losing enteropathy.

Common variable immunodeficiency or anot.normalized_text: Common variable immunodeficiency or another primary immunodeficiency with nodular lymphoid hyperplasia
Common variable immunodeficiency or anot.description: Primary immune disorders can cause chronic infectious or inflammatory diarrhea, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the bowel, malabsorption, protein loss, anemia, and occasionally inflammatory bowel disease-like colitis.

Dupuytren disease (Dupuytren contracture.description: A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia that produces nodules and cords, progressively causing flexion contractures, most often involving the ring and little fingers.

Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosyn.description: A condition in which thickening of the flexor tendon or A1 pulley causes painful catching, locking, or difficulty extending an affected finger.

Flexor tendon contracture or post-trauma.normalized_text: Flexor tendon contracture or post-traumatic scar contracture
Flexor tendon contracture or post-trauma.description: Shortening or scarring of flexor tendons and surrounding soft tissues can produce persistent finger flexion deformities, usually after trauma, surgery, infection, or immobilization.

Camptodactyly.description: A congenital or developmental condition characterized by flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint, commonly affecting the little finger.

Syphilitic lymphadenitis (secondary syph.description: Lymph-node involvement by Treponema pallidum, often occurring in secondary syphilis. It can cause prominent inguinal lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, follicular hyperplasia, plasmacytosis, and demonstrable spirochetes on immunohistochemical staining.

Lymphogranuloma venereum.description: A sexually transmitted Chlamydia trachomatis infection, usually caused by serovars L1-L3, that can produce painful unilateral inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms.

HIV-associated lymphoma.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, can occur in people with HIV and may present with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes and constitutional symptoms.

Mycobacterium avium complex lymphadeniti.description: Disseminated or localized MAC infection can cause fever, night sweats, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV-related immunosuppression.

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.icd11_title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

Solitary osseous Langerhans cell histioc.normalized_text: Solitary osseous Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma) of the rib
Solitary osseous Langerhans cell histioc.description: A localized form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects bone in children and adolescents. Rib lesions can cause focal pain, lytic bone destruction, chest-wall inflammation, and reactive pleural effusion.

Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewi.normalized_text: Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewing sarcoma/Askin tumor)
Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewi.description: An aggressive malignant small round cell tumor of bone and soft tissue that often occurs in adolescents. Rib involvement may produce chest pain, a chest-wall mass, pleural effusion, and respiratory symptoms.

Rib osteomyelitis.description: Infection of a rib, usually bacterial and less commonly tuberculous, which can cause focal bone pain, tenderness, adjacent soft-tissue inflammation, and reactive pleural effusion.

Rib stress fracture or occult traumatic.normalized_text: Rib stress fracture or occult traumatic rib fracture with reactive pleural effusion
Rib stress fracture or occult traumatic.description: Repetitive mechanical loading, such as intense dance activity, can cause a stress fracture of a rib. Rib fractures produce focal pain and tenderness and may rarely be associated with pleural irritation, hemothorax, or effusion.

Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelit.normalized_text: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) / chronic nonbacterial osteitis involving a rib
Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelit.description: A sterile autoinflammatory bone disorder affecting children and adolescents, particularly girls. It can involve the clavicle, spine, and ribs, causing recurrent focal bone pain and tenderness.

Primary splenic classical Hodgkin lympho.description: A rare extranodal presentation of classical Hodgkin lymphoma confined predominantly to the spleen, characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells that are typically CD30-positive and associated with systemic inflammatory symptoms.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma, ALK-nega.description: A mature T-cell lymphoma composed of large pleomorphic CD30-positive malignant cells. ALK-negative disease more often affects older adults and may present with systemic symptoms and extranodal involvement.

Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.normalized_text: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the spleen
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can arise primarily in the spleen or involve it secondarily, often causing a splenic mass, constitutional symptoms, and anemia.

Splenic tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis can rarely involve the spleen, causing fever of unknown origin, weight loss, splenomegaly, focal splenic lesions, and elevated inflammatory markers; it is more common in immunocompromised patients or disseminated infection.

Visceral leishmaniasis.description: A systemic protozoal infection that can cause prolonged fever, weight loss, marked splenomegaly, anemia, and hyperferritinemia. Diagnosis is usually made by finding intracellular amastigotes in splenic or bone marrow samples.

Fabry disease (cardiac and renal involve.description: An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation. It commonly causes progressive renal disease, proteinuria, concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities, atrial arrhythmias, and myocardial fibrosis.

Fabry cardiomyopathy.description: Cardiac manifestation of Fabry disease characterized by glycosphingolipid deposition in cardiomyocytes and conduction tissue, producing concentric ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, atrial enlargement, arrhythmias, and myocardial ischemia or fibrosis.

Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevati.normalized_text: Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevati.description: Acute myocardial injury due to ischemia, usually from coronary atherosclerotic plaque rupture or supply-demand mismatch. It can present with chest pressure, gastrointestinal symptoms, arrhythmia, and elevated cardiac troponin.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe hy.normalized_text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe hypertensive left-ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe hy.description: A condition with abnormal thickening of the left ventricular wall, caused either by genetic sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or chronic pressure overload from hypertension. It may produce diastolic dysfunction, an S4, chest pain, and atrial arrhythmias.

Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.normalized_text: Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery territory infarction)
Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left.description: An acute focal cerebral infarction caused by arterial occlusion, most commonly involving the middle cerebral artery in term neonates. MRI diffusion restriction in a unilateral cortical-subcortical distribution supports this diagnosis.

Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.description: Brain injury from impaired oxygen delivery and/or cerebral perfusion around birth. HIE commonly produces encephalopathy, seizures, and bilateral or watershed-pattern brain abnormalities rather than a single focal arterial-territory lesion.

Neonatal intracranial hemorrhage.description: Bleeding within the brain or intracranial spaces can provoke seizures in newborns. Causes include birth trauma, coagulation disorders, vascular malformations, or hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke.

Infective aortic-valve endocarditis comp.normalized_text: Infective aortic-valve endocarditis complicated by aortic root abscess and aorto-left atrial fistula
Infective aortic-valve endocarditis comp.description: Infection of the aortic valve can destroy valve tissue and extend into the aortic root, forming an abscess or pseudoaneurysm that may rupture into an adjacent cardiac chamber. Severe aortic regurgitation and abnormal aorta-to-left-atrium flow can cause acute heart failure and respiratory failure.

Acute severe aortic regurgitation due to.normalized_text: Acute severe aortic regurgitation due to destructive aortic-valve disease
Acute severe aortic regurgitation due to.description: Acute severe leakage of the aortic valve causes a sudden volume overload of the left ventricle and left atrium, rapidly producing pulmonary edema, low forward cardiac output, tachycardia, and cardiogenic respiratory failure. In this case, valve destruction from infection or aortic-root pathology would be a likely cause.

Infected aortic pseudoaneurysm (mycotic.normalized_text: Infected aortic pseudoaneurysm (mycotic aneurysm) with systemic arterial septic embolic disease
Infected aortic pseudoaneurysm (mycotic.description: A bacterial infection involving the aortic wall or aortic root may produce pseudoaneurysms, dissection-like defects, rupture, and embolic vascular lesions. Multifocal abnormal arterial findings on CT can occur when endocarditis or bacteremia seeds arterial walls.

Aortic dissection or intramural aortic i.normalized_text: Aortic dissection or intramural aortic injury with secondary severe aortic regurgitation
Aortic dissection or intramural aortic i.description: A tear or injury involving the ascending aorta and aortic root can disrupt aortic-valve support, cause acute aortic regurgitation, and lead to heart failure. Extension into thoracic or abdominal aortic segments may cause back, flank, or shoulder pain and abnormal CT angiographic findings.

Large-vessel vasculitis or inflammatory.normalized_text: Large-vessel vasculitis or inflammatory aortitis, such as Takayasu arteritis
Large-vessel vasculitis or inflammatory.description: Inflammatory disease of the aorta and its major branches can cause arterial wall thickening, stenosis, aneurysm formation, and aortic regurgitation. Takayasu arteritis primarily affects young women and may involve the thoracic and abdominal aorta.

Torsion with infarction of an accessory.normalized_text: Torsion with infarction of an accessory spleen (torsed splenunculus)
Torsion with infarction of an accessory.description: An accessory spleen can twist around its vascular pedicle, causing venous obstruction, ischemia, and infarction. This can produce acute abdominal pain and inflammatory changes on CT, particularly in a patient with known splenunculi after splenectomy.

Infarction of ectopic splenic tissue (sp.normalized_text: Infarction of ectopic splenic tissue (splenosis or accessory spleen infarction without complete torsion)
Infarction of ectopic splenic tissue (sp.description: Ectopic splenic tissue after traumatic splenectomy may undergo spontaneous vascular compromise or infarction, producing localized abdominal pain and an inflammatory response.

Mesenteric panniculitis (sclerosing mese.description: Mesenteric panniculitis is inflammation of mesenteric fat that can cause abdominal pain, nausea, raised inflammatory markers, and CT evidence of increased mesenteric attenuation or a focal inflammatory mesenteric mass.

Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastriti.normalized_text: Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastritis
Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastriti.description: Inflammation or ulceration of the stomach or duodenum commonly causes epigastric pain, nausea, dyspeptic symptoms, and belching. It may not respond immediately to proton pump inhibitor treatment if another process is present or if complications develop.

Hematocolpos due to imperforate hymen.description: Accumulation of menstrual blood within the vagina caused by congenital obstruction at the hymen. Ultrasound typically shows a large midline pelvic cystic structure with homogeneous low-level internal echoes.

Hematometrocolpos from a transverse vagi.normalized_text: Hematometrocolpos from a transverse vaginal septum
Hematometrocolpos from a transverse vagi.description: Congenital vaginal obstruction from a transverse septum may cause retained menstrual blood in the vagina and uterus, producing cyclic or progressively worsening pelvic pain and a pelvic mass.

Hydrocolpos or hydrometrocolpos.description: Distension of the vagina, with or without uterine distension, by retained fluid due to congenital genital outflow obstruction. Contents may appear simple or mildly echogenic on ultrasound.

Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.normalized_text: Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly (OHVIRA syndrome)
Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral re.description: A congenital Müllerian anomaly, usually involving uterine didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina, leading to hematocolpos and recurrent pelvic pain after menstruation begins; it is often associated with a same-side renal anomaly.

Acute appendicitis.description: Inflammation of the appendix causing acute abdominal pain, usually beginning centrally and later localizing to the right lower quadrant, often with nausea, vomiting, fever, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.

Potocki-Shaffer syndrome.description: A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome caused by loss of material from chromosome 11p11.2, typically including EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple exostoses, parietal foramina or skull defects, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, craniofacial differences, and growth impairment.

Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, most often caused by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, characterized by multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the growth plates of long bones.

Craniofrontonasal dysplasia due to ALX4-.normalized_text: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia due to ALX4-related parietal foramina
Craniofrontonasal dysplasia due to ALX4-.description: ALX4-related disorders can cause enlarged parietal foramina and other calvarial ossification defects, sometimes accompanied by craniofacial differences. Isolated ALX4-related disease does not usually cause multiple exostoses or profound neurodevelopmental impairment.

PHF21A-related Potocki-Shaffer-like neur.description: Loss-of-function variants or deletions involving PHF21A can cause developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, behavioral abnormalities, and characteristic craniofacial features. Skeletal exostoses and parietal foramina generally require involvement of neighboring genes such as EXT2 and ALX4.

Crusted scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei infes.description: A severe, highly contagious form of scabies with a very high mite burden, often occurring in immunocompromised patients. It can present with widespread crusted, erosive, ulcerated, or hyperkeratotic lesions and may have little or no itch. The biopsy image demonstrates a mite within the stratum corneum.

Classic scabies.description: A superficial infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei mites that typically causes intensely pruritic papules, burrows, and excoriations, often involving the finger webs, wrists, waistline, genital area, and ankles.

Bacterial ecthyma.description: Ecthyma is a deeper ulcerative bacterial skin infection, usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, producing crusted ulcers. It is more likely in patients with impaired host defenses.

Ecthyma gangrenosum.description: A necrotic ulcerative skin infection classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia in severely neutropenic or critically ill patients. Lesions often evolve rapidly into hemorrhagic bullae and necrotic eschars.

ANCA-negative pauci-immune crescentic gl.description: A rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis characterized by severe glomerular inflammation and crescent formation, usually with little or no immune-complex deposition. It may occur despite negative ANCA testing and can rapidly cause kidney failure.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (.description: A clinical syndrome of rapidly declining kidney function over days to weeks, usually associated with nephritic urinary findings and glomerular crescents on kidney biopsy.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.normalized_text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (anti-GBM disease/Goodpasture-spectrum disease)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane diseas.description: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target the glomerular basement membrane, causing severe crescentic glomerulonephritis and sometimes pulmonary hemorrhage.

IgA nephropathy with crescentic transfor.description: IgA nephropathy is an immune-complex glomerulonephritis that commonly causes hematuria and may rarely progress to a rapidly progressive crescentic form with acute kidney failure.

Thrombotic microangiopathy, including he.normalized_text: Thrombotic microangiopathy, including hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Thrombotic microangiopathy, including he.description: A disorder of small-vessel platelet-rich thrombosis that can cause acute kidney injury, hypertension, anemia, and thrombocytopenia; renal biopsy may show glomerular and arteriolar thrombotic injury.

Primary hepatic histiocytic sarcoma.description: A rare aggressive malignancy of mature histiocytes/macrophages that may arise in the liver and infiltrate the porta hepatis or intrahepatic bile ducts, producing obstructive jaundice. Tumor cells are typically CD45-positive and lack B-cell, T-cell, NK-cell, and precursor lymphoid markers.

Primary hepatic diffuse large B-cell lym.normalized_text: Primary hepatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Primary hepatic diffuse large B-cell lym.description: An extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the liver, sometimes presenting as a hilar or periportal mass that compresses bile ducts and causes cholestatic jaundice. Most cases express CD45 and B-cell markers such as CD20 or PAX5.

Cholangiocarcinoma.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bile ducts. Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma commonly causes obstruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to painless jaundice and a cholestatic liver-test pattern.
